spine: Experiment, one change at a time
ml-dl-q1.testing: whether you investigate before you optimise, and whether you know one symptom can have several root causes.
ml-dl-q1.trap: opening with "I'd add dropout and regularization." It sounds right and skips the diagnosis.
ml-dl-q1.spoken:
"A 27-point gap between train and test tells me the model isn't generalising, and my first hypothesis is overfitting, but I wouldn't reach for regularization yet.

First I'd make sure the gap is real. I'd check the split for leakage: duplicates across train and test, a feature derived from the label, preprocessing fitted on the full dataset, or the same customer on both sides. I'd also check the test set is big enough and drawn from the same distribution.

Then I'd confirm it with evidence: train and validation loss curves over epochs, and a learning curve over training-set size. Training loss falling while validation loss rises is overfitting. I'd also look past accuracy to per-class recall and a baseline, because on imbalanced data 99% can mean nothing.

Once it's confirmed, I'd run controlled experiments, one change at a time: early stopping, then weight decay or dropout, then a smaller model, then better or more representative data, tracking each against validation.

Finally I'd pick the winner on validation, evaluate once on the untouched test set, compare against the baseline, and ship with drift monitoring. The goal isn't a smaller gap for its own sake. It's reliable performance on real, unseen data."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: a generalisation gap, hypothesis: high variance
stages.html:
"Twenty-seven points is a generalisation gap. My working hypothesis is overfitting, but it's a hypothesis, not a diagnosis."

  • Train 99%: the model fits the data it learned from almost perfectly.
  • Test 72%: it loses a quarter of that on unseen data.
  • Overfitting = the model learned the training set too specifically, including noise and accidental patterns. It's the student who memorises the practice paper and scores 72% on a new exam.
  • Keep three rivals open: data leakage, distribution shift and an unreliable test set. All three produce the same two numbers.

Why this matters: naming the rivals up front is what earns you the right to investigate before fixing.

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: audit the split before the model
stages.html:
"Before I touch the model, I validate the pipeline. A flawed split can't be fixed by architecture."

Ask:

  • Are train and test genuinely independent? Any duplicates or near-duplicates across them?
  • Is any feature leaking the label, computed from or after the outcome?
  • Was preprocessing (scaler, encoder, imputer) fitted on train only?
  • Does the split match the data's structure: chronological for time series, group-based for users or devices?
  • Is the test set big enough and representative? 72% on 200 rows is a wide interval.

Example: in fraud detection, if one customer's transactions sit in both train and test, the model learns that customer, not fraud. Use a group split.

Why this matters: leakage usually inflates both scores. If validation is high and only test is low, suspect the split or the test set before variance.

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.claim: curves, data and the right metric
stages.html:
"I don't diagnose from two final numbers. I read the curves."

  • Loss curves over epochs: train loss falling while validation loss rises = overfitting. Loss shows confidence problems that accuracy hides.
  • Learning curve over training-set size: gap narrowing as data grows = more data will help. Gap flat = it's capacity, not data.
  • Data checks:
Look at What it reveals
Class balance, train vs test imbalance or label shift
Feature distributions covariate shift (clear train images, blurry test images)
Label quality noisy or inconsistent labels the model memorised
Test composition unusually hard or unrepresentative slices
  • Metrics: precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix, PR-AUC for rare classes, and per-class numbers. Always against a baseline (majority class or a simple model). In fraud, "always legitimate" can hit 99% accuracy.

Why this matters: overfitting and distribution shift are different problems with different fixes, and they can co-exist.

stages.name: Experiment, one change at a time
stages.html:
"Once overfitting is confirmed, I run controlled experiments, changing one factor at a time."

Experiment 1

Early stopping

I'd monitor validation loss and stop training when validation performance stops improving.

Why? The model may learn general patterns in early epochs and memorise training-specific noise in later ones.

Best suited when validation performance peaks before training finishes.

Experiment 2

Regularization

I'd add techniques that discourage the model from fitting noise:

  • L2 regularization (weight decay): penalises large weights.
  • Dropout: randomly disables some neurons during training (neural nets).
  • L1 regularization: encourages sparse weights where that suits the model.
  • For trees: limit max_depth, raise min_samples_leaf, subsample rows and columns.

Why? These reduce the model's sensitivity to training-specific patterns, which improves generalisation.

Best suited when capacity is fine but the fit is too sharp.

Experiment 3

Reduce capacity

If the model is large relative to the data, I'd use fewer layers or units, a smaller model, or fewer features.

Why? A model with excess capacity can memorise the training set instead of learning robust patterns.

Best suited when the model is large relative to the data.

Experiment 4

Better, more representative data

I'd prioritise more representative, high-quality examples:

  • Targeted collection for weak-performing segments.
  • Relabelling and removing corrupted examples.
  • Augmentation where it's valid for the domain; class weighting for imbalance.

Why? More diverse examples help the model learn patterns that generalise instead of memorising a limited set.

Best suited when the learning curve says more data helps.

Experiment 5

Tune hyperparameters

Learning rate, batch size, weight decay, dropout rate and training length, all selected on validation.

Why? The right settings interact; tuning finds the combination, but only on data the final test never sees.

Best suited last, once the bigger levers above are in place.

Experiment Train acc Val acc
Baseline 99% 72%
Early stopping measure measure
Weight decay / dropout measure measure
Smaller model measure measure
More representative data measure measure

Why this matters: the goal isn't to drag train accuracy down to 72%. It's to raise validation while keeping what the model genuinely learned.

stages.name: Interpret the result
stages.html:
"This is where I show judgement: not every train–test gap has the same cause."

Observation Likely cause Next action
Train 99%, val 72%, val loss rising overfitting regularise, early stop, reduce capacity
Train 75%, val 72% underfitting more capacity, better features
Train and val high, test low leakage or split mismatch audit pipeline and split strategy
Val fine, test distribution differs distribution shift fix representativeness, reweight, collect data
Accuracy high, minority recall low class imbalance per-class metrics, weighting, resampling

If early stopping lifts validation from 72% to 80% (illustrative), I'd then test whether regularization or data closes more of the gap. Real validation numbers drive the next step.

stages.name: Validate once, then monitor
stages.html:
"The test set gets looked at once. Otherwise it quietly becomes a second validation set."

  • Select the model and hyperparameters on validation (or cross-validation).
  • Retrain on train (+ validation if appropriate) with the chosen configuration.
  • Evaluate once on the held-out test set, against the baseline and the business metric.
  • Check segments (region, device, customer tier) and calibration if scores drive decisions.
  • Deploy with monitoring: input drift (PSI/KS per feature), prediction drift, and delayed-label performance.

Why this matters: "fixed" means reliable on real traffic, not a nicer number on a test set you've tuned against.

followUps.question: Why not just reduce the number of epochs?
followUps.html: That's early stopping, and it's my first experiment, but only once I've shown overfitting is the cause. If the gap comes from leakage, a bad split or distribution shift, fewer epochs just produces a weaker model with the same gap. I let the validation-loss curve pick the stopping point rather than guessing a number.

followUps.question: Would you always add dropout?
followUps.html: No. Dropout is a neural-network tool, and its benefit depends on architecture and data size. It can hurt small models or ones already regularised by batch norm. For gradient-boosted trees it doesn't apply; I'd regularise with depth, leaf size and subsampling instead. Every technique is tested against the baseline, not assumed.

followUps.question: The learning curve is flat and you can't get more data. Now what?
followUps.html: A flat gap means data volume isn't the constraint, so I'd attack capacity and signal: stronger regularization, a simpler model, fewer and better-engineered features, or an ensemble like bagging to average variance away. I'd also check label noise, because a model can't generalise past inconsistent labels. And I'd sanity-check whether 72% is actually poor for this task against a baseline or human performance.

followUps.question: Can you get 99% / 72% without overfitting?
followUps.html: Yes. Distribution shift between train and test, a small or unrepresentative test set, or an evaluation-pipeline bug (different preprocessing at test time) all produce the same two numbers. That's exactly why I audit the split and read the curves first. The gap is a symptom, not a diagnosis.

followUps.question: How do you know an improvement is statistically meaningful?
followUps.html: First, size the noise: accuracy on n test rows has a standard error of √(p(1−p)/n), so at 72% on 1,000 rows the 95% interval is about ±2.8 points. Then compare the two models on the same examples with McNemar's test, or bootstrap a confidence interval of the difference. For small data, repeat across CV folds or seeds, so one lucky split doesn't decide it.

followUps.question: It's a gradient-boosted model, not a neural net. What changes?
followUps.html: The diagnosis is identical; the levers change. Instead of dropout and weight decay I'd use max_depth, min_child_weight / min_samples_leaf, row and column subsampling, a lower learning rate with more trees, and L1/L2 on leaf weights. Early stopping works the same way, on validation loss per boosting round.

followUps.question: How would you catch this before it reaches production?
followUps.html: Make it structural. Keep every transform inside a pipeline fitted per fold. Use group or time-based splits by default. Add a leakage checklist to review ("would I know this feature at prediction time?"). Hold out a final test set nobody tunes on. Then shadow-score live traffic before cut-over, so drift shows up against real inputs, not a static file.

dontSay: "I'd add dropout and regularization." (as the opening) — fixing before diagnosing is the trap this question sets.
"The model is 99% accurate on training, so it's learned well." — it may have memorised, and accuracy may hide imbalance.
"I'll keep tuning until test accuracy goes up." — that turns the test set into a validation set.
"Overfitting, definitely." — the gap alone doesn't prove it; leakage and shift look the same.

ml-dl-q2.testing: whether you know the ways an offline number can be optimistic, and check them in the right order.
ml-dl-q2.trap: "It's data drift, retrain on fresh data." Drift doesn't arrive pre-installed on day one.
ml-dl-q2.spoken:
"A drop from 0.94 to 0.71 with no code change tells me the offline number was probably never real, so I'd treat it as an evaluation problem before a model problem.

I'd check leakage first, because it's the most common cause of a gap this size. Is any top feature computed from or after the label? Was the scaler or encoder fitted on the full dataset before the split? Is the same customer, or future data, on both sides of the split?

Next, train–serve skew. Training features usually come from warehouse SQL, serving features from application code, and two implementations of 'the same' feature quietly disagree on nulls, time zones or windows.

Only then would I call it drift, by comparing production feature distributions against training with PSI or KS.

To prove which one it is, I'd log the features actually served, replay them through the offline pipeline, and compare scores row by row.

Finally I'd make the fix structural: every transform inside a pipeline fitted per fold, group or time-based splits, and one shared feature definition for training and serving, so the next model can't repeat this."

stages.name: Frame the gap
stages.claim: an optimistic offline number, not a broken model
stages.html:
"Twenty-three points on day one is too big and too sudden for drift. I assume the 0.94 was inflated until proven otherwise."

  • Ask when it dropped: from the first production day (evaluation problem) or gradually (drift).
  • Ask what 0.71 is measured on: same metric, same label definition, same population as offline?
  • Ask whether production labels are complete; a label delay makes recent rows look worse or better than they are.

Why this matters: the timing alone reorders the suspects. Day-one gaps are leakage or skew; slow decay is drift.

stages.name: Leakage first
stages.html:
"Leakage is the most common cause, so I go through its families one by one."

Family What it looks like How I check
Target leakage feature computed from or after the outcome (refund flag, "days since cancellation") for the top features: "would I know this at prediction time?"
Preprocessing contamination scaler, imputer or encoder fitted on all data before splitting is every transform inside the per-fold pipeline?
Temporal leakage random split on time-ordered data trains on the future re-score on a strict time holdout
Group leakage same user or device in train and validation re-score with GroupKFold on the entity id

Example: a churn model with "number of support tickets in the last 30 days" computed at the end of the label window looks brilliant offline and has nothing to use at serving time.

Why this matters: re-scoring on an honest split is cheap. If CV drops toward 0.71, you've found it without touching production.

stages.name: Then train–serve skew
stages.html:
"If the offline evaluation is honest, the next suspect is that production computes different features."

  • Training features from warehouse SQL; serving features from service code. Two code paths drift apart.
  • Typical differences: null defaults, time zones, aggregation windows, unit changes, categorical levels unseen offline.
  • A feature that exists in the warehouse but is not available at request time gets silently defaulted at serving.
  • Check per-feature null rates and distributions: served vs training.

Example: training uses avg_spend_30d from a nightly batch; the service computes it from a cache that resets on deploy, so half of production sees zero.

Why this matters: skew looks exactly like drift on a dashboard, but retraining won't fix it. It just trains on the bug.

stages.name: Drift last
stages.html:
"Only after leakage and skew are ruled out do I call it drift."

  • Covariate shift: input distributions moved. Detect with PSI or KS per feature, and prediction-distribution drift.
  • Label shift: the base rate changed. Compare predicted vs observed positive rate.
  • Concept drift: the relationship changed. Needs labels; watch rolling metrics per segment.

On day one, genuine drift is unlikely unless the launch population differs from the training population (a new market, a new client). That's worth asking.

stages.name: Prove it by replay
stages.html:
"I don't argue about which cause it is. I replay."

  1. Log the exact feature vectors served in production, plus the model version.
  2. Recompute the same rows through the offline feature pipeline.
  3. Compare feature by feature, and compare model scores row by row.
Result Diagnosis
Offline and served features match, scores match, metric still low leakage inflated the offline number
Features differ for some columns train–serve skew in those columns
Features match, distributions differ from training drift or a population change

Why this matters: it turns a debate into a diff, and it tells you which team owns the fix.

stages.name: Make it structural
stages.claim: so the next model can't do this
stages.html:
"The fix isn't this model. It's the process that let a fake 0.94 ship."

  • Every transform inside a Pipeline / ColumnTransformer, fitted per fold.
  • Group- or time-based splits by default; a final time-ordered holdout nobody tunes on.
  • One feature definition shared by training and serving (feature store or a shared library).
  • A leakage checklist in model review; shadow-score live traffic before cut-over.
  • Monitoring: feature nulls and PSI against the training profile, plus delayed-label metrics.

followUps.question: How would you find target leakage fast in a model with 300 features?
followUps.html: Sort by importance and interrogate the top ten: "would I know this at prediction time, and when is it written?" A feature with implausibly high importance, or one whose SHAP values separate classes almost perfectly, is guilty until proven innocent. Then drop the suspects and re-score on a time holdout; a large drop confirms it.

followUps.question: Why not just retrain on recent production data?
followUps.html: Because if the cause is leakage, the retrained model leaks the same way and the offline number stays fake. If it's skew, you train on production's broken features and bake the bug in. Retraining fixes covariate or label drift; it's the last step, after the diagnosis says drift.

followUps.question: CV is honest, replay shows features match, and it's still 0.71. Now what?
followUps.html: Then the population or the label differs. Check whether production users match the training population (new market, new client, new acquisition channel). Check the label: same definition, same horizon, fully observed? A 30-day churn label measured after 10 days looks like a model failure. Slice the metric by segment to find where the loss concentrates.

followUps.question: You don't have a feature store. How do you prevent skew?
followUps.html: Share one computation library or dbt layer between the training job and the service, so there's one definition. Better still, log the features the service actually computes and use those logs as training data ("log and wait"), which makes training and serving identical by construction. Add a nightly check comparing served-feature distributions with the training profile.

followUps.question: How do you tell drift from a pipeline break on a dashboard?
followUps.html: Pipeline breaks are abrupt and local: a step change on one or two features, often nulls or a unit change, aligned with a deploy or upstream schema change. Drift is gradual and spread across correlated features. Check null rates and value ranges first, and line the change up against the deploy log before you reach for PSI.

followUps.question: How do you catch this before shipping next time?
followUps.html: Evaluate the way you'll serve: a time-ordered final holdout, features computed by the serving path, and a shadow deployment scoring live traffic for a week before cut-over. If the shadow score doesn't match offline within a tolerance, the launch stops. That turns this incident into a gate.

dontSay: "It's data drift." (as the first answer) — drift doesn't explain a day-one gap.
"Let's retrain with more data." — retraining on leakage or skew reproduces it.
"Maybe production data is just noisier." — untestable; name a mechanism you can check.
"CV was 0.94, so the model is good." — CV measures the split you built, not production.

ml-dl-q3.testing: whether you know the framework and its limits in the deep-learning era.
ml-dl-q3.trap: reciting the U-curve as a universal law in 2026, or naming only two terms.
ml-dl-q3.spoken:
"For squared loss, expected test error splits exactly into three terms: bias squared, variance, and irreducible noise. Bias is systematic error from wrong assumptions, like fitting a line to a curve. Variance is how much the model changes if you retrain it on a different sample. Noise is the floor no model can beat.

The classical picture says capacity trades the two: more capacity lowers bias and raises variance, so test error is U-shaped and you pick the bottom.

That still governs most tabular work, but it misleads in two places. First, heavily over-parameterised models show double descent: past the point where the model can fit the training set exactly, test error falls again. So 'more parameters always overfit' is false for modern networks; I reason about effective capacity, which includes regularisation, the optimiser and data size, not parameter count. Second, the clean decomposition only holds for squared loss; for classification with 0–1 loss it's an analogy.

What survives is the diagnostic value. The train–validation gap reads variance; high error on both reads bias. Each has a different fix, so the framework's real job is telling me which one to attack."

stages.name: Decompose into three terms
stages.html:
"Expected squared error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise."

  • Bias: error from the model's assumptions. Averaged over many training sets, how far is the prediction from the truth? Underfitting.
  • Variance: how much the prediction moves when you retrain on a different sample. Overfitting.
  • Irreducible noise: randomness in the target itself. No model removes it.

Example: a linear model on a curved relationship has high bias; a depth-30 decision tree on 500 rows has high variance.

Why this matters: most candidates stop at two terms. Naming noise tells the interviewer you know where the floor is.

stages.name: The classical U-curve
stages.html:
"As capacity rises, bias falls and variance rises, so test error is U-shaped."

  • Pick the capacity at the bottom, using validation error, not training error.
  • This is the right first answer for trees, linear models, k-NN and most tabular problems.

stages.name: Where it misleads
stages.claim: double descent, and the wrong loss
stages.html:
"Two places the classical picture breaks."

  • Double descent: past the interpolation threshold (the model can fit the training data exactly), test error can fall again as capacity keeps growing. Modern networks live in that second descent.
  • Parameter count ≠ capacity. Effective capacity depends on the architecture, regularisation, the optimiser's implicit bias (SGD prefers simpler fits) and data size. So "a 1B-parameter model must overfit 10M rows" is not a valid argument.
  • Loss matters. The exact decomposition holds for squared error. For 0–1 classification loss, bias and variance interact, so the three-term split is an analogy.

Why this matters: saying this is the difference between a textbook answer and one that has read past the textbook.

stages.name: What survives
stages.html:
"Operationally, it's still the right lens for debugging a model."

Observation Dominant term Read
Train error low, validation high variance gap = variance
Both high and close bias model can't represent the signal
Both low, close healthy check against the noise floor
Gap shrinks as data grows variance, data-hungry more data helps

A learning curve (error vs training-set size) separates "needs more data" from "needs more capacity".

stages.name: Fix the dominant term
stages.html:
"Different terms, different fixes, and using the wrong one makes things worse."

  • High variance: more data, regularisation (L1/L2, dropout), early stopping, bagging, smaller model.
  • High bias: more capacity, better features, less regularisation, boosting.
  • Noise: better labels or measurement; no model change helps.

Example: adding dropout to an underfitting model raises bias further. That's why diagnosis comes first.

followUps.question: Why does bagging reduce variance but not bias?
followUps.html: Averaging many models trained on bootstrap samples cancels the part of their error that's uncorrelated, which is the variance. Every model shares the same systematic assumptions, so averaging biased models gives a biased average. That's why bagging wants deep, low-bias, high-variance trees.

followUps.question: So should I just make every model huge?
followUps.html: No. Double descent needs enough data, the right regularisation and the right optimiser, and it isn't guaranteed. The peak near the interpolation threshold is real and can be worse than a small model. For tabular data with modest rows, boosting still beats large networks. Capacity is a choice you validate, not a default.

followUps.question: How do you estimate the irreducible noise?
followUps.html: Look at label disagreement: duplicate or near-identical inputs with different labels, or inter-annotator agreement for human labels. Human-level or best-known performance is a practical proxy for the floor. If your error is already near it, more modelling won't help; better labels or new features might.

followUps.question: Where does regularisation sit in this picture?
followUps.html: It reduces effective capacity without changing the architecture: it adds a little bias to remove more variance. That's why the regularisation strength is a knob along the same U-curve. Weight decay, dropout, early stopping and data augmentation all move you left on it.

followUps.question: Does this matter for LLMs at all?
followUps.html: The framing shifts. Pretraining on huge corpora for one epoch usually sits in the underfitting regime, so the scale of data is the regulariser, and dropout is often set to zero. Variance problems reappear in fine-tuning on small datasets, where overfitting and memorisation are real, and in evaluation, where contamination fakes a low "variance".

dontSay: "There's a trade-off: more complex models always overfit." — double descent contradicts it.
"Bias and variance." (two terms only) — you dropped the noise floor.
"Deep models have low bias, so they're always better." — effective capacity and data size decide.
"The decomposition works the same for accuracy." — exact only for squared loss.

ml-dl-q4.testing: whether one split design can defeat two independent leakage risks at once.
ml-dl-q4.trap: stratified K-fold because the class balance looked nicer.
ml-dl-q4.spoken:
"The question names two separate risks, and a random split fails both.

The first is entity leakage: if the same user is in train and test, the model memorises the user instead of learning the behaviour. The second is temporal leakage: with seasonality, a random split trains on the future and tests on the past.

So I'd split by time first: train on everything up to a cutoff, validate on the next window, test on the most recent one. Within that, I'd keep users disjoint, so no user in the test window was seen in training. Whether I enforce that strictly depends on production: if the model will score existing users, some overlap is realistic, but their test rows must still come after their training rows.

I'd also respect the prediction horizon and label delay: features only use data up to the prediction time, and I drop recent rows whose label window isn't fully observed yet.

Then I'd validate walk-forward across several cutoffs instead of one, report the metric per time slice, and check the test window covers a comparable season.

The principle is that offline evaluation should mirror deployment exactly: train on the past, predict forward."

stages.name: Name the two leaks
stages.html:
"Two independent violations. Fix only one and the score is still fiction."

  • Entity leakage: a user appears in both sets. The model learns user identity (their habits, ID-correlated features) and scores well on "new" rows it has effectively seen.
  • Temporal leakage: random shuffling puts December in training and November in test. The model uses the future.
  • Seasonality adds a third subtlety: the test window must cover a comparable season, or you're measuring the calendar, not the model.

stages.name: Split by time first
stages.html:
"Time is the primary axis: train ≤ T, validate (T, T+Δ], test on the latest window."

|──────── train ────────|── val ──|── test ──|   time →
                        T        T+Δ
  • Mirrors deployment, where the model always predicts forward.
  • Leave a gap between train and validation equal to the prediction horizon, so labels from the train window can't overlap validation features.

stages.name: Keep users disjoint
stages.claim: decide it from the production case
stages.html:
"Then enforce user disjointness inside that time split, if production requires it."

Production scores… Split rule
mostly new users strict: no test-window user appears in training (GroupKFold-style on user id)
mostly existing users overlap allowed, but each user's test rows come strictly after their training rows

Example: a subscription-cancellation model scores the existing base monthly, so overlap is realistic; a sign-up fraud model sees only new users, so strict disjointness is the honest test.

Why this matters: "always group" and "never group" are both wrong. The split copies what production will see.

stages.name: Respect horizon and label delay
stages.html:
"Features stop at the prediction timestamp, and labels must be fully observed."

  • Point-in-time features: every feature is computed as-of the prediction time. Aggregates like "logins last 30 days" must not include days after it.
  • Label delay: a 30-day churn label isn't known for the last 30 days of data. Those rows look like non-churners, so drop them.
  • Watch features that change after the fact (account status, refunds): use their historical value, not today's.

stages.name: Walk forward and slice
stages.html:
"One cutoff is one sample. I validate across several."

  • Walk-forward CV: expanding or rolling windows across several origins; report mean and spread.
  • Per-slice reporting: metric per month in the test window. Steady decay tells you the retraining cadence you'll need.
  • Season check: make sure at least one validation window covers the same season as the deployment period.

stages.name: Mirror production
stages.html:
"If my CV doesn't look like production, its number is decoration."

Write the split rule into the pipeline, not a notebook: time cutoffs, user rule, horizon gap and label-completeness filter. Keep a final time-ordered holdout that no tuning touches.

followUps.question: Why not stratified K-fold? Class balance is identical across folds.
followUps.html: Balance isn't the risk. Stratified K-fold shuffles across time and users, so it trains on the future and lets users appear on both sides. The score will be optimistic in exactly the way production can't reproduce. Stratification is fine within a time-ordered, grouped split if positives are rare.

followUps.question: You only have 14 months of data. How many walk-forward folds?
followUps.html: Enough to cover a full season in validation at least once. With 14 months, perhaps train on the first 9–12 and validate on 3–4 rolling one-month windows. Fewer, honest folds beat many leaky ones. Report the spread, because with few folds the variance of the estimate is high.

followUps.question: A user's behaviour depends on account age. Does that break the user split?
followUps.html: No, but features must be computed point-in-time, so account age is its value at prediction time. And if production scores new and old users, report metrics separately for each cohort; a model that only works for tenured users will hide behind a pooled number.

followUps.question: How do you handle a label that takes 90 days to observe?
followUps.html: The newest training data is always 90 days old, so the model trains on stale behaviour. Options: use a shorter proxy label validated against the full one, accept the lag and retrain on a schedule, and monitor label-free signals (feature and prediction drift) in the meantime. Always drop rows whose window isn't complete.

followUps.question: How do you tune hyperparameters inside this scheme?
followUps.html: Nested inside the time structure: tune on the walk-forward validation windows, never on the final test window. The final test gets evaluated once. If data is scarce, use the walk-forward folds as the inner loop and hold the most recent window as the outer estimate.

dontSay: "Stratified K-fold with shuffle." — breaks both time order and user disjointness.
"Just group by user." — fixes one leak and ignores time.
"Use all the data up to today." — the last label window is incomplete.
"One train/test cut is enough." — one origin tells you nothing about stability across seasons.

spine: Fix: nested CV or an untouched holdout
ml-dl-q5.testing: whether you separate selecting a model from estimating its performance.
ml-dl-q5.trap: treating the best CV score as the expected production score.
ml-dl-q5.spoken:
"The number did two jobs. It was used to pick the hyperparameters, and then reported as the estimate of how well the model generalises. Once you select on a score, that score is optimistically biased.

The reason is the winner's curse. Every configuration's CV score is its true performance plus some fold noise. When you pick the maximum across many configurations, you systematically pick the ones that got lucky on those particular folds. The more configurations you try, the bigger the inflation: small if you tried three settings, large if Optuna tried three hundred.

The fix depends on how much data I have. With enough data, I keep a test set that nothing touches during selection and evaluate on it exactly once at the end. With scarce data, I use nested cross-validation: the inner loop tunes, the outer loop estimates the performance of the whole tuning procedure.

The same rule covers anything else chosen on those folds: feature selection, encoders, the decision threshold.

And when comparing two models, I'd treat differences inside the CV noise as ties, using repeated CV with confidence intervals or a paired test, not a single leaderboard number."

stages.name: Name the bias
stages.claim: selection and estimation used the same data
stages.html:
"The CV score was used to select, so it can no longer estimate."

  • The folds were held out for training, but not for selection. Selection is a form of fitting.
  • Reported number = score of the configuration that did best on these exact folds.
  • In production, the model meets new data with new noise, and the lucky part disappears.

stages.name: Why selection inflates
stages.html:
"Each CV score is true performance plus noise. The max of many noisy scores is biased upward."

The same effect makes a stock-picking fund's best past year a bad forecast.

stages.name: How big it gets
stages.html:
"The bias grows with how hard you searched and shrinks with how much data each fold has."

Situation Inflation
3 hand-picked configs, large folds small
300-trial Bayesian search, small data large
Many features selected on CV + tuning larger again, because both steps overfit the folds

Why this matters: you can say how worried to be, instead of treating it as always fatal or always negligible.

stages.name: Fix: nested CV or an untouched holdout
stages.html:
"Two honest options."

Option 1 — Untouched test set. Split off a test set first. Do all tuning with CV on the rest. Evaluate the final model once on the test set. Best when data is plentiful.

Option 2 — Nested CV. Outer loop splits data into k folds for estimation. Inside each outer training fold, an inner CV tunes hyperparameters. The outer score estimates the procedure (tune-then-train), not one configuration. Best when data is scarce. Cost: outer × inner × candidates fits.

  • Everything chosen on validation data goes inside the inner loop: feature selection, encoders, thresholds.
  • After nested CV, you still refit the tuning procedure on all data to get the model you ship.

stages.name: Compare models honestly
stages.html:
"Before claiming model A beats model B, I check the difference is bigger than the noise."

  • Repeated CV with different seeds: report mean ± spread.
  • Paired tests on the same folds or examples: McNemar's test, 5×2-CV paired t-test.
  • A 0.3-point gain inside a 1-point spread is a tie. Pick the simpler or cheaper model.

followUps.question: Nested CV is expensive. When is it worth it?
followUps.html: When the data is too small to spare a clean holdout and the decision is costly: a model going to a regulator, a paper, or a go/no-go on a product. For a large dataset, one untouched test set gives the same honesty much cheaper. The cost scales with outer folds × inner folds × candidates, so reduce the search space before nesting.

followUps.question: After nested CV, which hyperparameters do you ship?
followUps.html: Nested CV estimates the procedure, and each outer fold may pick different hyperparameters. To ship, rerun the inner tuning on the full dataset and train with the winner. The outer score is your honest estimate of how that procedure performs; if the outer folds chose wildly different settings, the tuning is unstable, which is itself a finding.

followUps.question: I also chose features using the same CV. Problem?
followUps.html: Yes, the same one, often worse. Feature selection on the full dataset before CV is leakage: the features were chosen with the validation rows' labels. Put selection inside the pipeline so it's refit per fold, or inside the inner loop of nested CV.

followUps.question: How much can you tune against a test set before it stops being a test set?
followUps.html: Strictly, once. Every decision you make after looking at it leaks information. Looking twice isn't catastrophic, but a team iterating against a fixed test set for months has turned it into a validation set. Refresh it or hold back a second, never-seen set for the final claim.

followUps.question: What's your threshold-tuning story here?
followUps.html: The decision threshold is a hyperparameter too. Choose it on validation data, using the cost of errors or an alert budget, and evaluate the chosen threshold once on the test set. Choosing it on the test set inflates precision and recall exactly the way tuning on CV inflated the score.

dontSay: "CV is unbiased, so the score is fine." — CV is unbiased for a fixed model, not a selected one.
"Just use more folds." — more folds don't remove selection bias.
"Nested CV always." — it's a budget decision; a clean holdout is often enough.
"Model B wins by 0.3%." — without a noise estimate that's not a result.

ml-dl-q6.testing: whether you frame from the business decision backwards, and have the judgement to say no.
ml-dl-q6.trap: accepting "predict churn" as the spec and jumping to model choice.
ml-dl-q6.spoken:
"'Reduce churn' is a goal, not a spec, so I'd work backwards from the decision.

First, the decision: who gets which intervention, when, and at what cost? A discount, a call from customer success, a product nudge. If nobody can act on a prediction, there's no project.

Second, the label and horizon. Churn meaning a cancellation event, or no activity for 30 days? Predicted how far ahead? And is that label available historically without leakage, and how long until we observe it?

Third, the unit: per user, per account or per subscription, scored daily, weekly or monthly.

Fourth, the cost of errors. A false positive wastes a discount on someone who'd have stayed; a false negative loses the customer. That cost matrix, plus how many people the team can actually contact, picks the metric and the threshold. I'd also ask whether we should predict churn at all or the uplift from the intervention.

Then I'd set a baseline, like a rule on recent inactivity, and a success threshold before modelling.

I'd say don't use ML when a stable rule captures most of the value, when there's no reliable label or feedback loop, or when the action is the same for everyone anyway."

stages.name: Pin the decision
stages.html:
"I start from what changes in the business if the prediction is right."

Ask:

  • What intervention exists? Discount, outreach call, onboarding fix, product change.
  • Who acts on it, and how many can they handle per week? (capacity constraint)
  • When must the prediction arrive to be useful? A week before renewal, not the day after.
  • What does one intervention cost?

Why this matters: the decision sets everything downstream: horizon, unit, metric and threshold.

stages.name: Define the label and horizon
stages.html:
"The label is a definition, and it's the most important modelling choice."

  • Event: explicit cancellation, non-renewal, or inactivity for N days? Do pauses or downgrades count?
  • Horizon: "will churn in the next 30 days" measured from the prediction date.
  • Availability: can we reconstruct it historically, point-in-time, without leaking post-outcome data?
  • Label delay: a 30-day label for last week's users isn't known yet.

Example: in B2B, "account churn" at renewal is quarterly and rare; in consumer apps, 14-day inactivity is frequent and noisy. Different problems.

stages.name: Choose the unit
stages.claim: what gets a score, how often
stages.html:
"The unit of prediction is a choice, not a given."

Option Fits when
Per user, weekly consumer app, cheap nudges
Per account, monthly B2B, account managers act
Per subscription at renewal-minus-30 renewal-driven businesses

Batch scoring on a schedule is usually enough for churn; say so, because it removes most of the serving infrastructure.

stages.name: Price the errors
stages.claim: the cost matrix picks the metric
stages.html:
"A false positive and a false negative have different prices, so accuracy is meaningless."

  • False positive: discount given to someone who'd have stayed (cost = discount + margin loss).
  • False negative: a churner missed (cost = lost lifetime value).
  • Capacity: if the team can call 200 people a week, the metric is precision@200, not AUC.
  • Uplift, not churn: the valuable users are the persuadable ones. Some churners leave whatever you do; some would stay anyway. If you can run experiments, model the treatment effect.

stages.name: Beat a baseline
stages.html:
"Before any model, I write down what we'd do without one, and what 'success' means."

  • Baselines: current process, a rule ("no login in 14 days and plan expires in 30"), a logistic regression on five features.
  • Success = measurable lift in retained revenue in an A/B test against the baseline, not an offline AUC.
  • If the rule gets most of the value, ship the rule and revisit later.

stages.name: Decide: ML or not
stages.html:
"'Don't use ML' needs conditions, not modesty."

Say no when Because
A simple stable rule captures most of the value ML adds cost and opacity for little gain
No reliable label, or it's hopelessly noisy nothing to learn from
No feedback loop to measure outcomes you can't tell if it works
The action is identical for everyone a prediction can't change the decision
Errors are costly and unbounded without human review put a human in the loop, or use rules

followUps.question: Why is predicting churn not the same as reducing it?
followUps.html: Because the intervention only helps some users. "Sure things" stay anyway, "lost causes" leave anyway, and "sleeping dogs" can be pushed to leave by a reminder. A churn model targets high-risk users, which includes lost causes. An uplift model targets users whose outcome the intervention changes. It needs randomised treatment data to train, so start with an experiment.

followUps.question: How do you avoid leakage in the churn label?
followUps.html: Compute every feature as-of the prediction date and never use information recorded after it: cancellation-flow visits, support tickets about cancelling, refund requests. Split by time. Drop recent rows whose label window hasn't closed. Then audit the top features: "would I know this on the prediction date?"

followUps.question: The business wants 95% accuracy. Your answer?
followUps.html: Accuracy is the wrong target: with 5% churn, "nobody churns" scores 95%. I'd reframe it as a business outcome, for example "retain N more customers per month at a cost below X", and agree on precision at the team's capacity as the model metric. Then set targets from a baseline, not from a round number.

followUps.question: How do you prove the model reduced churn?
followUps.html: A randomised holdout: score everyone, intervene on a random subset of high-risk users and not on a matched control. The difference in churn between them is the causal effect of model-plus-intervention. Offline metrics can't show this; only an experiment can. Keep a small permanent holdout to detect decay.

followUps.question: Batch or real-time scoring?
followUps.html: Batch, unless the intervention is triggered in-session (a save offer in the cancellation flow). Churn decisions are usually daily or weekly, so a nightly job writing scores to a table is simpler, cheaper and easier to monitor. Real-time adds an online feature path and skew risk for no business benefit.

followUps.question: There's no history of interventions, only of churn. Can you still build it?
followUps.html: You can build a churn-risk model, but not an uplift model, because you've never observed what the intervention does. So start with risk scoring plus a randomised pilot: treat a random half of high-risk users, hold out the rest. That pilot measures the intervention's effect and creates the training data for an uplift model later.

dontSay: "I'd train an XGBoost on user features." (first sentence) — model before framing.
"We'll optimise accuracy." — imbalanced label, and it ignores the cost of errors.
"ML is always better than rules." — the baseline decides.
"Predict who will churn and give them all a discount." — ignores capacity and persuadability.

ml-dl-q7.testing: whether you can translate a threshold-free metric into the decision the business actually makes.
ml-dl-q7.trap: defending the model with the metric instead of the decision.
ml-dl-q7.spoken:
"Both statements can be true, because ROC-AUC and the business are measuring different things.

ROC-AUC averages ranking quality over every possible threshold and is insensitive to class prevalence. If positives are rare, say half a percent, the false-positive rate's denominator is the huge negative class, so a model can flood the review queue with false alarms and still post 0.92.

The business lives at one operating point: 'my team can review a hundred cases a day'. So I'd measure what they experience: precision at that budget, recall at that budget, and the precision–recall curve, which has the positives in the denominator and exposes what ROC hides.

I'd also check calibration. If scores feed any downstream logic like 'act above 0.7', a good ranker with miscalibrated probabilities still breaks it. A reliability plot and the Brier score show that, and Platt or isotonic scaling fixes it.

Then I'd set the threshold from the cost of errors or the capacity constraint, not at 0.5.

The real lesson is framing: the operating metric should be agreed with the business before training. A metric mismatch discovered after launch is a framing failure, not a modelling one."

stages.name: Both are right
stages.html:
"AUC answers 'does the model rank positives above negatives?' The business asks 'is the list I act on worth acting on?'"

  • AUC = probability a random positive scores above a random negative.
  • It's threshold-free: averaged over all thresholds, most of which the business never uses.
  • The business sees one threshold and one queue.

stages.name: Check prevalence
stages.html:
"With 0.5% positives, a small false-positive rate is still a flood."

ROC reports "80% TPR at 5% FPR", which sounds excellent. The analyst sees 13 false alarms for every real case.

stages.name: Look where the business operates
stages.html:
"Evaluate at the operating point, not across all of them."

  • Precision@k, where k is daily review capacity.
  • Recall at that budget: what share of real cases we catch.
  • PR-AUC / average precision as the threshold-free summary, because precision uses positives in the denominator.
  • Slice by segment: the model may be useless for the segment the business cares about most.

stages.name: Check calibration
stages.html:
"If anyone acts on the score's value, the score has to mean what it says."

  • Reliability diagram: predicted probability vs observed frequency, binned.
  • Brier score: mean squared error of the probabilities.
  • Fix on a held-out set: Platt scaling (sigmoid, little data) or isotonic (flexible, more data).

Example: the business rule "escalate above 0.7" catches nothing if the model's scores cluster between 0.2 and 0.5.

stages.name: Set the threshold from cost
stages.html:
"The threshold is a business decision expressed in numbers."

  • Cost-based: pick the threshold that minimises FP cost × FP count + FN cost × FN count.
  • Budget-based: take the top k per day.
  • Revisit when costs, capacity or prevalence change; a threshold is not permanent.

stages.name: Agree the metric up front
stages.html:
"This was a framing failure. The metric should have been agreed before training."

Write down the decision, the capacity, the cost of each error and the target precision@k with the business. Report that number, with AUC as a secondary diagnostic.

followUps.question: When would you still prefer ROC-AUC?
followUps.html: When comparing rankers across datasets with different prevalence, since ROC is prevalence-insensitive; when classes are roughly balanced; or early on, before an operating point is known. It's a good diagnostic of ranking quality, just not a business metric.

followUps.question: PR-AUC is 0.12. Is the model bad?
followUps.html: Not necessarily. A random classifier's PR-AUC equals the prevalence, so at 0.5% prevalence, 0.12 is 24 times better than random. The question is whether precision at the business's budget is high enough to be worth the team's time. Compare against the current process, not against 1.0.

followUps.question: How do you pick k if the team's capacity varies?
followUps.html: Rank by score and let capacity decide the cut each day, so the threshold floats. Report precision and recall at several k values so the business can see the trade-off. If costs are known, give them the expected value at each k and let them choose.

followUps.question: Can you improve precision at the top without retraining?
followUps.html: Sometimes. Add a second-stage model or rules on the top candidates only, using expensive features you couldn't afford for everyone. Re-rank with business context (value at risk). Dedupe related alerts so the queue isn't padded. Retraining with a ranking objective focused on the top of the list is the longer fix.

followUps.question: Your AUC improved 0.92 → 0.94. Does the business care?
followUps.html: Only if precision or recall at their operating point improved. AUC gains can come entirely from reordering cases the business never looks at, far below the cutoff. I'd report the change in precision@k and in expected cost, and only claim a win if those moved.

dontSay: "0.92 is a great AUC, the business doesn't understand metrics." — the business is describing the operating point correctly.
"Let's use accuracy instead." — worse under imbalance.
"Set the threshold at 0.5." — arbitrary; costs and capacity set it.
"We need a better model." — maybe; first measure at the right operating point.

ml-dl-q8.testing: whether you know that the value of a probability matters as soon as money multiplies it.
ml-dl-q8.trap: "the AUC is 0.9, so the probabilities are good."
ml-dl-q8.spoken:
"The problem is that a model can rank perfectly and still lie about the probability. Expected value multiplies the probability by money, so any distortion becomes a wrong bid.

Boosted trees are often not calibrated. The scores come from an additive ensemble, and anything done to improve ranking makes it worse: class weights, resampling, early stopping on AUC. Resampling alone shifts the base rate, so every score is inflated.

AUC can't see this because it only measures ranking. I'd diagnose with a reliability diagram, predicted probability against observed frequency in bins, and the Brier score.

The fix is a post-hoc calibrator fitted on held-out data, never the training data: Platt scaling, a sigmoid, when data is limited, or isotonic regression when there's enough data, since it's more flexible but overfits small sets. If I resampled, I'd also correct the prior back to the true base rate.

Then I'd re-check the reliability curve and only then compute expected value.

Operationally, calibration drifts as the population changes, so I'd monitor predicted versus observed rates in production and recalibrate as part of retraining. The rule: whenever the probability itself enters a decision, calibration is a requirement."

stages.name: Ranking ≠ calibration
stages.html:
"Ranking asks 'which is more likely?' Calibration asks 'when I say 30%, does it happen 30% of the time?'"

  • AUC is invariant to any monotone transform of the scores. Squash them all into 0.4–0.6 and AUC doesn't move.
  • Expected value = p × payoff − cost. A 30% that's really 15% doubles the bid.

Example: in ad bidding, EV = p(click) × value. Overconfident p means overbidding on every impression.

stages.name: Why boosted scores lie
stages.html:
"Several common choices push boosted scores away from true frequencies."

Cause Effect on probabilities
Resampling / SMOTE base rate inflated, every score shifted up
scale_pos_weight / class weights same shift, in the loss
Many boosting rounds scores pushed toward 0 and 1 (overconfident)
Early stopping on AUC optimised for ranking, not probability

Logistic loss alone can be reasonably calibrated; it's the extra ranking-driven choices that break it.

stages.name: Diagnose with a reliability curve
stages.html:
"Plot what the model says against what happened."

  • Bin predictions (deciles), plot mean predicted vs observed rate.
  • Brier score summarises it; expected calibration error (ECE) gives one number per model.
  • Check per segment: calibration can be good overall and bad for a key segment.

stages.name: Calibrate on held-out data
stages.html:
"Fit a mapping from raw score to probability on data the model didn't train on."

Platt scaling. Fit a sigmoid on the raw scores. Two parameters, stable with little data. Best when distortion is a smooth S-shape.

Isotonic regression. Fit a monotone step function. Flexible, handles any monotone distortion, needs thousands of positives, can overfit. Best with plenty of calibration data.

  • In sklearn: CalibratedClassifierCV with cross-validation, or a dedicated calibration split.
  • Never fit the calibrator on training data; the model's scores there are overconfident by construction.

stages.name: Correct for resampling
stages.html:
"If I oversampled positives, the model thinks they're more common than they are."

Either calibrate on a held-out set with the real class balance (the calibrator absorbs the shift), or apply the prior correction analytically: rescale the odds by (true rate / training rate). Then check the mean predicted probability matches the observed base rate.

stages.name: Monitor calibration drift
stages.html:
"Calibration is fitted to one population. When the population moves, it drifts."

  • In production, compare mean predicted probability with the observed rate, per day and per segment.
  • Recalibrate on recent data at each retrain; it's cheap.
  • Alert when observed/predicted diverges past a tolerance; it's often the first sign of drift.

followUps.question: Platt or isotonic — how do you choose?
followUps.html: By data size and shape of the distortion. Platt has two parameters, so it's stable with a few hundred positives but can only fix sigmoid-shaped distortion. Isotonic fixes any monotone distortion but needs a lot of data and can overfit into a jagged step function. I'd compare both on a separate split by Brier score.

followUps.question: Does calibration change the AUC?
followUps.html: Platt doesn't, because it's a strictly monotone transform. Isotonic can change it slightly, because it creates ties (flat steps), but it doesn't improve ranking. Calibration fixes the numbers, not the ordering, so a bad ranker stays bad.

followUps.question: Which models are usually calibrated out of the box?
followUps.html: Logistic regression trained with log loss is typically close, if well specified. Naive Bayes and SVM scores are not probabilities at all. Random forests tend to be underconfident near 0 and 1. Deep networks trained long are often overconfident; temperature scaling is the standard fix there.

followUps.question: How do you calibrate with very few positives?
followUps.html: Use Platt rather than isotonic, calibrate with cross-validation so every positive contributes, and consider pooling segments that share behaviour. Report confidence intervals on the reliability curve, since high-score bins may have a handful of cases. If the decision is high-stakes, widen the margin in the EV rule.

followUps.question: The EV system worked for months, then started overspending. Where do you look?
followUps.html: Calibration drift. The base rate or population shifted, so probabilities that used to be right are now too high. Compare predicted vs observed rates by segment and over time. Recalibrate on recent data, and add that comparison as a standing alert so the next drift is caught before the budget is.

dontSay: "AUC is high, so the probabilities are fine." — AUC ignores calibration completely.
"Calibrate on the training set." — scores there are overconfident by construction.
"Just use a threshold of 0.5." — doesn't fix probabilities feeding EV math.
"Boosted trees output true probabilities." — only if nothing distorted them, and usually something did.

spine: Resample inside the training fold only
Measure with PR metrics at the budget
ml-dl-q9.testing: whether you know which imbalance mistakes silently invalidate the number.
ml-dl-q9.trap: SMOTE on the whole dataset before splitting, or evaluating on a rebalanced set.
ml-dl-q9.spoken:
"At 0.3% the binding constraint is how many positives each split contains, so every choice starts there.

For splitting, I'd stratify on the target so every fold gets its share of positives, and use repeated stratified K-fold, because with a few hundred positives a single split is noisy. If there's time or user structure, that comes first and stratification sits inside it.

For training, my first move is class weights or scale_pos_weight, plus threshold tuning, not synthetic data. It's cheaper and doesn't distort the data. If I do resample, it happens inside the training fold only, after the split. SMOTE before splitting leaks synthetic neighbours of test points into training.

The validation and test sets are never resampled. They must keep the real 0.3%, or the number describes a world that doesn't exist.

For metrics, accuracy is meaningless: predicting 'negative' scores 99.7%. I'd use PR-AUC and, more importantly, precision and recall at the real review budget, like the top 500 alerts a day.

I'd report confidence intervals, because a point of difference is often noise here. And I'd say the deliverable is really a ranked list under a capacity budget, not a classifier."

stages.name: Stratify every split
stages.html:
"With 0.3%, a random fold can end up with almost no positives."

  • 100k rows → ~300 positives; 5 folds → ~60 per fold. Unstratified, some folds get 40, some 80.
  • Stratified K-fold, repeated with different seeds, to stabilise the estimate.
  • If data has time or entity structure, split by that first, then stratify within it.

stages.name: Weight before you resample
stages.html:
"Class weights change the loss, not the data."

  • class_weight='balanced', scale_pos_weight = negatives / positives, or a focal-style loss.
  • No synthetic rows, no duplicated positives, no invented neighbours.
  • Combine with threshold tuning on validation; weighting shifts scores, so the default 0.5 is meaningless.
  • Weights distort probabilities; calibrate afterwards if scores feed decisions.

stages.name: Resample inside the training fold only
stages.html:
"Resampling is a training-time transform. It goes in the pipeline, per fold."

Mistake Why it's wrong
SMOTE before the split synthetic points are interpolations of test points, so the test set leaks into training
Resampling the validation/test set the metric describes a 50/50 world production never sees
Oversampling by duplication before CV the same positive appears in train and validation folds

Use imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline so the sampler runs only on each training fold. SMOTE also interpolates nonsense for categorical or high-dimensional features.

stages.name: Measure with PR metrics at the budget
stages.html:
"Measure what the operations team will experience."

  • Accuracy: 99.7% by predicting all-negative. Useless.
  • ROC-AUC: dominated by the huge negative class, so it flatters.
  • PR-AUC / average precision: random = 0.003, so compare against that.
  • Precision@k, recall@k at the real alert budget (the number of cases reviewed per day).
  • Per-segment recall: which kinds of positives do we miss?

stages.name: Report the noise
stages.html:
"With ~300 positives, a two-point difference in recall is a handful of cases."

  • Bootstrap confidence intervals on precision@k and recall.
  • Repeated CV spread across seeds.
  • Paired comparison (same folds) when choosing between models.

stages.name: Deliver a ranked list
stages.html:
"With extreme imbalance, the output is a prioritised queue under a capacity budget."

The business question isn't "is this fraud?" but "which 500 cases should analysts look at today?" Design the model, metric and threshold around that list.

followUps.question: Why is SMOTE before the split leakage?
followUps.html: SMOTE creates synthetic positives by interpolating between a positive and its nearest positive neighbours. If done before splitting, a synthetic training point can be a near-copy of a test positive. The model has effectively seen the test case, so recall on the test set is inflated.

followUps.question: When is undersampling the right call?
followUps.html: When the negative class is huge and training cost is the bottleneck, say billions of rows. Undersample negatives for training, keep all positives, then correct the scores for the changed prior or recalibrate on real-prevalence data. It throws away information, so check a learning curve that the discarded negatives weren't helping.

followUps.question: Is ROC-AUC ever fine here?
followUps.html: For comparing rankers where the operating point isn't fixed, it's a usable secondary diagnostic. But at 0.3%, two models can have near-identical ROC-AUC and very different precision in the top 500, which is what the business sees. PR metrics and precision@k decide.

followUps.question: Only 50 positives in total. What changes?
followUps.html: Supervised learning is barely viable. Use leave-one-out or repeated stratified CV, very simple models with strong regularisation, and domain rules. Consider anomaly detection or semi-supervised approaches, and invest in labelling: active learning on the model's most uncertain cases gets you more positives fastest. Report intervals honestly; they'll be wide.

followUps.question: Your weighted model's probabilities are off. Problem?
followUps.html: Only if the probabilities are used as probabilities, like expected cost or risk thresholds. Weighting inflates positive scores by design. Fix it with Platt or isotonic calibration on a held-out set with real prevalence. If you only rank, it doesn't matter.

dontSay: "I'd SMOTE the data to 50/50 and then split." — leakage.
"Balance the test set so the metric is fair." — the metric no longer reflects production.
"Accuracy is 99.7%." — the all-negative baseline gets that.
"ROC-AUC 0.95, done." — says little about the top of the queue.

ml-dl-q10.testing: whether you choose by conditions and evidence, not by reputation.
ml-dl-q10.trap: "XGBoost is better" and then spending a week tuning it with no baseline to beat.
ml-dl-q10.spoken:
"I don't pick by reputation. I'd train both with defaults, alongside a logistic regression as the floor, and let the gaps decide.

The axis is variance versus bias. Random Forest averages deep, decorrelated trees, which cuts variance. It's robust, needs almost no tuning, handles noisy labels well, trains in parallel and gives an honest out-of-bag score for free. It rarely embarrasses you.

Gradient boosting fits each tree to the ensemble's remaining errors, which cuts bias. It usually has a higher ceiling on tabular data and brings native missing-value handling, custom objectives like ranking or quantile loss, and regularisation. The price is a tuning budget: learning rate, depth, subsampling and early stopping on a validation set. LightGBM for large or wide data, CatBoost when categoricals dominate.

The failure modes are asymmetric. Random Forest's risk is mediocrity. Boosting's risk is overfitting noisy labels and exploiting leakage, because it chases residuals, and residuals of noise are noise.

So in practice: Random Forest is the baseline I must beat, boosting is usually the model I ship, and I only invest in tuning if the gap between them justifies it."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"They solve different problems."

  • Random Forest: bagging + random feature subsets → averages many high-variance trees → variance falls.
  • Gradient boosting: sequential trees fitted to residuals/gradients → bias falls.
  • Both are tree ensembles, so both handle nonlinearity, interactions and mixed scales without much preprocessing.

stages.name: Where Random Forest wins
stages.html:
"Random Forest is the strong default you can trust in an hour."

  • Near-zero tuning; defaults are usually close to optimal.
  • Robust to label noise and outliers, because averaging dampens them.
  • Embarrassingly parallel training.
  • OOB score: built-in validation without a separate split.
  • Stable across retrains, which matters for explainability and reason codes.

stages.name: Where boosting wins
stages.html:
"Boosting usually wins on accuracy when you can pay for tuning."

Need Why boosting
Highest accuracy on clean tabular data bias reduction; typical competition winner
Missing values native handling, learned default directions
Custom objectives ranking, quantile, Tweedie, Poisson losses
Large or wide data LightGBM (histograms, leaf-wise growth)
High-cardinality categoricals CatBoost (ordered target statistics)

Tuning core: learning rate + number of rounds with early stopping, max depth, row/column subsampling, L1/L2 on leaves.

stages.name: The failure asymmetry
stages.html:
"Their failure modes differ, and that matters in production."

  • Random Forest fails quietly: a few points below the best possible.
  • Boosting fails loudly: it will fit label noise, exploit a leaked feature harder, and can degrade faster under drift.
  • So a boosted model needs stricter validation (time splits, leakage audit) than a forest.

stages.name: How I actually decide
stages.html:
"Three models with defaults, one honest split, then read the gaps."

Result Read Next step
Logistic ≈ RF ≈ boosting signal is mostly linear or weak ship the simple model; work on features
RF ≫ logistic, boosting ≈ RF nonlinear, low ceiling left ship RF, skip tuning
Boosting > RF by a margin bias-limited, room at the top tune boosting, check stability
Boosting ≫ RF suspiciously possible leakage audit top features before celebrating

stages.name: What I'd pick here
stages.claim: usually boosting, with RF as the bar
stages.html:
"For most production tabular problems I ship boosting, after it beats the forest honestly."

Pick Random Forest when labels are noisy, tuning time is scarce, the team needs stable, low-maintenance models, or the accuracy gap is within noise.

followUps.question: Why not a neural network?
followUps.html: On tabular data, tree ensembles still routinely match or beat deep models, with less tuning and cost, and research on deep tabular models keeps re-finding that. I'd consider a network when there are rich unstructured inputs (text, images) alongside the table, or very large data with embeddings for high-cardinality IDs.

followUps.question: XGBoost, LightGBM or CatBoost?
followUps.html: Accuracy is usually similar after tuning. LightGBM is fastest on large, wide data because of histogram binning and leaf-wise growth, but leaf-wise trees overfit small data unless you cap leaves. CatBoost handles many categoricals natively with ordered statistics that avoid target leakage, and has good defaults. XGBoost is the mature, well-supported middle.

followUps.question: Boosting beats the forest by 8 points. Suspicious?
followUps.html: Worth auditing. Boosting exploits leaked features harder than forests do, so a big gap can be leakage amplified. Check the top features for availability at prediction time and re-score on a time-based holdout. If the gap survives, it's real bias reduction.

followUps.question: How does the number of trees behave in each?
followUps.html: In a Random Forest, more trees only reduce variance, so performance plateaus and never gets worse; it's a compute trade-off. In boosting, each tree adds fitting capacity, so too many rounds overfit. That's why boosting uses early stopping on validation loss and a small learning rate.

followUps.question: Which is easier to operate in production?
followUps.html: Random Forest: stable across retrains, fewer hyperparameters to drift, larger model files though. Boosting: smaller and faster to serve, but sensitive to tuning and data shifts, so it needs early-stopping discipline on each retrain and monitoring of feature importance stability. Both export cleanly (ONNX, Treelite).

dontSay: "XGBoost always wins." — conditions decide, and the forest is the bar.
"Random Forest is outdated." — it's the most reliable baseline in tabular ML.
"More trees in XGBoost is always better." — without early stopping it overfits.
"I'd start by tuning XGBoost." — no baseline, no idea if tuning is worth it.

spine: Consequences for tree depth and tuning
ml-dl-q11.testing: whether you can explain the mechanism, not recite "parallel vs sequential".
ml-dl-q11.trap: "bagging is parallel, boosting is sequential." That's the implementation, not why.
ml-dl-q11.spoken:
"Bagging trains many models on bootstrap samples and averages them. Averaging cancels errors that are uncorrelated between models, and variance is exactly the part of the error that changes from sample to sample. So variance falls. Bias doesn't, because every model shares the same systematic assumptions, and the average of biased models is still biased.

The variance reduction depends on how correlated the models are. Averaging n models shrinks variance roughly with n, but only the uncorrelated part. That's why Random Forest adds random feature subsets at each split: bootstrap alone leaves the trees too similar, so decorrelating them is the real lever.

Boosting works the other way. Each new learner is fitted to what the current ensemble still gets wrong: the residuals, or more generally the negative gradient of the loss. So each round corrects systematic error, and bias falls. Formally, it's gradient descent in function space, where each tree is one step.

That explains the design choices. Bagging wants deep, low-bias, high-variance trees, because it can average the variance away. Boosting wants shallow, weak learners, and since nothing cancels its variance, it needs a learning rate, subsampling and early stopping to avoid overfitting."

stages.name: Bagging averages errors
stages.claim: and variance is the averageable part
stages.html:
"Averaging removes what varies between models and keeps what they share."

  • Train each model on a bootstrap sample (sampling with replacement).
  • Each model's error = shared bias + its own sample-specific wobble (variance).
  • Averaging many wobbles that point in different directions cancels them. The shared bias survives intact.

Example: 100 deep trees each overfit different quirks of their bootstrap sample; the average keeps what they agree on, the real signal.

stages.name: Decorrelation is the real lever
stages.html:
"Averaging only helps as much as the models disagree."

For n models each with variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the variance of their average is:

Var(avg) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ² / n
  • As n grows, the second term vanishes, but ρσ² stays. Correlation sets the floor.
  • Bootstrap alone leaves trees similar (the same strong feature dominates every root split).
  • Random feature subsets per split (max_features) force trees to differ, lowering ρ. That's why max_features matters more than n_estimators.

stages.name: Boosting fits what's left
stages.html:
"Boosting is sequential because each learner depends on the ensemble's current mistakes."

  • Start with a simple prediction (the mean).
  • Compute residuals: what the ensemble still gets wrong.
  • Fit a small tree to those residuals; add a scaled version to the ensemble.
  • Repeat. Systematic error is chipped away round by round, so bias falls.

AdaBoost does the same thing by reweighting misclassified examples; gradient boosting generalises it to any differentiable loss.

stages.name: Gradient descent in function space
stages.html:
"Each tree is a step along the negative gradient of the loss, taken in the space of functions."

  • For squared loss, the negative gradient is the residual.
  • For log loss, Huber or ranking losses, fit the tree to the negative gradient (pseudo-residuals).
  • The learning rate is the step size; smaller steps + more trees generalise better.
  • XGBoost adds a second-order (Newton) step and regularises leaf weights.

stages.name: Consequences for tree depth and tuning
stages.html:
Bagging / Random Forest Boosting
Base learner deep trees (low bias, high variance) shallow trees / stumps (high bias, low variance)
Reduces variance bias
More estimators never hurts, plateaus eventually overfits
Overfitting control decorrelation (max_features) learning rate, early stopping, subsampling, depth
Label noise robust fits the noise if unchecked
Parallelism trivial within-tree only

followUps.question: Why does boosting eventually overfit if it only reduces bias?
followUps.html: Because once the systematic error is gone, the residuals are mostly noise, and each new tree fits that noise. There's no averaging to cancel it. Learning rate shrinks each step, subsampling adds randomness (a little bagging inside boosting), and early stopping on validation loss stops before the noise-fitting starts.

followUps.question: Would bagging shallow stumps work?
followUps.html: Poorly. Stumps have high bias and low variance; averaging removes variance they don't have and leaves the bias. You'd get an average of many near-identical weak models. Bagging needs high-variance base learners to have anything to average away.

followUps.question: What does subsampling do in gradient boosting?
followUps.html: Row and column subsampling per tree (stochastic gradient boosting) makes consecutive trees less correlated and injects randomness, which reduces variance, the same idea as bagging. It also speeds training. Typical values are 0.5–0.9 of rows and columns, tuned on validation.

followUps.question: Where does stacking fit?
followUps.html: Stacking trains a meta-model on the out-of-fold predictions of diverse base models. It can reduce both bias and variance, but only if the base models make different mistakes. It needs careful out-of-fold construction to avoid leakage, and the gain is often small relative to the operational cost.

followUps.question: In production, which ensemble degrades more under drift?
followUps.html: Generally boosting, because it fits fine-grained structure, including relationships that may not persist, and it exploits the strongest features hardest. Random Forest's averaging makes it more conservative. Either way, monitor feature distributions and retrain with early stopping recalibrated each time.

dontSay: "Bagging is parallel and boosting is sequential." (as the explanation) — that's how, not why.
"More trees in boosting always helps." — it overfits without early stopping.
"Bagging reduces bias too." — the average of biased models is biased.
"Random Forest is just bagging." — feature subsampling (decorrelation) is the point.
