spine: How I use them in production
ml-dl-q12.testing: the last clause. Whether you know explanation ≠ causation ≠ justification.
ml-dl-q12.trap: presenting a SHAP plot as "the drivers of churn" to a stakeholder.
ml-dl-q12.spoken:
"SHAP splits a prediction's difference from the baseline across features using Shapley values from game theory. It comes with guarantees: the attributions add up exactly to the prediction, and a feature that contributes more always gets more credit. For tree models, TreeSHAP computes it exactly and fast, which is why it dominates tabular work. Aggregating local values also gives a global view.

LIME perturbs the input around one example and fits a small interpretable model, usually sparse linear, to the black box's outputs there. It's model-agnostic and cheap, but it's unstable: the sampling and kernel width change the story, so two runs can disagree. So I default to SHAP where it's tractable and use LIME as a quick local check.

Both share a weakness: with correlated features, perturbing one feature at a time creates unrealistic inputs, and credit gets split between correlated features arbitrarily.

And what neither tells you is causality or fairness. They explain the model's function, not the world. A leaked feature or a proxy for a protected attribute shows up as 'important' with no flag that it's wrong to use. Explanation isn't justification, so a human still has to judge whether the model's reasons are acceptable reasons."

stages.name: SHAP: fair credit with guarantees
stages.html:
"SHAP answers: how much did each feature move this prediction away from the average?"

  • Based on Shapley values: a feature's credit = its average marginal contribution over all orderings of features.
  • Local accuracy: attributions sum to prediction − baseline.
  • Consistency: if a model changes so a feature contributes more, its attribution never drops.
  • TreeSHAP: exact and polynomial-time for tree ensembles. KernelSHAP for arbitrary models is slow and approximate.
  • Global view: mean |SHAP| per feature, beeswarm and dependence plots.

stages.name: LIME: a local surrogate
stages.html:
"LIME answers: what simple model mimics the black box near this one point?"

  • Perturb the instance, score the perturbations with the model, weight them by closeness.
  • Fit a sparse linear model; its coefficients are the explanation.
  • Model-agnostic, works on text and images (superpixels, words).
  • Unstable: kernel width, number of samples and random seed change the result. No consistency guarantee.

stages.name: Where each wins
stages.html:
Need Choose
Tree ensemble, tabular, need reason codes SHAP (TreeSHAP)
Global feature ranking with local detail SHAP
Quick look at one prediction from any black box LIME
Text or image, fast intuition LIME (or gradient-based methods for deep nets)
Regulated reason codes that must be reproducible SHAP, never a stochastic method

stages.name: The shared weakness: correlated features
stages.html:
"Both perturb features as if they were independent, and real features aren't."

  • Perturbing income while holding tax_paid fixed creates impossible people. The model's output on them is meaningless.
  • Credit splits arbitrarily between correlated features; one may look unimportant only because its twin took the credit.
  • Mitigation: group correlated features, use conditional/interventional SHAP deliberately, and say which one you used.

stages.name: What neither can tell you
stages.claim: causality, and whether the reason is acceptable
stages.html:
"They explain the model, not reality."

  • Not causal: "high SHAP for num_logins" means the model uses it, not that increasing logins reduces churn.
  • Not a fairness check: a zip-code feature acting as a proxy for race looks like an ordinary important feature.
  • Not a leakage detector by itself: a leaked feature appears very important, and only a human asks "should we know this at prediction time?"

That last clause is the answer the interviewer is waiting for.

stages.name: How I use them in production
stages.claim: debugging and reason codes, with review
stages.html:
• Debugging: an absurdly important feature is my first leakage suspect.
  • Reason codes: top SHAP contributions per decision, for customer or regulator explanations.
  • Monitoring: track global SHAP importance over time; a shift signals drift or a pipeline change.
  • Governance: a human reviews whether the top reasons are legitimate to use.

followUps.question: SHAP vs permutation importance?
followUps.html: Permutation importance measures how much a metric drops when a feature is shuffled: global, model-agnostic, tied to performance. SHAP attributes individual predictions and aggregates up. Both suffer with correlated features. Permutation importance on validation data is a good sanity check; impurity-based importance from trees is biased toward high-cardinality features.

followUps.question: The business wants "the drivers of churn" from your SHAP plot. Response?
followUps.html: I'd say the plot shows what the model relies on, which is correlational. To claim a driver, we need a causal design: an experiment, or at minimum causal-inference methods with stated assumptions. I'd offer SHAP as hypothesis generation and propose an A/B test on the most actionable feature.

followUps.question: Why are LIME explanations unstable, concretely?
followUps.html: They depend on random perturbation samples, the kernel width that defines "local", and the choice of surrogate complexity. Change any of them and a different sparse linear model fits best. You can reduce it with more samples and fixed seeds, but there's no guarantee two reasonable settings agree.

followUps.question: How would you explain a deep network's prediction?
followUps.html: For deep nets, gradient-based attributions like Integrated Gradients are the usual choice; DeepSHAP approximates Shapley values. For transformers, attention weights are not reliable explanations on their own. Whatever the method, validate it: remove the top-attributed features and check that the prediction actually changes.

followUps.question: Can explanations be gamed?
followUps.html: Yes. Because perturbation-based explainers query off-manifold points, a model can be built to behave innocently on those points while discriminating on real data, and LIME or KernelSHAP will report the innocent behaviour. That's why explanations support governance but don't replace fairness testing on real outcomes by group.

dontSay: "SHAP shows the causes of the outcome." — it shows the model's reliance, not causation.
"LIME and SHAP give the same answer." — LIME is unstable and has no consistency guarantee.
"Feature importance proves the model is fair." — proxies look like ordinary features.
"Attention weights explain the model." — not reliable on their own.

ml-dl-q13.testing: whether you design against train–serve skew structurally, not by being careful.
ml-dl-q13.trap: a "small" reimplementation of the feature in the serving service.
ml-dl-q13.spoken:
"The enemy is train–serve skew: training features computed in warehouse SQL, serving features in application code. Two implementations always drift, and the model degrades silently.

So the design goal is one feature definition, materialised twice. A feature store gives you that: an offline store for training and an online store, a low-latency key-value store, serving the same definitions at request time, kept in sync by one pipeline.

The offline side must be point-in-time correct: each training example gets feature values as they were at that example's timestamp, not as they are today. Otherwise you train on the future.

Stateless preprocessing, like scaling, encoding and imputation, ships inside the model artefact as a pipeline object, so the service can't reimplement it.

The model and its feature versions are deployed and rolled back together, behind a prediction service with a validated input schema.

And I'd still detect skew: log the features actually served, replay them offline, and compare distributions.

I'd also challenge the serving need. For something like churn, nightly batch scoring into a table removes the online path, and most of the skew risk, entirely."

stages.name: Name the enemy: skew
stages.claim: two code paths, one feature name
stages.html:
"Skew happens whenever the same feature is computed by two different pieces of code."

Where it hides Example
Defaults SQL treats null as 0; service drops the row
Time UTC in the warehouse, local time in the service
Windows "last 30 days" inclusive vs exclusive of today
Availability feature exists in the warehouse but not at request time, so it's defaulted
Library versions tokenizer or encoder changed on one side

It doesn't raise errors. It shows up as a model that's "worse in production".

stages.name: One definition, two materialisations
stages.html:
"Write each feature once; let the platform compute it for both paths."

            feature definition (one place)
                 │                 │
          batch pipeline     streaming / on-demand
             │        │              │
     offline store   online store ◀──┘
  (point-in-time,    (low latency,
    for training)      for serving)
             │              │
         training     prediction service

Feast and Tecton implement this; the pattern matters more than the product.

stages.name: Point-in-time correctness
stages.claim: features as they were at the event
stages.html:
"Training joins must use feature values as of each label's timestamp."

  • A naive join attaches today's value of lifetime_spend to an event from last March. That's future leakage.
  • Offline stores do an as-of join: for each event, take the latest feature value with timestamp ≤ event time.
  • Also account for feature latency: if a feature lands in the online store with a 2-hour delay, the offline join should apply the same delay.

stages.name: Ship preprocessing with the model
stages.html:
"Anything stateless travels inside the artefact."

  • sklearn Pipeline / ColumnTransformer, or preprocessing layers exported with the model.
  • The service passes raw inputs; the artefact applies the exact fitted transforms.
  • Same for tokenizers in NLP: version-pinned and bundled.

stages.name: Version together, roll back together
stages.html:
"A model trained on feature set v3 must never be served v4."

  • Model registry entry records the feature definitions and versions it was trained on.
  • Prediction service validates the input schema (types, ranges, required fields).
  • Deploy and roll back model + feature versions as one unit.

stages.name: Detect it anyway
stages.html:
"Design reduces skew; monitoring catches what design missed."

  • Log served feature vectors with the model version.
  • Nightly: compare served distributions and null rates with the training profile (PSI/KS).
  • Periodically replay logged requests through the offline pipeline and diff feature values row by row.

followUps.question: You don't have a feature store and can't buy one.
followUps.html: Share one computation library, or a dbt layer, imported by both the training job and the service, so there's one definition. Or use "log and wait": have the service compute and log features, and train on those logs, which makes training and serving identical by construction at the cost of waiting to accumulate data.

followUps.question: Batch or online scoring for churn?
followUps.html: Batch. Churn decisions are daily or weekly, so a nightly job scoring everyone into a table is enough. It uses one pipeline for training and scoring, so skew almost disappears, and it's cheaper and easier to monitor. Online only makes sense if the intervention happens in-session, like a save offer in the cancellation flow.

followUps.question: How do you handle a feature that needs to be fresh within seconds?
followUps.html: Compute it as a streaming aggregation (Flink, Kafka Streams, or the feature store's streaming path) writing to the online store, and backfill the same logic offline for training. The hard part is proving the streaming and batch versions agree; test them on the same event log.

followUps.question: How do you know skew is the cause of a production drop?
followUps.html: Replay. Take served requests with their logged features, recompute features offline for the same entities and timestamps, and compare. If features differ, it's skew; if they match but distributions differ from training, it's drift; if both match, the offline evaluation was optimistic.

followUps.question: What does a feature store cost you?
followUps.html: Operational complexity: another system to run, materialisation jobs, online-store latency and cost, and a learning curve. For a single batch model it's overkill; for many models sharing real-time features it pays for itself. I'd adopt it when skew or duplicated feature work is a demonstrated cost, not by default.

dontSay: "We'll just reimplement the feature carefully in the service." — two implementations always diverge.
"Join the latest feature values to the training labels." — future leakage.
"A feature store solves skew automatically." — only if every feature goes through it and joins are point-in-time.
"We need real-time serving." (without checking) — often batch is enough.

ml-dl-q14.testing: whether you treat drift as an operational decision loop, not "retrain nightly".
ml-dl-q14.trap: a nightly retrain cron as the answer to drift.
ml-dl-q14.spoken:
"I'd treat it as a decision loop with four questions.

First, is the drop real? Are labels complete, or is the most recent period still waiting on delayed labels? Is the metric computed the same way, on the same population?

Second, is it drift at all, or an impostor? A pipeline break, a schema change upstream, a new client version or a product change all produce the same symptom, and retraining would just bake them in. I'd check feature null rates and value ranges and line changes up against deploys.

Third, which drift? Covariate shift, where the input mix moved; label shift, where the base rate moved; or concept drift, where the relationship between inputs and outcome changed. Input and prediction drift are visible without labels through PSI or KS per feature; concept drift needs labels.

Fourth, where? Slice by segment, because a 6-point average drop is often a 20-point drop in one segment.

Then the response: retraining on recent data fixes covariate and label shift; concept drift may need new features or a rethink. Every retrain goes through the same offline gate and canary as a new model.

And I'd run this as a loop with time-to-detect and time-to-recover as SLOs."

stages.name: Is it real?
stages.html:
"Before diagnosing the model, I check the measurement."

  • Label delay: if outcomes take weeks to arrive, the latest period looks worse (or better) until labels land.
  • Metric definition: same metric, same threshold, same filters as before?
  • Population: did a new market, client or acquisition channel change who's being scored?
  • Noise: is 6 points outside normal week-to-week variation? Look at the confidence interval.

stages.name: Rule out the impostors
stages.html:
"Retraining on a broken pipeline trains the model on the bug."

Impostor Signature
Upstream schema/unit change step change in one feature, aligned with a deploy
Broken join / missing source null rate jumps; defaults flood in
New client/app version a segment's features change shape overnight
Product or pricing change behaviour changed on purpose; the model needs to be told
Train–serve skew served features differ from recomputed offline features

Abrupt + local = break. Gradual + broad = drift.

stages.name: Classify the drift
stages.html:
"Three different things can move, with different detection and different fixes."

Type What moved Detect Retraining fixes it?
Covariate shift P(X): input mix PSI/KS per feature, no labels needed usually yes
Label shift P(y): base rate predicted vs observed positive rate yes, plus recalibration
Concept drift P(y|X): the relationship rolling metrics once labels arrive maybe not; may need new features

Example: after a pricing change, users with the same activity churn at a different rate. That's concept drift; retraining on old data won't capture it until enough post-change labels exist.

stages.name: Localise it
stages.html:
"Aggregate metrics hide localised rot."

  • Slice by segment: region, device, customer tier, acquisition channel, tenure.
  • Find which features drifted most (PSI ranking) and which segments lost most.
  • Often a single segment explains most of the drop, and the fix is targeted.

stages.name: Decide the response
stages.claim: match the fix to the cause
stages.html:
Diagnosis Response
Pipeline break fix the pipeline; don't retrain
Covariate or label shift retrain on recent data; recalibrate
Concept drift new features, new label definition, or model redesign; short-term, retrain on post-change data
One segment segment-specific model or features; or route that segment to a fallback
Within noise watch; no action

stages.name: Retrain through a gate
stages.html:
"A retrained model is a new model and goes through the same checks."

  • Offline gate: beats the incumbent on a recent time-ordered holdout, per segment.
  • Shadow or canary on live traffic before full rollout.
  • Trigger options: scheduled (simple), drift/metric-triggered (responsive, needs good monitors), continual (rarely worth the validation risk).

stages.name: Run it as a loop
stages.html:
"Drift response is an operational loop, not an event."

  • Monitor labels-free signals (feature PSI, prediction distribution) daily; delayed-label metrics as they land.
  • Define time-to-detect and time-to-recover as SLOs.
  • Keep a runbook: check impostors → classify → localise → respond → gate.

followUps.question: Why not just retrain every night?
followUps.html: It doesn't fix pipeline breaks or concept drift without new features, it can quietly ship a regression if there's no gate, and it hides the diagnosis, so you never learn why performance moves. Scheduled retraining is fine as a baseline cadence, but each retrain still needs evaluation and a canary.

followUps.question: PSI says a feature drifted but performance is fine. Act?
followUps.html: Not necessarily. Drift in an unimportant feature, or drift the model handles well, doesn't need action. Weight drift alerts by feature importance, and alert on prediction drift and performance, not raw PSI alone. Otherwise the alerts become noise and get ignored.

followUps.question: Labels arrive 60 days late. How do you detect problems sooner?
followUps.html: Use label-free proxies: feature drift, prediction distribution shift, and calibration against any early signal. Build a short-horizon proxy label that correlates with the real one (7-day engagement for 60-day churn) and monitor that. And track business metrics that react faster than the label.

followUps.question: How much recent data should the retrain use?
followUps.html: Trade freshness against sample size. Compare training windows (last 3, 6, 12 months) on a recent holdout, or weight recent data more heavily. After concept drift, pre-change data can actively hurt, so a shorter window wins once there are enough post-change labels.

followUps.question: Who owns this loop?
followUps.html: The team that owns the model owns detection and response, with on-call like any service. Upstream data owners sign data contracts (schema, freshness, ranges), so breaks are caught at the source. Without clear ownership, drift alerts get routed nowhere and time-to-recover is measured in months.

dontSay: "Set up a nightly retrain." — not a framework; it can ship regressions and hides causes.
"It's concept drift." (without evidence) — check impostors and label delay first.
"Retraining will fix it." — not for pipeline breaks, and not reliably for concept drift.
"Monitor accuracy." — labels may be late; you need label-free signals too.

spine: Suspect the label in the feature
Why high cardinality makes it worse
ml-dl-q15.testing: whether a suspiciously good result triggers an audit, not a celebration.
ml-dl-q15.spoken:
"Target encoding replaces each category with a statistic of the target itself, usually its mean. So if a row's own label contributed to its encoding, that feature partly is the answer, and a big AUC jump is often self-leakage rather than signal.

High cardinality makes it worse. With 5,000 levels, many appear only a handful of times, and a level seen once is encoded as exactly that row's label.

To test it, I'd check how the encoding was computed: if it was fit on the full training set, or before the CV split, the validation score is contaminated. I'd recompute it honestly and re-score, ideally on a time-ordered holdout, because random CV is exactly where this failure hides.

The safe construction is out-of-fold encoding: each row is encoded using statistics from folds it isn't in, computed strictly inside each training fold. Rare levels get smoothing toward the global mean, weighted by how often the level appears, and unseen levels at serving time fall back to the prior.

Then I'd compare against leak-free alternatives: frequency encoding, feature hashing, or CatBoost's ordered target statistics.

If the jump survives an honest time-split evaluation, I'll believe it."

stages.name: Suspect the label in the feature
stages.html:
"A feature built from the target is guilty until proven innocent."

  • Target encoding: city → mean(churned) for that city.
  • If computed using all rows, row i's encoding includes row i's own label.
  • The model learns "encoding high → label 1" partly because the encoding was made from the label.

stages.name: Why high cardinality makes it worse
stages.html:
"With 5,000 levels, most have few rows, and few rows means the encoding is the label."

Level count Encoding without smoothing
1 row exactly that row's label (0 or 1)
3 rows mean of 3 labels, heavily includes this row
10,000 rows stable; self-contribution negligible

The long tail of rare levels produces near-perfect separation on training data and nothing at serving time.

stages.name: Test it honestly
stages.html:
"I don't argue about it. I rebuild it properly and see if the jump survives."

  • Was the encoder fit before the split, or on the full training set outside CV? Then validation is contaminated.
  • Put the encoder inside the pipeline, fitted per fold, and re-score.
  • Re-score on a time-ordered holdout; random CV hides encoding leakage because the same levels and labels sit on both sides.
  • Compare to the same model with frequency encoding. A large gap that collapses under honest evaluation was leakage.

stages.name: Encode safely
stages.html:
"Each row's encoding must come from rows that aren't it, and from training data only."

Out-of-fold encoding. Split training data into k parts; encode each part using statistics from the other k−1. Default choice.

Leave-one-out. Encode each row with the level mean excluding itself. Cheaper but can still leak through the row's own absence; add noise.

  • Nest it: inside each CV training fold, run the out-of-fold encoding again. The validation fold is encoded with the full training fold's statistics.
  • sklearn's TargetEncoder (1.3+) does internal cross-fitting for fit_transform.

stages.name: Handle rare and unseen levels
stages.html:
"Rare levels shrink toward the global mean; unseen levels get the prior."

encoded = (n · level_mean + m · global_mean) / (n + m)
  • n = rows for the level, m = smoothing strength (tuned on validation).
  • Unseen at serving: use the global mean, or a parent-level mean if a hierarchy exists (city → region).
  • Optional Gaussian noise on training encodings adds regularisation.

stages.name: Compare the leak-free alternatives
stages.html:
Option Trade-off
Frequency / count encoding no leakage; captures popularity only
Feature hashing bounded width; collisions are a controlled cost
CatBoost ordered target statistics target encoding done safely by design
Entity embeddings good in neural models; need data per level
Group rare levels into "other" simple; loses tail information

followUps.question: Why doesn't random CV catch this?
followUps.html: If the encoder is fit before CV, every fold's validation rows helped create the encoding. Even if it's fit per fold, random splits put the same levels with similar label patterns on both sides, so memorised level effects look like generalisation. A time split shows whether level effects persist into the future.

followUps.question: Why not one-hot the 5,000 levels?
followUps.html: 5,000 sparse columns inflate memory and training time, and most columns are nearly empty, so linear models overfit rare levels and trees struggle to split on them. It also breaks at serving time when new levels appear. For trees, one-hot on high cardinality is usually the worst option.

followUps.question: How does CatBoost avoid this leakage?
followUps.html: Ordered target statistics: it processes rows in a random permutation and encodes each row using only the rows before it in that order, so a row never sees its own label. Multiple permutations reduce the variance this introduces. It's out-of-fold encoding taken to the limit.

followUps.question: The honest AUC is still higher than without the feature. Ship?
followUps.html: Then the category has real signal, so yes, with conditions: smoothing tuned on validation, a fallback for unseen levels, and monitoring of the share of unseen levels in production. If new levels arrive constantly (new merchants, new devices), the feature's value will decay, so watch it.

followUps.question: How would you catch this class of bug in review?
followUps.html: Any feature derived from the target is flagged in model review and must be computed inside the per-fold pipeline. Add a standard check: train with and without the suspect feature on a time-split holdout. And treat any single feature change that moves AUC by several points as a leakage suspect until audited.

dontSay: "Great, target encoding really helped." — without an honest re-score, you don't know.
"I fit the encoder on the whole training set, then ran CV." — that's the leak.
"Rare levels are fine, the model will handle it." — rare levels encode their own labels.
"Unseen categories won't happen." — they always do in production.

spine: Offline data is biased by the old policy
ml-dl-q16.testing: whether you understand that logged data isn't a neutral test set for a ranking system.
ml-dl-q16.trap: trusting an offline ranking metric as the launch decision.
ml-dl-q16.spoken:
"Offline-up, online-down is expected in recommenders, and there are three classic mechanisms.

First, feedback-loop bias. The offline data was logged under the old model: users only clicked on what the old model showed. Items it never showed have no labels. So offline evaluation rewards agreeing with the old model more than being right, and a genuinely different ranker can look worse, or a subtly worse one better.

Second, position bias. Clicks in logs are inflated for items that were shown near the top, regardless of relevance. NDCG on those clicks treats them as pure relevance. When the new model reshuffles positions, it loses that borrowed advantage.

Third, diversity collapse. NDCG scores each list independently. A model that maximises it can converge on similar popular items. Users get staler, more repetitive feeds, and click less over a session, which per-query metrics can't see.

I'd also rule out the boring causes: train–serve skew in features, a latency regression that cut impressions, or a population mismatch between offline and online.

The rule is that offline metrics gate a launch and the online A/B decides it. Long term, I'd log propensities, the probability each item was shown, so offline evaluation can be corrected counterfactually."

stages.name: Offline data is biased by the old policy
stages.claim: you can only grade what was shown
stages.html:
"Logged data records the old model's choices, not the world."

  • Users click only among items the old model displayed.
  • Items the new model wants to show but the old model never did have no labels, so they count as irrelevant offline.
  • Offline evaluation therefore favours rankers that imitate the old one. This is the off-policy evaluation problem.

Example: a new model that surfaces fresh long-tail content scores poorly offline because the logs contain no clicks on it.

stages.name: Position bias
stages.claim: clicks measure rank, not just relevance
stages.html:
"Rank 1 gets clicks because it's rank 1."

  • Click-through falls sharply with position regardless of quality.
  • Logged clicks at high positions overstate relevance; NDCG treats them as ground truth.
  • The new model moves items; those items lose the positional boost they had in the logs.
  • Fix direction: estimate position propensities and reweight clicks (inverse propensity scoring), or use randomised position experiments to measure the bias.

stages.name: Diversity collapse
stages.html:
"NDCG rewards each list; users experience the feed."

  • Optimising per-query relevance can concentrate on popular, near-duplicate items.
  • Users see repetition, get bored, and click less across the session.
  • Novelty, coverage and diversity metrics, plus session-level engagement, catch it; NDCG doesn't.

stages.name: Rule out the boring causes
stages.html:
Check Why
Train–serve skew online features differ from offline replay
Latency regression slower ranking → fewer impressions → lower CTR
Population mismatch offline NDCG on all users; CTR dominated by heavy users
Candidate generation online candidate set differs from what offline ranked
Metric definition CTR counted differently after the deploy

stages.name: Let the A/B decide
stages.html:
"Offline metrics are a filter, never a verdict."

  • A/B test on the business metric (CTR, engagement, retention), long enough to see novelty effects fade.
  • Interleaving (mix results from both rankers in one list) detects preference with far less traffic, useful for comparing many candidates.
  • Guardrail metrics: latency, diversity, revenue.

stages.name: Fix the evaluation loop
stages.html:
"Log what you need for counterfactual evaluation."

  • Log propensities: the probability each item was shown at each position.
  • Use IPS / doubly robust estimators to evaluate new policies offline.
  • Reserve a small exploration slice (randomised items) so logs contain data outside the current policy.
  • Track diversity and coverage alongside NDCG.

followUps.question: How does inverse propensity scoring work here?
followUps.html: Each logged click is weighted by 1 / (probability the item was shown at that position under the logging policy). Rarely shown items get large weights, correcting for the fact they had few chances to be clicked. It's unbiased in expectation but high-variance, so clip the weights or use doubly robust estimators.

followUps.question: CTR dropped but time-on-site rose. Did the model fail?
followUps.html: Not necessarily. Fewer, better clicks can mean users found what they wanted faster or engaged more deeply. CTR may be the wrong north-star metric. I'd check downstream metrics (conversions, retention, dwell time) and agree with product which metric the ranker should serve.

followUps.question: Why not just train on more logged data to fix it?
followUps.html: More logged data from the same policy carries the same bias, so the model learns to imitate the old ranker even more closely. You need data outside the current policy: exploration traffic, randomisation, or counterfactual reweighting.

followUps.question: How long should the A/B test run?
followUps.html: Long enough to reach statistical power on the primary metric and to see past novelty or primacy effects, usually at least one to two full weekly cycles. Check the effect over time; a gain that decays after a week was novelty. Pre-register the metric and duration to avoid peeking.

followUps.question: How do you add diversity without hurting relevance too much?
followUps.html: Re-rank the top candidates with a diversity-aware step, such as maximal marginal relevance or determinantal point processes, trading a little per-item relevance for coverage. Tune the trade-off with online tests, since the right balance depends on how users react, not on offline NDCG.

dontSay: "NDCG went up, so the model is better." — offline data is biased toward the old policy.
"Users are being irrational." — position and presentation effects are predictable.
"Retrain on more click logs." — same bias, more of it.
"Offline metrics should decide launches." — they gate; A/B decides.

ml-dl-q17.testing: whether you say "chain rule" and "reuse" in the same breath.
ml-dl-q17.trap: "the error propagates backwards through the network" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q17.spoken:
"Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to a computation graph, run in reverse, with the intermediate results reused.

A network is a chain of simple operations, each of which knows its own local derivative. In the forward pass, I compute the output and the loss, and cache every intermediate activation.

In the backward pass, I start from the loss and walk the graph in reverse. Each operation receives the gradient of the loss with respect to its output, multiplies it by its local derivative, and passes the result to its inputs. When I reach a weight, that product is the weight's gradient.

It's dynamic programming: each upstream gradient is computed once and reused by everything below it. That's why one backward sweep gives the gradient for every parameter at roughly the cost of two forward passes, no matter how many parameters there are.

Two clarifications. Backprop only computes gradients; the optimiser, like SGD or Adam, decides how to update. And because the forward activations must be kept for the backward pass, activations, not weights, dominate training memory, which is what gradient checkpointing trades back for recompute."

stages.name: Chain rule over a graph
stages.html:
"A network is a composition of functions; its derivative is a product of local derivatives."

x ──W1──▶ h = σ(W1·x) ──W2──▶ ŷ ──▶ L(ŷ, y)

∂L/∂W1 = ∂L/∂ŷ · ∂ŷ/∂h · ∂h/∂W1

Every operation (matmul, add, ReLU, softmax) implements two things: forward, and "given dL/d(output), return dL/d(inputs)".

stages.name: Forward pass caches
stages.claim: keep what the backward pass will need
stages.html:
"The forward pass computes the loss and stores every intermediate value."

  • Local derivatives depend on forward values: ReLU needs to know which inputs were positive; matmul needs the input activations.
  • So activations are cached per layer, per example in the batch.

stages.name: Backward pass reuses
stages.html:
"Walk the graph in reverse; each node multiplies and passes down."

  • Start with ∂L/∂L = 1.
  • Each node: receive upstream gradient → multiply by its local Jacobian → send to its inputs.
  • Where a value feeds several nodes, gradients from each path are summed.
  • At a parameter, the arriving gradient is ∂L/∂θ.

stages.name: Why it's cheap
stages.html:
"One backward sweep yields every parameter's gradient."

Mode Cost for gradient of one scalar loss w.r.t. n parameters
Finite differences n+1 forward passes
Forward-mode autodiff ~n passes (one per input direction)
Reverse-mode (backprop) ~2–3× one forward pass, independent of n

This is memoisation: each intermediate gradient is computed once and shared.

stages.name: What it isn't
stages.html:
"Backprop computes gradients. The optimiser uses them."

  • SGD, Momentum, Adam and AdamW are separate, swappable components.
  • Backprop also doesn't guarantee good gradients: vanishing and exploding gradients are properties of the network, which backprop faithfully computes.

stages.name: The memory consequence
stages.html:
"Training memory is mostly cached activations, which is why batch size and sequence length drive it."

  • Activation memory grows with batch × sequence length × depth × width.
  • Gradient (activation) checkpointing: store only some activations, recompute the rest during the backward pass. Trades compute for memory.
  • Inference needs no cache for gradients, which is why inference fits where training doesn't.

followUps.question: Why do activations dominate training memory?
followUps.html: Because the backward pass needs forward values to compute local derivatives, so every layer's activations are stored for the whole batch until the backward pass reaches them. Weights are stored once; activations scale with batch size and sequence length. Checkpointing recomputes activations instead of storing them.

followUps.question: Why reverse mode and not forward mode?
followUps.html: Neural networks have millions of parameters and one scalar loss. Reverse mode costs one sweep per output, so one sweep total. Forward mode costs one sweep per input direction, so millions. Forward mode wins only when there are few inputs and many outputs.

followUps.question: What happens to the gradient at a ReLU?
followUps.html: It passes through unchanged where the input was positive and becomes zero where it was negative. At exactly zero the derivative is undefined, and frameworks pick 0 by convention. Units that are always negative get zero gradient forever: dead ReLUs.

followUps.question: Is backprop how the brain learns?
followUps.html: Probably not directly; it needs symmetric backward weights and a separate backward phase, which biology doesn't obviously have. But that's irrelevant to engineering: backprop is an exact, efficient algorithm for computing gradients of a differentiable program.

followUps.question: How does autograd in PyTorch implement this?
followUps.html: The forward pass records a dynamic graph of operations with saved tensors. loss.backward() traverses it in reverse topological order, calling each op's backward function and accumulating gradients into .grad. That's why you zero gradients between steps and why in-place ops on saved tensors raise errors.

dontSay: "The error flows back through the network." (alone) — no mechanism.
"Backprop is how the network learns." — it computes gradients; the optimiser learns.
"It's expensive because it computes each gradient separately." — the point is reuse.
"Weights take most of the training memory." — activations do.

ml-dl-q18.testing: whether you can derive the mechanism from the chain rule, not just name it.
ml-dl-q18.spoken:
"That's vanishing gradients, and it falls straight out of backprop.

The gradient reaching layer 1 is a product of one factor per layer above it: the layer's weights times the activation's derivative. The sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, and much smaller when the unit saturates. Multiply twelve of those together and the gradient at the bottom is orders of magnitude smaller than at the top. So the last layers learn and the first barely move. The same product explodes if the weight scales sit above one; vanishing and exploding are two ends of one mechanism.

I'd confirm it by logging per-layer gradient norms: a clean exponential decay toward the input is the signature.

Then the fixes, in the order I'd try them. One: switch to ReLU-family activations, whose derivative is 1 in the positive region, so they don't shrink the signal. Two: use variance-preserving initialisation, He for ReLU, so activations and gradients keep their scale across depth. Three: add normalisation layers to keep activations in a healthy range. And for real depth, residual connections, which give the gradient an identity path around each layer.

Raising the learning rate doesn't fix it; it just destabilises the top layers."

stages.name: Name it: vanishing gradients
stages.html:
"Symptom pattern: last layers' weights change, first layers' weights stay near their initial values."

  • Loss decreases slowly and plateaus early.
  • Early layers act like fixed random features.
  • Common with sigmoid or tanh in deep plain stacks.

stages.name: The multiplicative mechanism
stages.html:
"The gradient at layer 1 multiplies one Jacobian per layer above it."

∂L/∂h1 = ∂L/∂h12 · Π (k=2..12) [ W_k · σ'(z_k) ]

σ'(z) ≤ 0.25   →   0.25^11 ≈ 2.4 × 10⁻⁷   (before weights)
  • Saturated sigmoids (|z| large) have σ' ≈ 0, making it worse.
  • If ‖W · σ'‖ > 1 per layer, the product explodes instead.
  • The underlying quantity is the spectral radius of the layer Jacobians.

stages.name: Confirm with per-layer gradient norms
stages.html:
"Log the gradient norm of each layer's weights for a few steps."

Pattern Diagnosis
Exponential decay toward input vanishing gradients
Exponential growth, NaNs, loss spikes exploding gradients
Uniform but tiny everywhere learning rate or loss scaling issue
One layer near zero dead units or a bug in that layer

Also check activation statistics: sigmoid outputs pinned near 0 or 1 = saturation.

stages.name: Fix: activations, init, normalisation, residuals
stages.html:
Fix 1 — ReLU-family activations. Derivative is 1 for positive inputs, so no per-layer shrink. Leaky ReLU or GELU avoid dead units. Cheapest, try first.

Fix 2 — Variance-preserving initialisation. He init (variance 2/fan_in) for ReLU, Xavier for tanh. Keeps signal and gradient scale stable at the start. Needed with any activation.

Fix 3 — Normalisation. BatchNorm or LayerNorm keeps pre-activations centred and scaled, so units don't saturate. Also stabilises and speeds training.

Fix 4 — Residual connections. h = x + f(x) gives the gradient a direct identity path around every block. What made truly deep networks trainable.

Gradient clipping helps the exploding case, not vanishing.

stages.name: Verify
stages.html:
"After the fix, per-layer gradient norms should be within an order of magnitude of each other, and the first layers' weights should move."

Re-run the same logging; compare training curves; check that early-layer weights change meaningfully across epochs.

followUps.question: Which fix made truly deep networks possible?
followUps.html: Residual connections. With h = x + f(x), the Jacobian of each block is I + ∂f/∂x, so even if ∂f/∂x is small, the identity term carries the gradient through. That's what let networks go from tens to hundreds of layers, and it's the backbone of every transformer.

followUps.question: Why not just increase the learning rate for early layers?
followUps.html: The ratio between layers can be 10⁶ or more and changes during training, so a fixed per-layer rate can't track it, and a large global rate destabilises the top layers. Adaptive optimisers like Adam partly normalise per-parameter scale, which helps, but they don't fix the signal loss in the forward pass. Fix the architecture.

followUps.question: Does ReLU have its own failure mode?
followUps.html: Yes, dead ReLUs: a unit whose input is always negative outputs zero with zero gradient, so it never recovers. Causes include a high learning rate or poor init. Leaky ReLU, GELU or careful init reduce it. Monitor the fraction of units that never activate.

followUps.question: How does this relate to RNNs forgetting long sequences?
followUps.html: Same mechanism, worse. Backprop through time multiplies the same recurrent Jacobian once per time step, so over 500 steps the product vanishes or explodes even faster than across 12 different layers. LSTMs add an additive cell path for the same reason residuals help MLPs.

followUps.question: Where does BatchNorm cause problems?
followUps.html: Small batches (noisy statistics), sequence models with variable lengths, and train/inference mismatch if running statistics are wrong or eval mode isn't set. That's why transformers use LayerNorm, which normalises per example and doesn't depend on the batch.

dontSay: "The learning rate is too low." — the ratio between layers is the problem, not the global scale.
"Add more layers so it learns better." — deepens the product that's vanishing.
"Use gradient clipping." — that's for exploding gradients.
"Sigmoid is fine if you train longer." — the early layers' signal is gone, not slow.

ml-dl-q19.testing: whether you can give the mechanism, not "it just works better".
ml-dl-q19.trap: "cross-entropy is for classification, MSE is for regression" with no reason.
ml-dl-q19.spoken:
"Two reasons: one statistical, one about gradients.

The statistical reason: a classifier outputs a probability distribution, and cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the true label under that distribution. Minimising it is maximum-likelihood estimation for a Bernoulli or categorical model, the principled loss for probability outputs.

The gradient reason is the one interviewers want. Take a sigmoid output p. With MSE, the gradient with respect to the logit is (p − y) times σ'(z). That σ' term goes to zero when the sigmoid saturates, which happens exactly when the model is confidently wrong: say it predicts 0.001 for a true positive. The error is huge, but the gradient is tiny, so learning stalls.

With cross-entropy, the σ' cancels, and the gradient with respect to the logit is simply p − y. Big error, big step. The same holds for softmax with categorical cross-entropy.

Cross-entropy also punishes confident wrong answers heavily, because log p goes to minus infinity, which is the behaviour you want.

The practical corollary: use the fused, numerically stable loss that takes logits, like BCEWithLogitsLoss or CrossEntropyLoss, never a hand-written log of a softmax."

stages.name: The principled reason: maximum likelihood
stages.html:
"Cross-entropy is what you get when you ask for the most likely parameters."

  • Binary: L = −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)], the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli.
  • Multiclass: L = −log p_true, the NLL of a categorical.
  • Equivalent to minimising KL divergence from the label distribution to the model's.
  • MSE is the NLL of a Gaussian, the right assumption for continuous targets, not labels.

stages.name: The gradient mechanism
stages.html:
"Differentiate both through the sigmoid and look at what's left."

p = σ(z)

MSE:  L = ½(p − y)²          ∂L/∂z = (p − y) · σ'(z)
CE:   L = −y log p − ...     ∂L/∂z = (p − y)

The σ'(z) = p(1−p) factor is what MSE keeps and cross-entropy cancels.

stages.name: Where MSE stalls
stages.html:
Case p y MSE ∂L/∂z CE ∂L/∂z
Confidently wrong 0.001 1 ≈ −0.999 × 0.001 ≈ −0.001 −0.999
Unsure 0.5 1 −0.5 × 0.25 = −0.125 −0.5
Confidently right 0.999 1 ≈ 0 ≈ −0.001

The worst mistakes get the weakest correction under MSE. That's the killer argument.

stages.name: Landscape and penalties
stages.html:
• For logistic regression, CE is convex in the weights; MSE through a sigmoid is not, with flat plateaus.
  • CE's penalty grows without bound as p → 0 for the true class, so confident errors dominate the loss.
  • MSE caps the per-example loss at 1, treating a confident error almost like an unsure one.

stages.name: The practical corollary
stages.html:
"Pass logits to the fused loss; never compute log(softmax(x)) by hand."

  • BCEWithLogitsLoss, CrossEntropyLoss (PyTorch) use the log-sum-exp trick internally.
  • Hand-composed log(softmax) underflows to log(0) = −inf for large logits.
  • Label smoothing is a small, useful modification when models become overconfident.

followUps.question: Is MSE ever acceptable for classification?
followUps.html: It can work, especially with a linear output and well-scaled targets, and some work has shown MSE competitive in certain settings. But it loses the likelihood interpretation and the clean gradient, and it tends to produce poorly calibrated probabilities. Cross-entropy is the default for good reasons; use MSE only with evidence.

followUps.question: What does label smoothing do to cross-entropy?
followUps.html: It replaces one-hot targets with (1−ε) on the true class and ε spread over the others. The model stops pushing logits to infinity for the true class, which reduces overconfidence and often improves calibration and generalisation. The cost: the model's probabilities no longer target the true frequencies exactly.

followUps.question: Why is log(softmax) numerically dangerous?
followUps.html: Softmax of large logits overflows (exp(1000)), and for very negative logits it underflows to 0, so the log becomes −inf and the gradient NaN. The log-sum-exp trick subtracts the max logit first and computes log-softmax directly, which fused losses do for you.

followUps.question: Cross-entropy with severe class imbalance?
followUps.html: Plain CE is dominated by the majority class. Options: class-weighted CE, or focal loss, which down-weights easy, well-classified examples so training focuses on hard ones. Both distort probabilities, so recalibrate if scores are used as probabilities.

followUps.question: How does this connect to LLM training?
followUps.html: LLMs are trained with next-token cross-entropy over the vocabulary: the NLL of the true next token. Perplexity is just exp of the average cross-entropy. The same gradient property, p − y at the logits, is why that objective trains stably at scale.

followUps.question: Why not train directly on accuracy, since that's what we report?
followUps.html: Accuracy is a step function of the parameters: small weight changes usually don't flip any prediction, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the flips. Gradient descent can't use it. Cross-entropy is a smooth, differentiable surrogate that also rewards confidence in the right answer. Report accuracy, optimise cross-entropy.

dontSay: "Cross-entropy just works better." — no mechanism.
"MSE is for regression, CE for classification, that's the rule." — a rule, not a reason.
"I compute softmax then take the log." — numerically unstable.
"The two losses give the same gradients." — MSE carries σ', CE doesn't.

spine: The layer collapses to one neuron
ml-dl-q20.testing: whether you separate breaking symmetry, setting scale, and determinism.
ml-dl-q20.trap: confusing reproducibility with a constant initial value.
ml-dl-q20.spoken:
"The network won't learn anything useful, because of symmetry.

If every weight in a layer starts at zero, every neuron in that layer computes the same output and receives exactly the same gradient. They update identically, so they stay identical forever. A layer of 512 units behaves like a single unit repeated 512 times. With ReLU it's even worse: zero inputs give zero outputs and zero gradients, so nothing moves. Any constant has the symmetry problem, not just zero.

Random initialisation breaks the symmetry. But the real job of initialisation is scale: keeping the variance of activations and gradients stable from layer to layer, so signals neither vanish nor explode before training even starts. That's what the named schemes do. Xavier or Glorot scales by fan-in and fan-out and suits tanh or sigmoid. He initialisation uses variance 2 over fan-in for ReLU, where the factor of two compensates for ReLU zeroing half its inputs.

As for reproducibility, that comes from seeding: fix the seeds for Python, NumPy and the framework, and enable deterministic kernels where needed. A seeded random init is perfectly reproducible and actually trains."

stages.name: Symmetry never breaks
stages.html:
"Same weights → same outputs → same gradients → same updates, forever."

  • All hidden units in a layer compute w·x + b with the same w: identical outputs.
  • Backprop gives each the same gradient.
  • After the update they're still identical. No step can ever separate them.
  • With zeros specifically, many gradients are exactly zero too (e.g. through ReLU, or the product of zero weights).

stages.name: The layer collapses to one neuron
stages.html:
"Effective capacity = one unit per layer, whatever the width."

Setting Result
Zero init, ReLU outputs 0, gradients 0: nothing trains
Zero init, sigmoid all units output 0.5; they move, but together
Constant c ≠ 0 symmetric, same collapse
Only biases zero, weights random fine; common practice

stages.name: What init is really for
stages.html:
"Randomness breaks symmetry; the scale is what the schemes are about."

  • Too large → activations and gradients explode through layers.
  • Too small → they shrink toward zero: vanishing signal before training starts.
  • Target: Var(output of a layer) ≈ Var(input), and similarly for gradients going backwards.

stages.name: Pick the scheme by activation
stages.html:
Scheme Variance Use with
Xavier / Glorot 2 / (fan_in + fan_out) tanh, sigmoid (symmetric around 0)
He / Kaiming 2 / fan_in ReLU family (half the inputs zeroed)
Scaled residual init output projections scaled down by depth transformers: start close to identity

Framework defaults are usually sensible; check them when using unusual activations.

stages.name: Get reproducibility the right way
stages.html:
"Determinism is a property of the run, not of the initial values."

  • Seed Python random, NumPy, and the framework (torch.manual_seed), including data-loader workers.
  • Enable deterministic algorithms (torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)) where exact repeatability matters; some GPU ops are otherwise non-deterministic.
  • Log seeds, library versions and hardware with each run.

followUps.question: Is initialising biases to zero also a problem?
followUps.html: No. Symmetry is broken by the random weights, so zero biases are the standard default. Some practitioners use a small positive bias for ReLU layers to avoid dead units at the start, and output-layer biases are sometimes set to the log of the class prior to speed up early training.

followUps.question: Why the factor of 2 in He initialisation?
followUps.html: ReLU zeroes roughly half of its inputs, which halves the variance of the signal passing through. Doubling the weight variance compensates, so the output variance of each layer matches its input variance. Without it, the signal shrinks by half per layer.

followUps.question: With good initialisation, do we still need BatchNorm?
followUps.html: Initialisation sets good statistics at step zero; normalisation keeps them good as the weights change during training. For deep networks you want both, plus residual connections. Some architectures train without normalisation using careful init and scaling, but that's the exception.

followUps.question: Two seeded runs still give slightly different results. Why?
followUps.html: Non-deterministic GPU kernels (atomic adds in some convolutions and scatter ops), multi-threaded data loading, different library or driver versions, or different hardware. Enable deterministic algorithms, fix worker seeds, pin versions. Expect small floating-point differences across hardware even then.

followUps.question: How does initialisation work when fine-tuning a pretrained model?
followUps.html: The pretrained weights are the initialisation; only new layers (like a classification head) are initialised fresh, usually small so they don't disrupt the pretrained features. LoRA adapters are a good example: one matrix is random, the other starts at zero, so the adapter begins as a no-op without symmetry problems, since the random side breaks it.

dontSay: "Zero init is fine, the optimiser will fix it." — identical neurons stay identical.
"Reproducibility needs constant initial weights." — seeds give reproducibility.
"Any random init works." — scale matters; badly scaled init vanishes or explodes.
"Only zero is a problem." — any constant has the same symmetry.

ml-dl-q21.testing: whether you know inverted dropout precisely enough to predict the bug's symptom.
ml-dl-q21.trap: chasing a data bug when the symptom is run-to-run variance on the same input.
ml-dl-q21.spoken:
"In train mode, dropout zeroes each unit with probability p on every forward pass and scales the survivors by 1 over 1 minus p. That's inverted dropout. The scaling keeps the expected activation the same as without dropout, and randomly removing units stops them co-adapting; effectively you train a shifting ensemble of sub-networks.

Because the scaling already happened at training time, eval mode should be the identity: no zeroing, no scaling, fully deterministic, using the whole network.

If dropout is left on at evaluation, every forward pass samples a different random sub-network. The same input gives different predictions on each run, and average quality drops, because each prediction comes from a thinned network rather than the full one.

That's exactly the classic symptom: two 'identical' evaluation runs give different numbers with no data, code or seed change. BatchNorm is the twin bug: in train mode it normalises with the current batch's statistics instead of the running averages, so predictions depend on what else is in the batch.

The fix is model.eval() before evaluation, which flips both, plus torch.no_grad() or inference mode. And I'd guard it: an evaluation helper that sets eval mode itself, and a test asserting two passes on the same input match."

stages.name: What train mode does
stages.html:
"Each forward pass drops units at random and scales up the rest."

train:  h' = h · mask / (1 − p)      mask ~ Bernoulli(1 − p)
        E[h'] = h                    (expected value preserved)
  • Prevents co-adaptation: units can't rely on specific partners.
  • Interpretable as training an ensemble of 2^n sub-networks with shared weights.

stages.name: What eval mode must be
stages.html:
"Because scaling happened in training, evaluation is just the full network."

  • No mask, no scaling, deterministic.
  • (Original, non-inverted dropout scaled at test time instead; modern frameworks use inverted dropout so inference needs no change.)

stages.name: What leaving it on does
stages.html:
"Each prediction comes from a different thinned network."

Effect Why
Different output each run on the same input new random mask per forward pass
Lower average accuracy each thinned network is weaker than the full one
Noisier metrics across evaluation runs variance from masks, not from data
Surprising in production users see non-deterministic answers

stages.name: The symptom and its twin
stages.html:
"Non-reproducible eval numbers with nothing changed is the fingerprint."

  • BatchNorm in train mode uses the batch's mean and variance, not the running averages. Predictions depend on batch composition and batch size; batch size 1 can break outright.
  • Both are flipped by model.eval(); both are forgotten by the same mistake.

stages.name: Fix and guard
stages.html:
"Fix the call, then make it impossible to forget."

  • model.eval() + torch.no_grad() (or torch.inference_mode()) for every evaluation and serving path.
  • Evaluation helper functions set the mode themselves and restore it after.
  • Test: two forward passes on the same input must be identical in eval mode.
  • Serving: export the model in eval mode (TorchScript/ONNX export after .eval()).

followUps.question: Is dropout at inference ever intentional?
followUps.html: Yes: Monte Carlo dropout. Run many forward passes with dropout on and use the spread of predictions as an uncertainty estimate. It's deliberate, done with many samples averaged, and documented, which is very different from accidentally leaving it on for a single pass.

followUps.question: Why is dropout often zero in large LLM pretraining?
followUps.html: Single-epoch pretraining on huge corpora usually underfits: the model never sees an example twice, so there's little memorisation to prevent. The data scale is the regulariser, and dropout would slow learning. Dropout reappears in fine-tuning on small datasets, where overfitting is real.

followUps.question: Does torch.no_grad() turn off dropout?
followUps.html: No. no_grad only disables gradient tracking. Dropout and BatchNorm behaviour is controlled by the module's training flag, set by model.train() / model.eval(). You need both: eval mode for correct behaviour, no_grad for speed and memory.

followUps.question: Where does dropout sit in a transformer?
followUps.html: On attention weights, on the outputs of attention and feed-forward sub-layers before the residual add, and on embeddings. All of it must be off at inference, which the same model.eval() handles.

followUps.question: How would you catch this in CI?
followUps.html: A determinism test on the evaluation and serving paths: load the model through the same code the service uses, run the same input twice, assert identical outputs. Also assert model.training is False at the serving entry point. Cheap tests, and they catch both the dropout and BatchNorm versions.

dontSay: "Dropout at eval just adds a bit of noise." — it evaluates a weaker random sub-network.
"Scale the outputs by (1 − p) at test time." — not with inverted dropout; you'd double-scale.
"no_grad fixes it." — it doesn't touch dropout.
"Must be a data-loading bug." — the same input varying is the dropout fingerprint.

spine: Gap vs no gap: two diseases
Open with the one-batch overfit test
Model B: optimisation or bug path
ml-dl-q22.testing: whether "loss is high" triggers a structured triage, not random tuning.
ml-dl-q22.trap: treating both as one diagnosis, or tuning hyperparameters before checking the pipeline works.
ml-dl-q22.spoken:
"They're two different diseases.

Model A, train 0.1 and validation 2.3, has a huge gap: it has memorised the training set. Model B, stuck at 2.3 on both, has no gap: it isn't learning at all, which is underfitting or a broken pipeline.

For both, my first move is the same five-minute experiment: try to overfit a single small batch to near-zero loss. If the model can't, there's a bug: in the loss, the labels, the architecture wiring or the data pipeline, and no tuning will help.

For model A, the gap path: first rule out a bad validation set, like leakage, a distribution mismatch or mislabelled data. Then more or better data and augmentation, then regularisation: weight decay, dropout, early stopping on validation loss, and a smaller model last.

For model B, the no-gap path: sweep the learning rate first, since it's the most common cause in both directions. Check the labels are aligned with the inputs and actually learnable, check input normalisation and the loss wiring, and only then add capacity or training time.

I'd also read the number itself. 2.3 is suspiciously close to ln(10), the loss of uniform guessing over ten classes, which would mean model B has learned nothing."

stages.name: Gap vs no gap: two diseases
stages.html:
Model Train Val Reading
A 0.1 2.3 memorisation: high variance
B 2.3 2.3 not learning: bias, optimisation or a bug

"The gap is the first split. Everything after depends on it."

stages.name: Open with the one-batch overfit test
stages.html:
"Take 8–32 examples, turn off regularisation, train until loss → ~0."

Result Meaning
Loss goes to ~0 the model and pipeline can learn; problem is data or optimisation scale
Loss plateaus above 0 bug: labels misaligned, wrong loss, frozen layers, broken data pipeline

Five minutes, and it separates "broken" from "undertuned" before you waste a day on hyperparameters.

stages.name: Model A: variance path
stages.html:
Step 0 — Check the validation set. Leakage between train and val (duplicates), distribution mismatch, noisy val labels.

Step 1 — Data. More examples, better labels, augmentation.

Step 2 — Regularise. Weight decay, dropout, early stopping on validation loss.

Step 3 — Capacity. Smaller model or fewer features, last.

Watch the validation loss curve: if it bottomed out early and rose, early stopping alone recovers a lot.

stages.name: Model B: optimisation or bug path
stages.html:
"If the one-batch test passes, it's usually the learning rate."

  • LR sweep (or LR range test): too low → flat; too high → noisy plateau or divergence.
  • Labels: shuffled independently of inputs? Wrong class mapping?
  • Inputs: normalised? Any NaNs or constant features?
  • Loss wiring: softmax applied twice? Logits passed where probabilities expected? Wrong reduction?
  • Architecture: frozen layers, dead ReLUs, vanishing gradients (check per-layer gradient norms).
  • Then capacity and training time.

stages.name: Read the loss against baselines
stages.html:
"Compare the loss with what trivial predictors score."

Baseline Cross-entropy
Uniform over K classes ln K (ln 10 ≈ 2.30, ln 50,000 ≈ 10.8)
Predicting class frequencies entropy of the label distribution

A loss sitting exactly at ln K means the model outputs uniform probabilities: a bug or zero learning.

stages.name: Verify each fix
stages.html:
• Change one thing, re-run, compare curves.
  • A: validation loss should fall while train rises slightly.
  • B: training loss should start dropping below the trivial baseline within the first epochs.

followUps.question: Why is the one-batch overfit test so valuable?
followUps.html: Because any correctly wired model with enough capacity can memorise a handful of examples. If it can't, the problem isn't generalisation or tuning; it's that gradients don't reach the right place or the targets are wrong. It turns a vague "not learning" into a yes/no question in minutes.

followUps.question: Model A's validation set came from a different source. Does the plan change?
followUps.html: Yes. The gap may be distribution shift, not overfitting. Regularisation won't close a shift. I'd compare feature or input distributions between the sets, evaluate on a validation split drawn from the training source, and if the gap shrinks, the fix is representative training data or domain adaptation.

followUps.question: The learning rate sweep didn't help model B. Next?
followUps.html: Go back to data and wiring: verify a few input-label pairs by eye, check the loss function's expected inputs (logits vs probabilities), confirm the optimiser actually receives the model's parameters, and check gradient norms per layer for vanishing or zero gradients.

followUps.question: Should I just add dropout to model B too?
followUps.html: No. Model B isn't overfitting; regularisation raises bias and makes underfitting worse. Regularisation is for a gap. With no gap and high loss, reduce regularisation, fix optimisation, or add capacity.

followUps.question: What's the LLM-era version of model A?
followUps.html: In single-epoch pretraining, classic overfitting is rare; the gap disease tends to be data duplication or benchmark contamination, where the model has seen test-like text. The fix is deduplication and contamination checks, not dropout. In fine-tuning on small datasets, classic overfitting returns.

dontSay: "Both have high loss, so tune the hyperparameters." — two diseases, two paths.
"Add regularisation to both." — makes model B worse.
"Train model B for longer." — first prove it can learn at all.
"2.3 is just a high loss." — it's the uniform-guessing baseline for 10 classes.

ml-dl-q23.testing: the multiplicative argument, and why it's worse than depth in an MLP.
ml-dl-q23.trap: "RNNs have short memory" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q23.spoken:
"The forgetting is a training problem: the gradient from the end of the document can't reach the beginning.

To train an RNN, you unroll it over the sequence, which turns it into a very deep network with one layer per time step, and backpropagate through time. The gradient from step T back to step 1 is a product of T Jacobians, one per step, and they all involve the same recurrent weight matrix.

Multiplying by the same matrix hundreds of times is worse than a deep MLP, where layers at least differ. If the matrix's largest singular value, combined with the activation derivative, is below one, the product shrinks exponentially and early tokens get essentially zero gradient: the model can't learn long-range dependencies no matter its capacity. Above one, it explodes, which shows up as loss spikes.

Exploding is easy to patch with gradient clipping. Truncated backprop caps the horizon, which admits the problem rather than fixing it. Vanishing is the hard one.

LSTMs and GRUs address it with a gated cell state updated additively, so the gradient can flow through time without being repeatedly multiplied. That's a longer leash, not an unlimited one.

And there's a second, independent failure: each step depends on the previous one, so training can't be parallelised across the sequence. Attention fixed both, which is why transformers won."

stages.name: Unroll in time: BPTT
stages.claim: an RNN is a deep network in time
stages.html:
"Training unrolls the recurrence into T copies with shared weights."

h_t = tanh(W_h · h_{t−1} + W_x · x_t)

x1 → [h1] → [h2] → … → [hT] → loss
        W_h    W_h        W_h      (same matrix every step)

Backpropagation through time (BPTT) is ordinary backprop on this unrolled graph.

stages.name: One matrix, multiplied T times
stages.html:
"The gradient to step 1 is a product of T Jacobians sharing W_h."

∂h_T/∂h_1 = Π (t=2..T) diag(tanh'(z_t)) · W_h
  • Same W_h every step, so the product behaves like W_h^T.
  • Largest singular value (with tanh' ≤ 1) below 1 → exponential decay; above 1 → exponential growth.
  • Worse than an MLP, whose layers have different weights and fewer multiplications.

stages.name: Vanish vs explode
stages.html:
Vanishing Exploding
Symptom early tokens don't influence learning; long dependencies never learned loss spikes, NaNs
Detectable quietly; model just underperforms on long contexts loudly
Patch architecture change needed gradient clipping

"Exploding is loud and easy. Vanishing is silent and hard."

stages.name: The patches: clipping, truncation
stages.html:
• Gradient clipping rescales the gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold. Fixes exploding, does nothing for vanishing.
  • Truncated BPTT backpropagates only k steps. Saves memory and compute, and explicitly gives up on dependencies longer than k.

stages.name: Gated cells: an additive path
stages.html:
"LSTMs replace repeated multiplication with a gated addition."

c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ g_t
  • The cell state c is updated additively; when the forget gate f ≈ 1, the gradient passes through nearly unchanged (the "constant error carousel").
  • Gates are learned, so the network decides what to keep.
  • Result: dependencies of hundreds of steps become learnable. Still finite, still degrading with distance.

stages.name: The second failure: sequential compute
stages.html:
"Even a perfect RNN can't be trained in parallel across time."

  • h_t needs h_{t−1}, so the T steps run in sequence on a GPU built for parallel work.
  • Attention connects every position to every other in one step: path length 1 for gradients, and fully parallel training.
  • The cost moves to O(T²) attention compute and memory, which modern variants attack.

followUps.question: Why is the RNN case worse than a deep MLP?
followUps.html: In an MLP, each layer has its own weights, so the Jacobians differ and don't systematically compound in one direction; depth is typically tens of layers. In an RNN, the same matrix is multiplied at every step, for hundreds or thousands of steps, so its dominant singular value is effectively raised to a huge power.

followUps.question: Does gradient clipping fix vanishing gradients?
followUps.html: No. Clipping only caps gradients that are too large. A vanished gradient is tiny; clipping never touches it. The information from early tokens is already gone from the gradient.

followUps.question: GRU vs LSTM?
followUps.html: A GRU merges the cell and hidden state and uses two gates instead of three, so it has fewer parameters and trains faster; performance is often similar. LSTMs have a separate cell state and output gate, sometimes better on very long dependencies. In practice, try both, or use attention.

followUps.question: Do transformers have no long-range problem at all?
followUps.html: They have a different one. Gradients reach any position in one step, but the context window is finite, attention cost grows quadratically with length, and models still use information in the middle of long contexts less reliably. The limit moves from training dynamics to compute, context length and learned attention patterns.

followUps.question: Where would you still use an RNN today?
followUps.html: Streaming or on-device settings where you process one step at a time with constant memory and latency, like keyword spotting or some sensor pipelines. State-space models (the Mamba family) revive recurrence with parallelisable training for long sequences, which is the modern version of this trade-off.

dontSay: "RNNs just have a short memory." — no mechanism.
"Clipping solves it." — only the exploding half.
"LSTMs have infinite memory." — a longer leash, not unlimited.
"Transformers won because they're bigger." — parallelism and path length won.

spine: Frame it as a judgement call
ml-dl-q24.testing: judgement, not knowledge. Can you argue against the fashionable tool, with conditions?
ml-dl-q24.spoken:
"Deep learning earns its cost when the data is unstructured, like images, audio or text, and plentiful. Outside that, I'd argue against it in four situations.

First, tabular data with up to a few hundred thousand rows. Gradient-boosted trees still match or beat deep models there, train in minutes on a CPU, need less tuning and are easier to explain. Research on deep tabular models keeps re-finding this.

Second, small data where the structure is known. If I can write down the relationship, a physical law, a business rule, seasonality, then a simple model with that structure built in beats a network that has to learn it from few examples.

Third, when I need interpretability I can defend to a regulator or a customer, like credit decisions. A scorecard or a monotone-constrained boosted model gives reasons I can stand behind; post-hoc explanations of a network are harder to defend.

Fourth, when the inference bill is the constraint: tight latency, high volume or an edge device. A smaller model or a well-engineered classical one may give most of the value at a fraction of the cost.

And the strongest version of this answer names the alternative: I'd benchmark a boosted model and a simple baseline first, and only move to deep learning if the gain justifies the cost."

stages.name: Frame it as a judgement call
stages.html:
"Deep learning has real costs: data, compute, tuning, opacity and operations. It has to earn them."

  • DL shines with unstructured, high-dimensional data and lots of it: vision, speech, language.
  • Everywhere else, benchmark it against cheaper options before committing.

stages.name: Tabular data
stages.html:
"For typical tabular problems, gradient boosting is the default to beat."

  • Handles mixed types, missing values and irregular feature scales natively.
  • Trains fast on CPU, strong with defaults, strong with modest tuning.
  • Deep tabular models occasionally match it at large scale; they rarely justify their tuning cost at moderate scale.
  • Exception: tables with rich text or image columns, or very high-cardinality IDs where learned embeddings help.

stages.name: Small data with strong structure
stages.claim: encode the prior, don't learn it
stages.html:
"If I know the shape of the relationship, I build it in."

Structure you know Better choice
Physical or accounting law parametric or physics-informed model
Seasonality and trend classical time-series models or boosting with lags
Monotone business rules monotone-constrained GBM, scorecards
Few hundred labelled examples regularised linear models, or a pretrained model fine-tuned

The last row is the nuance: with pretrained foundation models, small unstructured datasets can use DL via transfer learning.

stages.name: Interpretability you must defend
stages.html:
"When I must explain each decision, the model's structure has to be explainable."

  • Credit, insurance, hiring, healthcare: adverse-action reasons, audits, fairness reviews.
  • Scorecards, GAMs, monotone-constrained GBMs give stable, defensible reasons.
  • Post-hoc explanations (SHAP on a network) are approximations and harder to defend in an audit.

stages.name: Cost, latency and the edge
stages.html:
"At high volume, the model's cost is paid on every request."

  • Tight latency budgets (single-digit milliseconds), millions of calls a day, or on-device constraints.
  • Options: classical models, distillation into smaller networks, rules plus a model for hard cases.
  • Measure cost per decision against the value of the accuracy gained.

stages.name: Say what you'd ship instead
stages.html:
"Name the decision process, not just the objection."

  1. Baseline: rules or logistic regression.
  2. Strong classical model: gradient boosting.
  3. Deep learning only if it beats (2) by a margin that justifies data, compute, latency and explainability costs.

Best of all, name a real project where you argued against DL and what you shipped instead.

followUps.question: With LLMs available, isn't DL always the answer now?
followUps.html: No. LLMs are excellent for language tasks and for bootstrapping labels, but for a structured prediction on tabular data they're slower, costlier and usually less accurate than a boosted model. A common good pattern is using an LLM to extract features from text, then a classical model on top.

followUps.question: Small image dataset of 500 examples. DL or not?
followUps.html: DL, but via transfer learning: a pretrained vision backbone, frozen or lightly fine-tuned, with a small head. Training from scratch on 500 images would overfit. Structure you know (augmentation invariances) still helps. So "small data" isn't automatically "no DL" when a relevant pretrained model exists.

followUps.question: How do you convince a team that wants a neural network?
followUps.html: With evidence, not opinion: run the boosted baseline and the network on the same honest split, then compare accuracy, training cost, inference latency and cost per decision, and explainability. Frame it as "what's the cheapest model that meets the target?" If the network wins by enough, great; the benchmark decides.

followUps.question: When does DL win on tabular data?
followUps.html: Very large datasets, mixed modalities (text or images alongside columns), many high-cardinality categorical IDs that benefit from embeddings, or multi-task setups sharing representations. Recommendation systems are the classic case: embedding-based deep models dominate there.

followUps.question: What's the operational cost people forget?
followUps.html: GPUs for training and often serving, longer and less stable training runs, harder reproducibility, more complex monitoring, and specialised skills to maintain it. A boosted model runs on a CPU, retrains in minutes and has fewer failure modes. That total cost of ownership belongs in the decision.

dontSay: "It depends on the use case." (and stop) — name the conditions.
"Deep learning is always more accurate." — not on typical tabular data.
"Neural networks can't be explained, so never use them in finance." — too absolute; say what's defensible.
"We'd use deep learning to be future-proof." — cost without evidence.
