What I built around the model
ml-dl-q25.testing: whether you see ML as a system (decision, data, latency, evaluation, failure), not a model.
ml-dl-q25.trap: telling it as a modelling story ("I tried three models and tuned…"). They asked about everything else.
ml-dl-q25.spoken:
"At Velocit AI I built VhAIre, an agentic AI interviewer that runs a live spoken interview. The models were the easy part: we called GPT-4-class models and Groq through APIs, and picking between them took days. Everything around them took months.

The constraint was turn-taking. A conversation stops feeling human if the response takes more than about a second, and a single turn chains voice detection, streaming speech-to-text, a reasoning step, the LLM call and text-to-speech.

I weighed a single monolithic LLM call per turn against a LangGraph state machine, and chose <fill: which, and the deciding factor>. For the models, I routed <fill: which turn types went to Groq for latency and which to GPT-4.1 for quality>.

Most of the work was around the model: streaming partial transcripts so the model could start early, handling barge-in when the candidate interrupts, checkpointing the interview state, and a fallback when a provider returned errors. We also had to decide how to evaluate interview quality at all: <fill: human rubric, automated checks, or both>.

What broke in production was <fill: the scar>, and we changed <fill: what changed after>.

The result was <fill: p50/p95 turn latency and one business outcome>. The lesson I took: the model is a component; latency, state and evaluation are the product."

"Name the constraint before the solution. It's what makes the story senior."

  • Sub-second turn-taking is the product; above ~1 s the conversation stops feeling human.
  • The turn is a pipeline: mic → VAD → streaming STT → partial transcript → graph node → LLM → TTS → playback.

spine: What it does to training and data
ml-dl-q26.testing: whether you connect textbook taxonomy to latency, memory and cost in production.
ml-dl-q26.trap: "non-parametric means no parameters." It means the number of parameters isn't fixed in advance.
ml-dl-q26.spoken:
"The cleanest way to say it is: what grows when the data grows?

A parametric model has a fixed number of parameters no matter how much data you have: linear and logistic regression, naive Bayes, a neural net of fixed size. It makes strong assumptions, needs less data, and inference is constant-time and cheap.

A non-parametric model's complexity grows with the data: kNN, decision trees grown to purity, kernel SVMs, Gaussian processes. Fewer assumptions and more flexibility, but more variance, more data needed, and memory and inference cost that grow with n. Non-parametric doesn't mean no parameters; it means the count isn't fixed in advance.

The second axis is when the work happens. Model-based learning compresses the data into parameters at training time. Instance-based learning, like kNN, stores the data and does all the work at query time.

Operationally that decides artifact size, p99 latency, whether you can serve on CPU or on a device, and whether retraining can be incremental. kNN is the extreme: zero training cost, expensive queries. That's why production kNN becomes an approximate-nearest-neighbour index like FAISS or HNSW, which is really a retrieval system."

stages.name: Define by what grows
stages.html:
"Ask what gets bigger as n grows."

Parametric Non-parametric
Parameter count fixed grows with data
Examples linear/logistic regression, naive Bayes, fixed-size NNs kNN, deep trees, kernel SVM, Gaussian processes
Assumptions strong (functional form) weak
Bias / variance higher bias higher variance
Data needed less more

stages.name: Instance-based vs model-based
stages.html:
"Eager learners compress at training time; lazy learners compute at query time."

  • Model-based (eager): training summarises data into parameters; the data can be thrown away.
  • Instance-based (lazy): keep the data; every prediction compares against stored examples (kNN, kernel methods).
  • A tree is non-parametric but model-based: it grows with data yet compiles into a structure you query cheaply.

stages.name: What it does to serving
stages.html:
"This is where the distinction earns its interview slot."

  • Artifact size: a logistic model is kilobytes; a kNN model is the dataset.
  • Latency: parametric inference is O(features); exact kNN is O(n · d) per query.
  • Hardware: fixed-size models fit on CPU or edge; instance-based needs memory for the whole corpus.
  • Production kNN: becomes an approximate nearest neighbour index (FAISS, HNSW, ScaNN), trading exactness for sub-linear queries.

stages.name: What it does to training and data
stages.html:
• Instance-based "retrains" by inserting rows: trivially incremental.
  • Parametric models need refitting, or partial_fit for SGD-trained ones.
  • Non-parametric models keep improving with more data; parametric ones plateau once their assumptions bind.

stages.name: Pick by the operational constraint
stages.html:
Constraint Lean toward
Tight latency, CPU or device parametric
Little data, strong prior parametric
Lots of data, complex boundary non-parametric (trees/ensembles)
Similarity search over a corpus instance-based via ANN index
Frequent additions, no retraining instance-based

followUps.question: Is a neural network parametric?
followUps.html: Yes, formally: a fixed architecture has a fixed parameter count regardless of n. In practice people scale model size with data, which blurs the line, but for any trained network inference cost doesn't grow with the training set, and that's the operational meaning.

followUps.question: Is a random forest parametric?
followUps.html: No. Trees grow with the data: deeper and more splits with more examples. But it's model-based: at inference you traverse fixed trees, not stored examples. That's why "non-parametric" and "slow inference" aren't the same thing.

followUps.question: How does HNSW make kNN viable at scale?
followUps.html: It builds a layered proximity graph; queries greedily walk from coarse upper layers to fine lower ones, visiting a tiny fraction of points. You trade some recall for logarithmic-ish query time, tuned with parameters like ef and M. Memory is the cost: the graph lives in RAM alongside the vectors.

followUps.question: Where do Gaussian processes fit, and why are they rare in production?
followUps.html: They're non-parametric and give calibrated uncertainty, which is lovely, but exact inference is O(n³) in training and O(n) per prediction with an n×n kernel matrix. Beyond tens of thousands of points you need sparse approximations. They shine in small-data settings like Bayesian optimisation of hyperparameters.

followUps.question: Which would you pick for an on-device keyboard suggestion model?
followUps.html: Parametric: fixed memory, constant latency, no stored user corpus on disk. A small neural or n-gram model, quantised. An instance-based approach would need the whole history on the phone and scale query cost with usage.

dontSay: "Non-parametric models have no parameters." — the count just isn't fixed.
"kNN is cheap because it has no training." — you pay at every query.
"Parametric means linear." — neural nets are parametric and non-linear.

spine: Decouple feature freshness from weight freshness
ml-dl-q27.testing: whether you split two constraints the question fuses, and default to the operable option.
ml-dl-q27.trap: "the data is streaming, so we need online learning."
ml-dl-q27.spoken:
"There are two separate constraints hiding in that sentence, and they have different answers.

The first is size: the data doesn't fit in memory. That's an out-of-core problem: stream it in chunks with mini-batch training, partial_fit, or a distributed trainer. It says nothing about how often the model changes.

The second is recency: new data keeps arriving and the world may drift. That's a retraining-cadence question. Streaming data doesn't automatically mean online learning.

My default is scheduled batch retraining, daily or weekly, because it's reproducible, you can validate the new model before shipping it, A/B it and roll it back.

True online learning, updating weights on every event, breaks in specific ways: no clean train/test split, a bad burst of data can drag the model off a cliff, poisoning risk, no reproducibility, and a learning rate that has to be right forever. You lose validate-before-ship.

The architect move is to decouple freshness of features from freshness of weights. A model retrained daily but fed real-time features, like 'transactions in the last five minutes', usually beats an online-updated model with stale features, and it's far easier to operate."

stages.name: Separate size from recency
stages.html:
Constraint Question it raises Answer family
Size can I train on data bigger than RAM? out-of-core / mini-batch / distributed
Recency how fast must the model reflect new data? retrain cadence, online learning

stages.name: Size: out-of-core
stages.claim: stream the data, not the model
stages.html:
• Chunked readers (Parquet row groups, Arrow datasets), partial_fit for SGD-based linear models and naive Bayes, mini-batch deep learning, distributed trainers (Spark, Ray, XGBoost distributed).
  • Caveats: shuffling is hard, so chunks may be correlated; scaling needs running statistics; many algorithms (vanilla Random Forest, kernel SVM) don't fit incrementally.
  • Often simpler: train on a well-drawn sample, then check with a learning curve whether more data would help.

stages.name: Recency: retrain cadence
stages.html:
"Scheduled retraining keeps every safety property of offline ML."

  • Train on a recent window, validate on the newest slice, compare to the incumbent, canary, promote.
  • Cadence comes from measured decay: how fast does the metric drop over time?
  • Trigger-based retraining (on drift) when decay is irregular.

stages.name: What online learning breaks
stages.html:
• No held-out evaluation before a change reaches users.
  • Catastrophic drift: one bad burst (a bot, an outage) pulls weights far off.
  • Poisoning: adversaries can steer the model with crafted traffic.
  • Reproducibility: you can't recreate yesterday's model exactly.
  • Hyperparameters forever: the learning rate must suit every future regime.

Legitimate uses: bandits, ad click models with heavy guardrails, and systems where hours of staleness genuinely cost money.

stages.name: Decouple feature freshness from weight freshness
stages.html:
"Most of the value of 'online' comes from fresh inputs, not fresh weights."

  • Real-time features (counts in the last N minutes, session state) through a streaming feature pipeline.
  • Weights retrained on a schedule with full validation.
  • You get responsiveness without giving up reproducibility or rollback.

followUps.question: The business insists on minute-level adaptation. Now what?
followUps.html: First check whether real-time features deliver it. If weights truly must move, use online updates with guardrails: bounded learning rate, update only from validated/filtered events, shadow-evaluate the updated model against a frozen baseline continuously, and auto-revert on metric drops. Keep periodic full retrains to reset accumulated drift.

followUps.question: Which sklearn models support incremental fitting?
followUps.html: Those with partial_fit: SGDClassifier/SGDRegressor, MultinomialNB/GaussianNB, MiniBatchKMeans, PassiveAggressive, Perceptron, MLPClassifier. Random forests and gradient boosting in sklearn don't; XGBoost and LightGBM can continue training from an existing booster but that's not the same as online learning.

followUps.question: Why is shuffling a problem out-of-core?
followUps.html: Data often arrives sorted by time or user, so consecutive chunks share structure. Mini-batches then aren't i.i.d., gradients are biased per chunk, and the model oscillates. Fix with a shuffle buffer, pre-shuffled shards, or randomising the order of files and row groups.

followUps.question: Doesn't daily retraining risk shipping a regression every day?
followUps.html: Only without a gate. Every retrain passes the same offline checks against the incumbent on the newest data, per segment, then a canary. If it fails, the incumbent stays. Automation without evaluation is the risk, not frequency.

followUps.question: How do you pick the training window length?
followUps.html: Compare windows (last 1, 3, 6, 12 months) on a recent holdout, or weight recent data more. Longer windows give more data; shorter ones track change. After a known regime change (pricing, policy), drop or down-weight pre-change data.

dontSay: "Streaming data means online learning." — size and recency are separate.
"Online learning is more advanced, so it's better." — it trades away validation and rollback.
"Just get a bigger machine." — sometimes right, but name out-of-core and sampling first.

ml-dl-q28.testing: whether you run EDA toward decisions under a time box, not a plot gallery.
ml-dl-q28.trap: listing plots ("histograms, box plots, a heatmap…").
ml-dl-q28.spoken:
"I'd frame the day around the decisions EDA has to produce: what the target's base rate is, which columns are unusable, what the split strategy is, what each feature needs, and whether anything leaks.

I'd start by sampling, stratified on the target, so it fits in memory and iterates fast. Then a schema and type audit: numbers that are really IDs, dates stored as strings, sentinel values like minus 999 or 1900-01-01.

Next, missingness per column and jointly, because missingness is often informative. The target distribution and base rate. Cardinality of categoricals. Duplicates and near-duplicates. Then per-feature relationships with the target, correlation clusters, and temporal coverage: does each column exist across the whole time range, or appear after some date?

The thing I actively hunt is leakage: features that are too good, near-perfectly correlated with the target, are guilty until proven innocent.

I'd use an automated profiler like ydata-profiling for the first pass to save hours, but I don't treat its report as the analysis.

By end of day I deliver a written data-quality note with issues and decisions, a split strategy, a feature shortlist, and a trained baseline, because a baseline model is the fastest way to learn which columns matter."

stages.name: Frame EDA as decisions
stages.html:
By end of day I must be able to answer:

  • What is the target and its base rate?
  • Which columns are unusable (leaky, constant, broken)?
  • What's the split strategy (time? groups?)?
  • What does each kept feature need (encoding, transform, imputation)?

stages.name: Sample and audit the schema
stages.html:
• Stratified sample (e.g. 1–2M rows) to iterate in memory; confirm conclusions on the full data later.
  • Types: numeric IDs, zip codes as ints, dates as strings, booleans as "Y"/"N"/"".
  • Sentinels: −999, 0, 1900-01-01, "unknown" masquerading as values.
  • Constant or near-constant columns → drop candidates.

stages.name: Missingness, target and cardinality
stages.html:
Check Why
Missingness per column and co-missingness informative missingness, broken sources
Target distribution, base rate metric choice, imbalance handling
Categorical cardinality encoding strategy, leakage risk (IDs)
Duplicates / near-duplicates split leakage, inflated metrics
Temporal coverage per column schema changes, features that appear late

stages.name: Hunt leakage and traps
stages.claim: the part that saves the project
stages.html:
• Too-good features: anything with near-perfect target correlation or AUC on its own.
  • Post-outcome fields: timestamps or statuses written after the label event.
  • Units and scales changing mid-series.
  • Categorical levels that only exist after a date.

stages.name: Automate the first pass
stages.html:
• ydata-profiling, sweetviz on the sample: distributions, correlations, missingness in an hour.
  • Then targeted manual work on the suspicious columns the report flagged.

stages.name: Deliver by end of day
stages.html:
1. Data-quality note: issues found and the decision for each.
  2. Split strategy with the reason.
  3. Feature shortlist with needed transforms.
  4. Baseline model (logistic or a quick GBM) with feature importance: which columns actually carry signal.

followUps.question: Why train a model during EDA?
followUps.html: Because it's the fastest honest signal of which columns matter and whether any leak. A feature that dominates importance on day one is either your best feature or leakage, and you want to know which before building on it. It also sets the bar future models must beat.

followUps.question: How big should the sample be?
followUps.html: Big enough to keep rare classes and rare categorical levels represented: stratify on the target and cap per-level counts if needed. A few million rows usually suffices for distributions; confirm anything surprising on the full data with a SQL aggregate.

followUps.question: A feature has AUC 0.99 on its own. What now?
followUps.html: Assume leakage. Find out when and how it's written relative to the label. If it's recorded after the outcome or derived from it, drop it. If it's genuinely available at prediction time, the problem may be trivial, which is also worth telling the business.

followUps.question: How do you check missingness is informative?
followUps.html: Compare the target rate when the value is missing versus present; train a baseline with and without missing-indicator features. If the indicator carries signal, missingness isn't random, and imputation alone would throw that signal away.

followUps.question: What would you do on day two?
followUps.html: Validate the split with a quick CV sanity check, build the feature pipeline properly (inside a Pipeline), agree the metric with the business, and set up data-quality checks for the columns that showed problems, so they're monitored rather than rediscovered.

dontSay: "I'd make a pairplot of all 300 columns." — unreadable and slow.
"The profiling report covers it." — it's a first pass, not the analysis.
"EDA doesn't need a model." — a baseline is the fastest EDA tool.

spine: The rule: what the model computes with values
ml-dl-q29.testing: whether you reason from the algorithm's arithmetic instead of habit.
ml-dl-q29.spoken:
"The rule is: scaling matters when the algorithm compares or combines feature magnitudes, and it's a no-op when the algorithm only uses their order.

It matters in three families. Distance-based models: kNN, K-means, RBF SVMs, where a feature measured in thousands swamps one measured in fractions. Gradient-descent-trained models: linear and logistic regression with SGD, neural nets, where unscaled features make the loss surface badly conditioned and training slow or unstable. And regularised linear models, because the penalty is scale-sensitive: an unscaled feature gets shrunk more or less than it should.

It's a no-op for tree-based models: random forests, gradient boosting. Splits depend on ordering, not magnitude, so scaling them is ritual.

For which scaler: standardisation by default; min-max when you need a bounded range; robust scaling when outliers would distort the mean and standard deviation; and log or Box-Cox/Yeo-Johnson when the problem is skew, which changes the shape, not just the scale.

And the operational rule: fit the scaler on the training data only, inside the pipeline and inside each CV fold. PCA is the sneaky case: it maximises variance, so unscaled features with big units dominate the components."

stages.name: The rule: what the model computes with values
stages.html: "Distances, gradients and penalties see magnitude. Splits see order."

stages.name: Where it matters
stages.html:
Family Why scale matters
Distance-based: kNN, K-means, SVM-RBF large-unit features dominate the distance
Gradient-trained: linear/logistic via SGD, NNs ill-conditioned loss, slow or unstable convergence
Regularised linear: Ridge, Lasso, Elastic Net penalty shrinks features unequally by unit
PCA variance is unit-dependent; big units hijack components

stages.name: Where it's a no-op
stages.html:
• Decision trees, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost: splits are thresholds on sorted values, invariant to monotone transforms.
  • Naive Bayes per-feature likelihoods: largely unaffected (Gaussian NB fits each feature's own mean and variance).

stages.name: Which scaler
stages.html:
Scaler Use when
StandardScaler (z-score) default
MinMaxScaler need a bounded range (e.g. some NN inputs, images)
RobustScaler (median, IQR) outliers would distort mean/std
Log / Box-Cox / Yeo-Johnson heavy skew; changes shape, not just scale

stages.name: Fit it inside the fold
stages.html:
• Fit on training data only; transform validation and test with those statistics.
  • Put it in a Pipeline so CV refits it per fold automatically.
  • Ship the fitted scaler inside the model artifact so serving applies the identical transform.

followUps.question: Does scaling help gradient boosting at all?
followUps.html: Not for the splits. It can matter slightly for histogram binning edge cases and for linear boosters, but for standard tree boosters it's wasted work. What can help trees is transforming the target, not the features.

followUps.question: Why does Lasso need scaled features?
followUps.html: The L1 penalty is the sum of absolute coefficients. A feature in small units needs a large coefficient to have the same effect, so it's penalised more and dropped first, regardless of importance. Standardising puts every coefficient on the same footing.

followUps.question: Scale before or after the train/test split?
followUps.html: After, and fit on train only. Fitting on all data lets test-set statistics (mean, variance) influence training, which is mild but real leakage, and it breaks the guarantee that serving can reproduce the transform from training data alone.

followUps.question: Do neural nets need input scaling if they have BatchNorm?
followUps.html: BatchNorm normalises activations inside the network, not the first layer's inputs, so badly scaled inputs still hurt the first layer's conditioning and initialisation assumptions. Scale inputs anyway; it's cheap and removes a failure mode.

followUps.question: How do you handle a feature with extreme skew, like income?
followUps.html: Log or Yeo-Johnson first to compress the tail, then standardise if the model needs it. For trees, leave it alone. Check whether capping extremes is appropriate, which is a data decision, not a scaling one.

followUps.question: How do you guarantee serving scales inputs exactly like training did?
followUps.html: Ship the fitted scaler inside the model artifact (a Pipeline), never reimplement it in the service. Log the scaler's fitted means and variances with the model version, and monitor served feature distributions against them: a drifting mean means the scaling no longer centres production data, which is both a skew and a drift signal.

dontSay: "Always scale." — trees don't care.
"Scaling fixes skew." — standardising keeps the shape; you need a transform.
"I scaled the whole dataset first, then split." — leakage.

ml-dl-q30.testing: whether you see pipelines as correctness and deployment guarantees, not style.
ml-dl-q30.spoken:
"Two guarantees, and neither is about tidiness.

The first is leakage-free cross-validation. A Pipeline refits every transform, imputers, scalers and encoders, inside each CV fold, so they never see the validation rows. Doing preprocessing once up front and then cross-validating is the classic silent leak; the Pipeline makes the correct thing the default.

The second is train-serve consistency. The fitted pipeline is one serialised artifact containing preprocessing and model together, so serving applies byte-identical transforms. It's the small-scale version of what a feature store does for a platform.

ColumnTransformer adds declarative wiring: numeric, categorical and text columns each get their own path in one object, bound by column name, so there's no hand-maintained index bookkeeping to drift.

A bonus: hyperparameter search covers preprocessing choices too, like the imputation strategy or encoder type, so you tune the whole function, not just the estimator.

Architecturally, the pipeline is a contract: raw schema in, prediction out. That makes it testable, versionable and swappable behind an API."

stages.name: Guarantee 1: leakage-free CV
stages.html:
pipe = Pipeline([("prep", preprocess), ("model", LogisticRegression())])
cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5)   # imputer/scaler/encoder refit on each training fold

Without it: scaler.fit(X) on all rows → every fold's validation data shaped the scaler.

stages.name: Guarantee 2: one artifact for serving
stages.html:
• joblib.dump(pipe) stores fitted preprocessing and model together.
  • The service calls pipe.predict(raw_df): no hand-coded transforms to drift.
  • Version the pipeline; roll back model and preprocessing atomically.

stages.name: ColumnTransformer: declarative wiring
stages.html:
preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer()), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols),
])
  • handle_unknown="ignore" makes unseen categories safe at serving.
  • New columns can't silently shift positions.

stages.name: Tune the whole function
stages.html:
• param_grid = {"prep__num__impute__strategy": ["mean", "median"], "model__C": [0.1, 1, 10]}
  • Encoder choice, feature selection k, polynomial degree: all searchable in one CV loop.

stages.name: The pipeline as a contract
stages.html:
• Unit-testable: fixed input frame → expected output.
  • Schema validation at the edge (pandera, pydantic) before the pipeline.
  • Swappable behind an API: the service doesn't care what's inside.

followUps.question: What leaks if you impute before CV?
followUps.html: The imputed values (means, medians, KNN neighbours) are computed with validation rows included, so validation data influences the training features. Target encoding is the extreme case: the encoding contains validation labels.

followUps.question: How do you add a custom transform?
followUps.html: Write a class with fit and transform (inherit BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin), or use FunctionTransformer for stateless functions. Keep any learned state in fit so it's refit per fold.

followUps.question: What doesn't belong in the pipeline?
followUps.html: Things that need data unavailable at prediction time, row filtering that changes the target (do that before splitting, deliberately), and heavy feature computations shared across models, which belong in a feature store or upstream job.

followUps.question: Pickled pipelines break across sklearn versions. How do you manage that?
followUps.html: Pin library versions in the model's environment and record them with the artifact. For long-lived or cross-language serving, export to ONNX or a portable format, and add a load-and-predict test in CI for each new version.

followUps.question: Where do resamplers like SMOTE go?
followUps.html: In an imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline, which applies samplers only during fit. sklearn's Pipeline would also resample at predict time, which is wrong. Resampling must happen on training folds only.

dontSay: "Pipelines are just for clean code." — they're correctness and deployment guarantees.
"I preprocess the full dataset, then run CV." — leakage.
"The service reimplements the preprocessing." — train-serve skew waiting to happen.

spine: You can't prove it from data
ml-dl-q31.testing: whether imputation choices follow from assumptions, not habit.
ml-dl-q31.trap: "fill with the mean and move on."
ml-dl-q31.spoken:
"The mechanism decides which methods are unbiased, so it decides what you're allowed to do.

MCAR, missing completely at random, means missingness is independent of everything, observed or not. Then dropping incomplete rows is unbiased, just wasteful. It's the only case where deletion is safe, and it's the rarest in practice.

MAR, missing at random given the observed data, means other columns explain the missingness, for example older customers skip a field more often. Then model-based imputation like KNN or MICE is justified, because the observed columns carry the signal needed to recover the value.

MNAR, missing not at random, means missingness depends on the unobserved value itself, like income left blank because it's high. Then no imputation is unbiased. The honest move is a missing-indicator feature, plus a sentinel or 'missing' category, so the model can learn from the missingness itself.

You can't prove the mechanism from data alone. You reason from how the data was generated, form logic, sensor behaviour, and check whether missingness correlates with other columns.

And whatever you choose, the imputer is fitted on training data only, lives in the pipeline, and the serving path handles a column being entirely absent, not just NaN."

stages.name: Ask what missingness depends on
stages.html:
Mechanism Missingness depends on Example
MCAR nothing random sensor dropout
MAR observed columns older users skip "social handle"
MNAR the missing value itself high earners skip "income"

stages.name: MCAR: deletion is safe
stages.html:
• Complete-case analysis is unbiased; you lose rows and power.
  • Simple imputation (mean/median) is fine too, though it shrinks variance.

stages.name: MAR: model-based imputation
stages.html:
• KNN imputer: borrow values from similar rows.
  • MICE / IterativeImputer: model each column from the others, iterate.
  • Mean imputation here is biased: it ignores the relationship the MAR assumption relies on.

stages.name: MNAR: missingness is signal
stages.html:
"The fact that it's missing tells you something about the value."

  • Add a missing indicator column.
  • Fill with a sentinel or "missing" category (or let GBMs route NaN natively).
  • Consider modelling the missingness process explicitly if inference matters.

stages.name: You can't prove it from data
stages.html:
• Test MCAR against MAR: does missingness correlate with observed columns? (Little's test, or a classifier predicting missingness.)
  • MNAR is untestable from observed data alone: argue from how the value is produced.

stages.name: Ship it in the pipeline
stages.html:
• Imputer fitted per training fold; stored in the artifact.
  • Serving handles NaN and absent columns.
  • Monitor production missingness rates against training.

followUps.question: Why not always add missing indicators?
followUps.html: It's often a good default, especially for trees, and it's cheap. The costs are extra columns for wide data, and a risk: if missingness patterns differ between training and serving, the indicator becomes a skew channel. Monitor missingness rates in production.

followUps.question: Does XGBoost's native missing handling solve this?
followUps.html: It learns a default direction per split for missing values, which captures informative missingness well. It doesn't recover the true value, so for MNAR it effectively uses missingness as signal, which is what you want. It doesn't protect against train/serve differences in missingness rates.

followUps.question: Can MICE make things worse?
followUps.html: Yes, under MNAR: it imputes plausible values from observed columns, confidently wrong in a systematic direction. It's also slow on large data and can leak if fitted outside the fold. Validate imputation choices by downstream model performance.

followUps.question: How much missingness is too much to keep a column?
followUps.html: There's no fixed cutoff. A column 90% missing can still be valuable if its presence is informative. Judge by whether the column (plus indicator) improves validation performance, and whether its missingness rate is stable in production.

followUps.question: In medical data, why does the mechanism matter beyond accuracy?
followUps.html: Because conclusions and fairness depend on it. If a lab test is missing because doctors only order it for sicker patients, imputing a "normal" value misrepresents patients and can bias decisions for groups tested less often. The mechanism affects validity, not just metrics.

dontSay: "I always mean-impute." — biased except under MCAR.
"I dropped rows with nulls." — safe only under MCAR.
"I tested and it's MNAR." — MNAR can't be confirmed from observed data alone.

spine: It's a skew question, not imputation
ml-dl-q32.testing: whether you diagnose why the rates differ before filling the hole.
ml-dl-q32.spoken:
"This isn't an imputation question yet. A gap from 2% to 30% means training and serving see different data, so I'd diagnose the discrepancy first.

My first suspect is availability timing. The training set was probably built from a warehouse where the value eventually arrives, say a device fingerprint that lands a few minutes after the transaction. At prediction time it isn't there yet. So the training feature effectively used the future, and the model learned to rely on something production rarely has.

The second suspect is a pipeline break: an upstream service or schema change started dropping the field.

If it's timing, imputation is a band-aid over leakage. The real fix is to rebuild the feature as it was available at prediction time, point-in-time correctness, and retrain.

If it's a break, I page the owning team, and meanwhile check the model degrades gracefully: gradient-boosted trees route missing values along a learned path, and a fitted imputer at least doesn't crash.

Either way I'd add monitors on per-feature null rates and distributions at serving time, compared against the training profile, because this failure is invisible in model metrics until fraud losses show up."

stages.name: It's a skew question, not imputation
stages.html: "Two different worlds are producing this feature." Before touching the model, find out why.

stages.name: Suspect availability timing
stages.html:
• Training data backfilled from a warehouse: the value is present because it arrived later.
  • Serving computes at request time: the value often hasn't arrived.
  • Check: compare the feature's write timestamp with the transaction timestamp in training rows.

stages.name: Rule out a pipeline break
stages.html:
• Did the null rate jump on a date? Line it up with deploys and schema changes.
  • Is it one client, region or app version?
  • A step change is a break; a constant gap since launch is availability skew.

stages.name: Fix point-in-time correctness
stages.html:
• Recompute training features using only data available at each event's timestamp (the as-of join a feature store enforces).
  • Retrain; the model now learns from the missingness rate it will actually see.
  • Add a missing indicator: in fraud, "fingerprint not yet available" can itself be a signal.

stages.name: Protect the model now
stages.html:
• Estimate current damage: score recent traffic with and without the feature; check precision at the review budget.
  • Temporary options: fall back to a model trained without the feature, tighten rules for affected traffic, or raise review capacity.

stages.name: Monitor null rates
stages.html:
• Per-feature null rate and distribution vs training profile, alerting on divergence.
  • Data contracts with upstream owners: freshness, completeness, schema.

followUps.question: Why not just impute with the training mean?
followUps.html: If the model relies heavily on that feature, a constant fill for 30% of traffic produces confident, wrong scores. And if the cause is leakage, imputing hides the real bug; the model's offline performance was never achievable in production.

followUps.question: How would a feature store have prevented this?
followUps.html: Training data would come from point-in-time joins, so a value that arrived minutes after the transaction wouldn't be in that row's features. Offline and online stores share one definition, so availability behaves the same in both.

followUps.question: Could missingness be the fraud signal?
followUps.html: Yes. Fraudsters may block device fingerprinting or use emulators. Then missingness is predictive, and an indicator feature helps, but only if its rate in training matches production. Model it deliberately, don't discover it by accident.

followUps.question: How fast would you have noticed without monitoring?
followUps.html: Possibly weeks, when chargebacks arrive, since fraud labels are delayed. That's why input monitoring matters most for delayed-label problems: null rates and score distributions are visible immediately, outcomes aren't.

followUps.question: What's in the post-incident review?
followUps.html: Root cause (timing or break), time to detect, business impact (missed fraud, false positives), and structural fixes: point-in-time training data, null-rate alerts, a data contract with the upstream team, and a pre-launch check comparing serving feature distributions against training.

dontSay: "Impute and retrain." (first) — hides the cause.
"Production data is just messier." — a 15× difference has a mechanism.
"The model metrics look fine." — fraud labels arrive late.

spine: Legitimate extremes: keep, cap or transform
ml-dl-q33.testing: whether you decide by origin and model, not by a z-score threshold.
ml-dl-q33.spoken:
"I classify the outlier by origin first, because the treatment follows from the origin, not from how many standard deviations away it is.

Error outliers, a sensor glitch, a unit mix-up, an age of 250, get corrected if I can, removed if I can't.

Legitimate extremes, a real customer who spends a hundred times the median, stay in the data. If they'd distort a scale-sensitive model like linear regression or kNN, I cap them with winsorisation or log-transform the feature. Tree models mostly don't care, so often the answer there is do nothing.

And sometimes the outlier is the whole point: in fraud or anomaly detection, the extremes are the positives. Removing them destroys the task.

Detection methods only flag. Z-scores assume normality, IQR is more robust, and Isolation Forest or LOF catch multivariate oddities. The decision still needs the origin.

Whatever I do lives in the pipeline, with thresholds fitted on training data only, and I log what was removed and why. Silently deleting inconvenient rows before the split is unreproducible and leaky, and it's how audit findings start."

stages.name: Classify by origin first
stages.html:
Origin Example Treatment
Error age 250, price in cents vs dollars correct or remove
Legitimate extreme whale customer, viral post keep; cap/transform for sensitive models
The phenomenon itself fraud, machine failure keep; it's the target

stages.name: Errors: correct or remove
stages.html:
• Impossible values violate domain rules: fix units, re-derive, or drop.
  • Report upstream; an error class that recurs is a data contract issue.

stages.name: Legitimate extremes: keep, cap or transform
stages.html:
Model Action
Linear, kNN, K-means, NNs winsorise at percentiles, or log / Yeo-Johnson
Trees, GBMs usually nothing
Regression target with heavy tail robust loss (Huber) or transformed target

stages.name: The signal itself: never touch
stages.html:
• Fraud, intrusion, equipment failure: outliers are what you're predicting.
  • Cleaning them away produces a model that's excellent at normal data and useless for the task.

stages.name: Detection only flags
stages.html:
Method Assumes / suits
Z-score roughly normal data
IQR / percentiles robust, univariate
Isolation Forest multivariate, fast, few assumptions
LOF local density differences
One-Class SVM small, clean normal data

stages.name: Make it a pipeline policy
stages.html:
• Thresholds fitted on training folds; applied identically at serving.
  • Log counts and reasons for removed or capped rows.
  • An outlier policy is a data-contract decision, reviewable like code.

followUps.question: Cap or remove a legitimate extreme in a regression target?
followUps.html: Usually neither. Keep the row and use a robust loss (Huber) or model a transformed target (log). Removing real high values biases predictions downward exactly where the business may care most.

followUps.question: Why is removing outliers before the split leaky?
followUps.html: The thresholds (mean, std, percentiles) are computed with test data, and you've altered the test distribution to be cleaner than production. The evaluation then overstates performance on real traffic, which will contain those extremes.

followUps.question: How do you handle outliers at serving time?
followUps.html: The same fitted transform: clip to training-derived bounds or apply the same log. Also alert on inputs far outside the training range; the model is extrapolating there, so predictions deserve lower trust or a fallback.

followUps.question: Isolation Forest flags 5% of rows. Remove them?
followUps.html: Not blindly. The contamination parameter sets roughly how many it flags; that's a setting, not a finding. Inspect a sample by origin; if they're legitimate, removing 5% of real behaviour hurts the model.

followUps.question: Who should own the outlier policy?
followUps.html: The model owner with the domain team: engineers can detect, but only domain experts know whether a value is impossible or rare. Document it with the data contract so changes are reviewed, not made in a notebook.

dontSay: "Anything beyond 3σ goes." — assumes normality and ignores origin.
"I clean outliers in the whole dataset first." — leaky and unreproducible.
"Outliers are noise." — sometimes they're the task.

ml-dl-q34.testing: whether you can name concrete mechanisms, not "more features is bad".
ml-dl-q34.spoken:
"Three concrete things break.

First, distances concentrate. As dimensions grow, the nearest and farthest neighbours of a point end up almost the same distance away, so distance stops discriminating. Anything built on distance degrades first: kNN, K-means, kernel methods, and quietly, vector similarity search.

Second, data becomes sparse. The volume you need to cover grows exponentially with dimensions, so any fixed dataset becomes a thin scatter. Local methods and density estimators starve: there's no neighbourhood with enough points in it.

Third, spurious correlations multiply. With many features and finite rows, some features correlate with the target by pure chance, so overfitting risk rises and feature selection becomes large-scale multiple testing.

Who resists? Regularised linear models, because the penalty handles more features than rows. Trees and boosting, because axis-aligned splits ignore irrelevant dimensions reasonably well. And models with built-in selection like Lasso.

My response ladder: prune with domain knowledge first, then filter, wrapper or embedded feature selection, and only then projection like PCA. Selection keeps interpretability; projection keeps variance but mixes features."

stages.name: Distances concentrate
stages.claim: near and far look the same
stages.html: Hit first: kNN, K-means, RBF-kernel SVMs, similarity search.

stages.name: Data becomes sparse
stages.html:
• To keep 10 bins per axis covered: 10 points in 1-D, 10¹⁰ in 10-D.
  • Density estimation, kNN and local regression find almost nothing in any neighbourhood.

stages.name: Spurious correlations multiply
stages.html:
• With 10,000 random features and 1,000 rows, some will correlate with any target.
  • Univariate filter selection becomes multiple testing: expect false discoveries unless corrected.

stages.name: Who breaks first, who resists
stages.html:
Suffers Resists
kNN, K-means, kernel methods (distance) L2/L1-regularised linear models
density estimators, local regression trees, GBMs (axis-aligned splits)
unregularised models with p ≈ n Lasso / Elastic Net (built-in selection)

stages.name: The response ladder
stages.html:
Step 1 — Domain pruning. Drop IDs, duplicates, near-constant and leaky columns.

Step 2 — Feature selection. Filter (mutual information, chi-square), wrapper (RFE), embedded (Lasso, tree importance). Keeps original, interpretable features.

Step 3 — Projection. PCA, or UMAP for visualisation. Keeps variance, loses interpretability.

Step 4 — Better representation. Learned embeddings for high-cardinality or text data.

followUps.question: Why do embedding search systems still work in 768 dimensions?
followUps.html: Real embeddings aren't uniform random points; they lie near a much lower-dimensional manifold, so distances keep meaning. Concentration hurts most on isotropic data. Cosine similarity on normalised vectors and ANN indexes also work well in practice for that reason.

followUps.question: How does regularisation help when p > n?
followUps.html: Without it, a linear model with more features than rows has infinitely many perfect fits. The penalty picks the smallest-norm (Ridge) or sparsest (Lasso) solution, trading a little bias for a lot less variance.

followUps.question: Feature selection or PCA for a regulated credit model?
followUps.html: Selection. Regulators and adverse-action reasons need named, original features; principal components are mixtures that can't be explained to a customer. PCA is fine for internal exploration, not for the explanation surface.

followUps.question: Does gradient boosting have no dimensionality problem?
followUps.html: It's more robust, not immune. Many irrelevant features dilute split search and increase the chance of fitting noise, especially with small data. Column subsampling and early stopping help; so does removing junk features first.

followUps.question: How do you avoid false discoveries in filter selection?
followUps.html: Do selection inside CV folds so validation data isn't used to pick features, correct for multiple testing or use stability selection (features chosen consistently across resamples), and compare against a permuted-target baseline.

dontSay: "More features always hurt." — trees and regularised models cope well.
"Just apply PCA." — it's the last rung, and it kills interpretability.
"Distance-based methods are fine with scaling." — scaling doesn't fix concentration.

links.label: PCA — Intuition, Math, Explained Variance & Limitations
links.target: 01-ML/05-Dimensionality Reduction/03-PCA — Intuition, Math, Explained Variance & Limitations

ml-dl-q35.testing: whether you know PCA's objective and its blind spots, not just "reduces dimensions".
ml-dl-q35.trap: using PCA before a classifier and assuming it keeps the useful signal.
ml-dl-q35.spoken:
"PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance in the data; equivalently, it's the linear projection with the smallest reconstruction error.

Mechanically, those directions are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, or more stably the right singular vectors from an SVD of the centred data. Each eigenvalue is the variance explained by its component.

It quietly assumes three things. Linearity: components are linear combinations of features. That variance equals relevance: the high-variance directions are the ones that matter. And comparable scales: a feature measured in large units hijacks the first component unless you standardise.

Where it silently fails: it's unsupervised, so the direction that separates your classes can live in a low-variance component you just threw away. It can't unfold non-linear structure like a swiss roll; that needs kernel PCA or UMAP. And components are mixtures of every feature, which is a real cost when you have to explain a model.

To choose k, use explained-variance thresholds or the scree plot, but if the downstream task is supervised, pick k by the downstream metric.

When labels exist and separation is the goal, LDA maximises class separation instead of variance."

stages.name: The objective
stages.html:
• First component: the direction along which projected data varies most.
  • Each next component: maximum remaining variance, orthogonal to the previous ones.
  • Same thing: the k-dimensional subspace that best reconstructs the data (least squares).

stages.name: The linear algebra
stages.html:
X centred (n × d)
C = XᵀX / (n − 1)            covariance
C v = λ v                    components v, variance λ
X = U Σ Vᵀ                   SVD: columns of V are components, λ = σ² / (n − 1)

SVD is preferred: numerically stabler and doesn't form XᵀX.

stages.name: Three assumptions
stages.html:
Assumption Violation Fix
Linear structure curved manifolds kernel PCA, UMAP
Variance = relevance signal in low-variance directions supervised methods, validate downstream
Comparable scales one big-unit feature dominates standardise first

stages.name: Where it silently fails
stages.html:
• Discarded signal: two classes separated along a low-variance axis collapse on top of each other.
  • Outliers: variance is squared-distance based; a few extremes rotate the components.
  • Interpretability: each component mixes all features, which is hard to defend to a regulator.
  • Leakage: fitting PCA on all data before CV.

stages.name: Choosing k
stages.html:
• Compression or visualisation: cumulative explained variance (e.g. 90–95%) or the scree elbow.
  • Feeding a supervised model: treat k as a hyperparameter, tuned by CV on the downstream metric.

stages.name: The supervised alternative
stages.html:
• LDA maximises between-class separation relative to within-class spread; at most (classes − 1) components.
  • Use it when labels exist and separation is the point.

followUps.question: Why centre the data before PCA?
followUps.html: Without centring, the first component points toward the mean rather than along the direction of spread, so it captures location, not variance. sklearn's PCA centres automatically; a raw SVD doesn't.

followUps.question: Does PCA help tree models?
followUps.html: Usually not, and it can hurt. Trees split on individual features; rotating features into mixtures destroys the axis-aligned structure they exploit and removes interpretability. It can help linear or distance-based models on correlated inputs.

followUps.question: How do you use PCA without leakage?
followUps.html: Put it in the pipeline after scaling, so it's fitted on each training fold only and the fitted projection ships with the model.

followUps.question: PCA vs t-SNE vs UMAP?
followUps.html: PCA is linear, deterministic, preserves global variance and can transform new points. t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods for visualisation only. UMAP is non-linear, faster, keeps a bit more global structure and can transform new points, but distances on its map still aren't trustworthy.

followUps.question: PCA on 10 million rows and 5,000 features?
followUps.html: Use randomized SVD or incremental PCA (IncrementalPCA) to avoid the full covariance, compute on a sample to choose k, then transform in batches. On GPU, cuML's PCA handles this comfortably.

dontSay: "PCA keeps the most important features." — it keeps the most variance, as mixtures.
"I don't need to scale for PCA." — big-unit features dominate.
"Explained variance tells me the right k for my classifier." — validate on the downstream metric.

spine: Use it as a picture, not a ruler
ml-dl-q36.testing: whether you know which properties of an embedding are meaningful.
ml-dl-q36.trap: agreeing that the plot's cluster sizes and gaps are findings.
ml-dl-q36.spoken:
"I'd tell them the plot is a good picture but a bad ruler.

t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods: points that are close in the original space stay close. It deliberately doesn't preserve anything else. Distances between clusters are meaningless. Cluster sizes and densities are artifacts, because the algorithm tends to equalise them. And the layout changes with the perplexity setting and the random seed; at the wrong perplexity you can see clusters in pure noise.

So the segment sizes and distances in the report aren't findings about customers.

The legitimate use is visualisation and hypothesis generation. The fix is to cluster in the original space, or a PCA-reduced version of it, then use t-SNE only to look at the result.

UMAP is faster, keeps a bit more global structure and can place new points, but the same rule applies: don't measure the map.

Then validate the segments properly: silhouette in the clustering space, stability across seeds and resamples, and above all, whether the segments differ on business variables the clustering never saw.

And I'd say it kindly: it's like measuring country sizes on a Mercator map. The map is useful; the measurement isn't."

stages.name: What t-SNE preserves
stages.html:
• It matches the probability that points are neighbours in the original space and in 2-D.
  • Neighbours stay neighbours; that's the whole promise.

stages.name: What it distorts
stages.html:
Plot feature Meaningful?
Which points sit together ✅ mostly
Gap between clusters ❌
Cluster size / area ❌ (densities equalised)
Cluster count ⚠️ depends on perplexity, can appear from noise
Layout, orientation ❌ changes with seed

stages.name: Use it as a picture, not a ruler
stages.html:
• Good for: spotting structure, outliers, label noise, a sanity look at embeddings.
  • Not for: sizes, distances, cluster definitions, or anything reported as a number.

stages.name: Cluster in the real space
stages.html:
• Scale features; optionally reduce with PCA.
  • Run K-means / GMM / HDBSCAN there.
  • Colour the t-SNE or UMAP plot by those cluster labels to show them.

stages.name: Validate the segments
stages.html:
• Internal: silhouette, Davies-Bouldin in the clustering space.
  • Stability: same clusters across seeds, bootstrap samples (ARI between runs).
  • External: significant differences on revenue, churn, product usage not used to build them.

stages.name: Say it kindly
stages.html: "The picture is right about neighbours and wrong about sizes, like a world map. Let's define segments in the data, then use the plot to show them."

followUps.question: What does perplexity control?
followUps.html: Roughly the effective number of neighbours each point considers. Low perplexity focuses on very local structure and can fragment data into spurious clusters; high perplexity merges them. Always compare several values before reading structure into a plot.

followUps.question: Is UMAP safe to cluster on?
followUps.html: Safer than t-SNE and sometimes used (UMAP then HDBSCAN is a common recipe), but distances and densities are still distorted by its parameters. If you do it, validate stability and external differences just as strictly, and don't report map distances.

followUps.question: Can new customers be placed on a t-SNE map?
followUps.html: Not properly. Standard t-SNE has no transform for new points; you'd have to rerun it, which moves everything. UMAP and parametric t-SNE can transform new data.

followUps.question: The stakeholders already loved the plot. How do you correct course?
followUps.html: Keep the visual, change the evidence. Re-derive segments properly, show that the key segments (maybe most of them) still hold, and present sizes and differences from the real clustering. Frame it as making the result defensible, not as wrong work.

followUps.question: What would make you trust a segmentation?
followUps.html: It's stable under resampling, segments differ meaningfully on variables they weren't built from, they persist over time, and each can be described in one actionable sentence.

dontSay: "Segment B is twice as big as segment C." (from the plot) — sizes are artifacts.
"These two groups are far apart, so very different." — inter-cluster gaps mean nothing.
"t-SNE is wrong, don't use it." — it's a fine visualisation tool.

spine: Ask what the model is for
Constant variance and normality break intervals
ml-dl-q37.testing: whether you separate what breaks coefficients, predictions, standard errors and interpretation.
ml-dl-q37.trap: reciting LINE as a checklist where every violation is fatal.
ml-dl-q37.spoken:
"Which assumptions matter depends on whether the model is for prediction or for explanation, because each one breaks something different.

Linearity breaks predictions. If the true relationship is curved, the model is simply wrong. You fix it with transforms, polynomial or spline terms, or a different model; a residuals-versus-fitted plot with structure is the tell.

Independence of errors breaks inference and validation. With time series or grouped data, errors are correlated, so standard errors and random cross-validation are wildly optimistic. It's the one people violate without noticing.

Constant variance and normality of errors break intervals, not point predictions. The coefficients stay unbiased; the confidence and prediction intervals lie. Fix with robust standard errors, weighted least squares, or modelling the variance.

Multicollinearity breaks interpretation. Correlated predictors give unstable, sign-flipping coefficients with huge VIFs while predictions stay fine. That's fatal if the deliverable is 'which factor matters', harmless if it's the forecast.

So for prediction I care most about linearity and independence; for explanation I need all of them."

stages.name: Ask what the model is for
stages.html:
Assumption Breaks Matters for prediction? For explanation?
Linearity predictions (bias) ✅ ✅
Independent errors standard errors, CV ✅ (validation) ✅
Homoscedasticity intervals, SEs only for intervals ✅
Normal errors small-sample inference rarely ✅ (small n)
No multicollinearity coefficient stability ❌ ✅

stages.name: Linearity breaks predictions
stages.html:
• Symptom: curved pattern in residuals vs fitted.
  • Fix: log/Box-Cox, polynomial or spline terms, interactions, or a non-linear model.

stages.name: Independence breaks validation
stages.html:
• Time series, repeated measures per customer, clustered data.
  • Symptoms: autocorrelated residuals (Durbin-Watson, ACF plot), CV scores far above production.
  • Fix: time/group-aware splits, lagged terms, mixed models, clustered standard errors.

stages.name: Constant variance and normality break intervals
stages.html:
• Heteroscedasticity: fan-shaped residuals; SEs and intervals wrong, coefficients unbiased.
  • Fix: robust (HC) standard errors, weighted least squares, log target.
  • Normality matters mainly for small-sample inference; by the CLT, less so at scale.

stages.name: Multicollinearity breaks interpretation
stages.html:
• VIF > 5–10: coefficients unstable, can flip sign between samples.
  • Fix for explanation: drop or combine correlated features, Ridge, or domain-driven selection.
  • For prediction: often leave it.

stages.name: Diagnose with residuals
stages.html: Residuals vs fitted, Q-Q plot, scale-location, residuals vs time/order. Plus VIFs. Ten minutes that tell you which conclusions you're allowed to draw.

followUps.question: Must the features be normally distributed?
followUps.html: No. The assumption is about the errors, not the inputs. Skewed features are fine; transforming them can help linearity, but normality of X isn't required.

followUps.question: Coefficients flip sign when you add a feature. Why?
followUps.html: Multicollinearity, or the new feature is a confounder. The coefficient now means "effect holding the new feature constant", which can differ in sign from the marginal relationship (Simpson's-paradox territory). Check VIFs and think causally before interpreting.

followUps.question: How does heteroscedasticity hurt a pricing model's prediction intervals?
followUps.html: If variance grows with price, a single interval width is too wide for cheap items and too narrow for expensive ones, so risk is underestimated exactly where money is largest. Model log price, or use quantile regression for the interval bounds.

followUps.question: Is R² a good check of assumptions?
followUps.html: No. R² measures variance explained, not validity; you can have high R² with badly autocorrelated or heteroscedastic residuals. Residual plots and out-of-sample error matter more.

followUps.question: An executive asks "what drives sales?" from your regression. What caveats do you give?
followUps.html: Coefficients are associations holding other variables fixed, not causal effects; confounders and collinearity can mislead; and intervals assume the error model holds. For decisions, pair it with an experiment or a causal design.

dontSay: "Features must be normally distributed." — it's the errors.
"Multicollinearity ruins predictions." — it ruins interpretation.
"Every assumption must hold or the model is useless." — depends on the use.

ml-dl-q38.testing: the geometric reason L1 gives zeros, and choosing by the structure of the truth.
ml-dl-q38.trap: "Lasso is better because it selects features."
ml-dl-q38.spoken:
"Both add a penalty on coefficient size, trading a little bias for a lot less variance. They differ in the shape of the penalty.

Ridge uses L2, the sum of squared coefficients. It shrinks everything smoothly toward zero but never exactly to zero. Geometrically the constraint region is a circle, with no corners for the loss contours to touch on an axis. It wins when there are many small, correlated effects: it spreads weight across correlated features and stabilises them.

Lasso uses L1, the sum of absolute values. Its constraint region is a diamond whose corners sit on the axes, so the optimum often lands exactly on a corner, with some coefficients at zero. That's built-in feature selection, and it wins when the truth is sparse: a few real drivers among many candidates.

Lasso's weakness: among correlated features it picks one arbitrarily and drops the rest, so the selection is unstable, and with more features than rows it selects at most n.

Elastic Net blends both: selection plus grouped stability for correlated features.

Two practicalities: all of them need standardised features, because the penalty is scale-sensitive, and lambda is chosen by cross-validation. For depth: Ridge is a Gaussian prior on coefficients, Lasso a Laplace prior."

stages.name: Both trade bias for variance
stages.html:
Ridge:        min ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ Σ βⱼ²
Lasso:        min ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ Σ |βⱼ|
Elastic Net:  min ‖y − Xβ‖² + λ [ α Σ |βⱼ| + (1 − α) Σ βⱼ² ]

stages.name: Ridge: smooth shrinkage
stages.html:
• Circle-shaped constraint: loss contours touch it at a point generally off the axes, so no exact zeros.
  • Closed form: β = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy; the λI term also fixes singular XᵀX.
  • Correlated features share weight instead of one hogging it.

stages.name: Lasso: exact zeros from corners
stages.html:
• Diamond corners lie on the axes; contours usually first touch at a corner.
  • Result: sparse β, automatic selection, easier explanation.
  • No closed form; solved by coordinate descent.

stages.name: Lasso's weakness
stages.html:
• Picks one of a correlated group arbitrarily; which one changes across resamples.
  • With p > n, selects at most n features.
  • Selection instability is a problem when "which features matter" is the deliverable.

stages.name: Elastic Net
stages.html:
• L1 part gives sparsity; L2 part groups correlated features so they enter or leave together.
  • Two hyperparameters (λ, α), both by CV.
Truth / data Pick
Many small correlated effects Ridge
Few strong drivers, low correlation Lasso
Sparse but correlated groups, p ≫ n Elastic Net

stages.name: Practicalities
stages.html:
• Standardise features, or the penalty shrinks by units rather than importance.
  • Tune λ on a log grid with CV (LassoCV, ElasticNetCV).
  • Bayesian view: Ridge = Gaussian prior, Lasso = Laplace prior on β.

followUps.question: Why exactly does L1 produce zeros and L2 doesn't?
followUps.html: In the penalty's gradient: L2's derivative 2λβ shrinks toward zero as β does, so it never pushes all the way. L1's subgradient is a constant λ·sign(β) regardless of size, so small coefficients get pushed to exactly zero and held there (soft-thresholding).

followUps.question: Should you trust Lasso's selected features as "the drivers"?
followUps.html: Cautiously. With correlated features the choice is arbitrary and unstable. Use stability selection (how often a feature is chosen across bootstraps) and Elastic Net before telling anyone these are the causes, and remember it's still association.

followUps.question: Is regularisation relevant for gradient boosting?
followUps.html: Yes, in its own form: XGBoost has L1 (alpha) and L2 (lambda) on leaf weights, plus depth, learning rate and subsampling. Same principle: constrain complexity to reduce variance.

followUps.question: How do you pick λ?
followUps.html: Cross-validation over a log-spaced grid. A common rule is the "one standard error" choice: the largest λ whose CV error is within one SE of the minimum, giving a simpler model with statistically equivalent performance.

followUps.question: Where does weight decay in neural nets fit?
followUps.html: Weight decay is L2 regularisation applied to network weights. With adaptive optimisers it must be decoupled from the gradient (AdamW) to behave like true L2 shrinkage, otherwise the effective penalty varies by parameter.

dontSay: "Lasso is always better because it selects features." — depends on the truth's structure.
"Ridge sets unimportant coefficients to zero." — it never reaches zero.
"No need to scale for regularisation." — the penalty is scale-sensitive.

spine: Three ways to estimate the gradient
Problem 2: one step size for all
What still dominates: the learning rate
ml-dl-q39.testing: whether you can name the two problems optimizers solve and which feature fixes which.
ml-dl-q39.spoken:
"The three variants differ in how much data each gradient estimate uses.

Batch gradient descent uses the whole dataset per step: exact gradient, deterministic, but one slow step per pass and memory-bound. Stochastic gradient descent uses one example: very cheap, very noisy. The noise helps escape shallow minima but makes convergence jittery. Mini-batch is the production compromise: vectorised on GPUs and less noisy, with batch size trading gradient noise against steps per second.

Vanilla SGD then has two separate problems. The direction is noisy and oscillates across narrow valleys; momentum fixes that by following an exponential moving average of gradients, which damps the zigzag and speeds up consistent directions.

The second problem: one learning rate for every parameter. AdaGrad and RMSProp fix that by dividing each parameter's step by a running magnitude of its past gradients, so rarely updated parameters get bigger steps. RMSProp's moving average stops AdaGrad's step size shrinking to zero.

Adam is momentum plus RMSProp, with bias correction for the first steps, so it solves both at once, which is why it's the default. The caveats: tuned SGD with momentum sometimes generalises slightly better, AdamW is the modern variant, and the learning-rate schedule still matters more than the choice between good optimizers."

stages.name: Three ways to estimate the gradient
stages.html:
Variant Data per step Pros Cons
Batch all n exact, deterministic slow per step, memory
Stochastic 1 cheap, noise escapes shallow minima noisy, poor hardware use
Mini-batch 32–4096 GPU-efficient, moderate noise batch size is a hyperparameter

stages.name: Problem 1: noisy direction
stages.html:
v ← β v + (1 − β) g          (β ≈ 0.9)
θ ← θ − η v
  • Averages out zigzags across steep, narrow valleys; accelerates along consistent slopes.
  • Nesterov: evaluate the gradient at the look-ahead position for slightly better corrections.

stages.name: Problem 2: one step size for all
stages.html:
s ← β₂ s + (1 − β₂) g²       RMSProp (AdaGrad sums instead: s ← s + g²)
θ ← θ − η g / (√s + ε)
  • Parameters with large gradients take smaller steps; rare features get larger ones.
  • AdaGrad's sum only grows, so its step size decays to zero; RMSProp's moving average avoids that.

stages.name: Adam = both fixes
stages.html:
m ← β₁ m + (1 − β₁) g        direction (momentum)
v ← β₂ v + (1 − β₂) g²       scale (RMSProp)
m̂ = m / (1 − β₁ᵗ),  v̂ = v / (1 − β₂ᵗ)      correct the zero-initialised start
θ ← θ − η m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)
  • AdamW: apply weight decay directly to θ, not through the gradient (see Q62).

stages.name: What still dominates: the learning rate
stages.html:
• A bad LR ruins any optimizer; a good schedule (warmup, then cosine or step decay) matters more than SGD vs Adam.
  • Batch size and LR interact: larger batches often need proportionally larger LR (linear scaling rule) plus warmup.

followUps.question: Why does SGD sometimes generalise better than Adam?
followUps.html: One common explanation: SGD's noise and uniform step size bias it toward flatter minima, which tend to generalise better, while Adam's per-parameter scaling can settle into sharper ones. It's task-dependent; for transformers, AdamW is the standard anyway.

followUps.question: What does bias correction fix?
followUps.html: m and v start at zero, so early moving averages are biased toward zero, especially v with β₂ = 0.999. Without correction the first steps would be the wrong size. Dividing by (1 − βᵗ) removes that bias; its effect fades after a few thousand steps.

followUps.question: How does batch size affect training?
followUps.html: Bigger batches give less noisy gradients and better hardware utilisation, but fewer updates per epoch and, beyond a point, diminishing returns and sometimes worse generalisation. Scale LR with batch size and use warmup when going large.

followUps.question: Is Adam's memory cost relevant?
followUps.html: Yes at scale: it keeps two extra fp32 states per parameter, about 8 bytes each parameter on top of weights and gradients. For a 7B model that's ~56 GB of optimizer state alone, which is why sharded optimizers (ZeRO) and 8-bit optimizers exist.

followUps.question: When would you still use plain SGD with momentum?
followUps.html: Computer-vision training of CNNs often still uses it with a well-tuned schedule, and when memory is tight it avoids Adam's extra state. For linear models on huge sparse data, SGD-based solvers are common too.

dontSay: "Adam is always better." — it solves two specific problems; the LR schedule still dominates.
"Mini-batch is just faster SGD." — it's a variance-throughput trade-off.
"Momentum adapts the learning rate." — that's the second moment's job.

spine: The loss is where business cost enters
ml-dl-q40.testing: whether you derive the loss from the cost structure.
ml-dl-q40.spoken:
"The sentence hides two requirements: robustness to a heavy tail, and asymmetry, because under-forecasting costs more than over-forecasting.

MSE fails both. It squares errors, so the occasional huge order dominates training, and it's symmetric. MAE fixes robustness, since it predicts the median and grows linearly, but it's still symmetric and its constant gradient makes optimisation cruder.

Huber blends the two: squared near zero, linear in the tails, with delta setting the crossover. That gives robustness with clean gradients, but it's still symmetric.

The direct answer is quantile, or pinball, loss. Training at, say, the 0.8 quantile penalises under-prediction four times as much as over-prediction, so the business asymmetry lives in the objective instead of a fudge added afterwards. Gradient boosting libraries support it natively.

An alternative for the tail is modelling log of order value, but you then need to correct the retransformation bias, and it's still symmetric in log space.

The meta-point I'd say out loud: the loss function is where business cost enters the model. Choosing it by convention instead of by the cost structure is the actual mistake."

stages.name: Two requirements in one sentence
stages.html:
Requirement Needs
"occasionally huge" a loss robust to large errors
"under-forecasting costs more" a loss whose penalty depends on the error's sign

stages.name: Why MSE and MAE fail
stages.html:
Loss Tail-robust Asymmetric Predicts
MSE ❌ ❌ mean
MAE ✅ ❌ median
Huber ✅ ❌ between mean and median
Quantile (τ) ✅ ✅ τ-quantile

stages.name: Huber for the tail
stages.html:
• Quadratic for |error| < δ, linear beyond.
  • δ chosen relative to the typical error scale; tune by CV.
  • Good when the tail is noise you don't want to chase.

stages.name: Quantile loss for the asymmetry
stages.html:
• Pick τ from the cost ratio: if under costs c_u and over costs c_o per unit, τ = c_u / (c_u + c_o). Under 4× over → τ = 0.8.
  • LightGBM / XGBoost: objective="quantile", alpha=0.8.

stages.name: Log target as an alternative
stages.html:
• Train on log(value): compresses whales, errors become roughly multiplicative.
  • Retransformation: exp(prediction) estimates the median, not the mean; apply a smearing correction if you need the mean.
  • Still symmetric in log space; combine with a quantile objective if asymmetry matters.

stages.name: The loss is where business cost enters
stages.html: Evaluate with the same cost: report expected business cost (asymmetric) on a holdout, not RMSE.

followUps.question: How do you get the quantile from the cost ratio?
followUps.html: The pinball loss at τ is minimised by the τ-quantile of the conditional distribution. Expected cost is minimised where the probability of being under equals c_o / (c_u + c_o), so τ = c_u / (c_u + c_o). With under-forecasting 4× as costly, τ = 0.8.

followUps.question: Why not train MSE and add a safety margin afterwards?
followUps.html: A constant margin ignores that uncertainty varies by order: small, predictable orders need little buffer, volatile ones need a lot. Quantile regression learns a conditional buffer per input, which is cheaper on average for the same protection.

followUps.question: Can you get prediction intervals this way?
followUps.html: Yes: train quantile models at, say, 0.1 and 0.9 for an 80% interval. Watch for quantile crossing (the lower above the upper) and check calibration: about 80% of holdout actuals should fall inside.

followUps.question: What metric do you report?
followUps.html: The business cost with the real asymmetry (e.g. 4 × under-units + 1 × over-units, in money), plus quantile coverage. RMSE on a quantile model is meaningless because it rewards predicting the mean.

followUps.question: When would you use Tweedie or Poisson loss instead?
followUps.html: When many orders are zero and the rest are positive and skewed, like spend per visitor. Tweedie models that mix of a point mass at zero and a continuous tail; you can still add asymmetry through a quantile-based decision on top.

dontSay: "MSE because it's the standard regression loss." — fails both requirements.
"Log the target and it's handled." — fixes the tail, not the asymmetry.
"We'll add 20% to every forecast." — ignores varying uncertainty.
