spine: Why it's first: it prices the problem
ml-dl-q41.testing: the mechanism, plus judgement about baselines and production value.
ml-dl-q41.trap: "it squashes a linear output through a sigmoid."
ml-dl-q41.spoken:
"Mechanically, it models the log-odds of the positive class as a linear function of the features. The sigmoid isn't the model; it's just the function that turns log-odds back into a probability. It's trained by maximum likelihood, which is the same as minimising cross-entropy, and each coefficient is a log-odds ratio: a directly interpretable effect size.

I train it first because it prices the problem. If gradient boosting only beats it by a hair, the signal is mostly linear and I ship the simple thing. If there's a big gap, that tells me the problem needs interactions and non-linearity, and by how much.

It also has operational virtues that keep it in production at serious companies. Its probabilities are reasonably calibrated out of the box, which trees' aren't. It scores in microseconds on any hardware, the artifact is tiny, it's stable across retrains, and it's easy to explain to model-risk teams and regulators.

And with regularisation and good feature engineering, interactions, binning or weight-of-evidence encoding, it stays genuinely competitive on wide, sparse data. Ads and credit-risk stacks relied on it for decades for exactly that reason."

stages.name: What it models: linear log-odds
stages.html:
log( p / (1 − p) ) = β₀ + β·x          the model
p = 1 / (1 + e^−(β₀ + β·x))            inverse link back to probability
  • A one-unit increase in xⱼ multiplies the odds by e^βⱼ.

stages.name: How it's trained: maximum likelihood
stages.html:
• Maximise Π p^y (1 − p)^(1−y) ⇔ minimise binary cross-entropy.
  • Convex: one global optimum, solved with L-BFGS, Newton or SGD.
  • Regularisation (L2 default in sklearn, C = 1/λ) prevents blow-up on separable data.

stages.name: Why it's first: it prices the problem
stages.html:
Logistic vs boosting gap Reading
tiny signal mostly linear; ship logistic
moderate interactions matter; boosting may be worth its cost
huge strongly non-linear, or check for leakage in the complex model

stages.name: Operational virtues
stages.html:
• Calibrated probabilities (with a well-specified model), good for thresholds and expected value.
  • Microsecond scoring, kilobyte artifact, CPU or edge.
  • Explainable coefficients and reason codes; auditors understand it.
  • Stable across retrains; small, reviewable changes.

stages.name: Making it competitive
stages.html:
• Interactions and polynomial terms for known effects.
  • Binning / weight-of-evidence for non-linear numeric effects (credit scorecards).
  • One-hot or hashed high-cardinality categoricals on sparse data, with L1/L2.
  • Multiclass: softmax (multinomial) or one-vs-rest.

followUps.question: Why cross-entropy and not MSE for logistic regression?
followUps.html: Cross-entropy is its likelihood, so it's the principled loss, and it's convex in the coefficients. MSE through a sigmoid is non-convex and has vanishing gradients when the model is confidently wrong. See Q19 for the gradient argument.

followUps.question: What happens with perfectly separable data?
followUps.html: Unregularised, the likelihood keeps improving as coefficients grow, so they diverge to infinity and probabilities become 0 or 1. Regularisation keeps them finite, which is one reason sklearn regularises by default.

followUps.question: Is it really calibrated out of the box?
followUps.html: When the model is well specified and not heavily regularised or class-weighted, typically close. Strong regularisation, class weights or resampling distort it. Always check a reliability curve before using probabilities in decisions.

followUps.question: How do you interpret a coefficient of 0.7 on a standardised feature?
followUps.html: One standard deviation increase multiplies the odds by e^0.7 ≈ 2, holding other features fixed. It's association, not causation, and correlated features make individual coefficients less stable.

followUps.question: When would you ship logistic over a better-scoring GBM?
followUps.html: When the gain is within noise or small in business terms, when regulators need transparent reasons, when latency or hardware is tight, or when stability and ease of monitoring outweigh a small accuracy win. Price the gap, then decide.

dontSay: "It squashes a linear score with a sigmoid." — that's the link, not the model.
"It's outdated." — it's the baseline and still a production workhorse.
"It can't model non-linearity." — with feature engineering it can.

ml-dl-q42.testing: breadth under time pressure, with a structural reason for each weakness.
ml-dl-q42.trap: long answers per model; this is rapid fire.
ml-dl-q42.spoken:
"Decision tree. Killer property: human-readable rules, handles mixed types and missing values, and needs no preprocessing. Weakness: high variance. Small changes in the data restructure the whole tree, so a single tree is almost always beaten by its own ensemble. Depth and minimum leaf size are its bias-variance dials.

kNN. Killer property: zero training and arbitrarily complex decision boundaries, which makes it a strong lazy baseline. Weakness: inference cost and the curse of dimensionality. It stores and searches the data at query time, distances lose meaning as dimensions grow, and it needs scaling. In production it becomes an approximate-nearest-neighbour index, at which point it's really a retrieval system.

Naive Bayes. Killer property: absurdly fast, works with tiny data and huge sparse vocabularies like text, and updates online. Weakness: the conditional-independence assumption makes its probabilities badly calibrated and overconfident, even when the ranking is decent. Fine as a filter, wrong as a probability source.

The pattern: each is a regime specialist. Trees for interpretable tabular rules, kNN when data is small and local structure is everything, naive Bayes for sparse counts. And all three are baselines that price the problem before boosting."

stages.name: Decision tree
stages.html:
• Killer: if-then rules anyone can audit; mixed types, missing values, no scaling.
  • Weakness: high variance; greedy splits change drastically with small data changes.
  • Dials: max_depth, min_samples_leaf, cost-complexity pruning.
  • Usually superseded by: Random Forest (variance) or boosting (bias).

stages.name: kNN
stages.html:
• Killer: instant "training", flexible boundaries, intuitive.
  • Weakness: O(n·d) per query, memory = the dataset, distance concentration in high d, needs scaling.
  • Production form: ANN index (FAISS/HNSW); recommendation and semantic search.

stages.name: Naive Bayes
stages.html:
• Killer: trains in one pass, tiny data, huge sparse features, online updates.
  • Weakness: assumes features independent given the class; correlated features double-count evidence → extreme probabilities.
  • Variants: Multinomial (counts, text), Bernoulli (binary), Gaussian (continuous).

stages.name: The pattern: regime specialists
stages.html:
Model Best regime Avoid when
Decision tree need readable rules accuracy matters more than readability
kNN small data, local structure high d, tight latency, huge n
Naive Bayes sparse text/counts, very little data calibrated probabilities needed

stages.name: Where each still ships
stages.html:
• Tree: policy rules, compliance-friendly models, surrogate explanations.
  • kNN: similarity search, recommendation candidates, embedding lookups.
  • Naive Bayes: spam and text triage, very-low-latency first-pass filters.

followUps.question: How do you fix naive Bayes calibration?
followUps.html: Post-hoc calibration on held-out data (Platt or isotonic), or reduce correlated features. For ranking-only uses like spam filtering with a tuned threshold, you may not need to.

followUps.question: Why does Random Forest fix the tree's weakness but not boosting's style?
followUps.html: Random Forest averages many deep, decorrelated trees, cancelling variance, which is the single tree's problem. Boosting attacks bias with shallow trees. Both beat one tree, for different reasons (see Q11).

followUps.question: How do you choose k in kNN?
followUps.html: Cross-validate; small k is low bias / high variance, large k smooths. Use odd k for binary classification to avoid ties, distance-weighted voting, and always scale features first.

followUps.question: Why does naive Bayes work well for text despite a false assumption?
followUps.html: Classification only needs the correct class to have the highest score, not correct probabilities. Violated independence distorts magnitudes but often preserves the ranking, and with huge sparse vocabularies its low variance beats more flexible models on small data.

followUps.question: Would you ship a single decision tree?
followUps.html: Yes, when the requirement is auditable rules: a compliance policy or a triage rule set humans must follow. I'd constrain depth, validate stability across resamples, and compare its accuracy to an ensemble so the trade-off is explicit.

dontSay: "Naive Bayes probabilities are good because it's Bayesian." — independence breaks calibration.
"kNN is cheap." — cheap to train, expensive to serve.
"Decision trees are the best because interpretable." — high variance alone.

ml-dl-q43.testing: whether you verify before debating, and price accuracy against operational cost.
ml-dl-q43.trap: debating ship-or-not before checking the 0.4 is real.
ml-dl-q43.spoken:
"Before arguing either side, I'd check the gain is real. The meta-learner must be trained on out-of-fold predictions from the base models; training it on in-sample predictions is leakage and the 0.4 could be fiction. Then I'd re-measure on a time-split holdout with a confidence interval, because 0.4 points is often inside the noise.

If it's real, the case for shipping: at high volume in ads, risk or pricing, 0.4 AUC can translate into real money that dwarfs the infrastructure cost. And genuinely diverse base models, say linear plus trees plus a neural net, hedge each other's failure modes.

The case against is an operations list. You now version, retrain, monitor and keep consistent several models instead of one. Inference latency and cost multiply. Debugging drift becomes 'which of five models moved?'. Explainability gets harder. And stacking gains often shrink under drift, because the meta-weights were fit to one period's error structure.

Middle paths: a simple weighted blend of two diverse models often captures most of the gain, or distil the ensemble into a single student model for serving.

The deciding move is to price the 0.4 in money and let the ops cost argue against it honestly."

stages.name: First, is the gain real?
stages.html:
• Out-of-fold meta-training: base models predict on folds they didn't train on; the meta-learner trains on those predictions.
  • Time-split holdout with a bootstrap CI on the AUC difference.
  • Keep the meta-learner simple (logistic, ridge); the diversity of bases does the work.

stages.name: The case for shipping
stages.html:
• High-volume decisions: small ranking gains compound (ads, credit, fraud, pricing).
  • Diverse bases reduce correlated failure modes.
  • The value is measurable in an A/B test.

stages.name: The case against
stages.html:
Cost Why it hurts
N models to retrain, version, monitor N× failure surface
Latency and compute sequential or parallel inference of all bases
Drift debugging which component moved?
Explainability reason codes across a blend
Gain decay meta-weights fit to one era

stages.name: Middle paths
stages.claim: most of the gain, less cost
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Weighted blend

Average two genuinely different models (e.g. GBM + logistic) with a weight tuned on validation.

Why? Most stacking gain comes from diversity, not a clever meta-learner.

Best suited when two diverse models are already in production or cheap to run.

Experiment 2

Distillation

Train one student model on the ensemble's predictions.

Why? Serve one model with most of the ensemble's accuracy.

Best suited when latency or ops cost is the main objection.

stages.name: Decide in money
stages.html: Convert 0.4 AUC into expected profit or loss at the operating point, subtract the added infra and team cost, and confirm with an A/B test. If it doesn't clear a pre-agreed bar, ship the single model.

followUps.question: Why must the meta-learner train on out-of-fold predictions?
followUps.html: In-sample predictions are overconfident because the bases saw those rows. The meta-learner learns to trust whichever base overfits most, a relationship that won't hold on new data. Out-of-fold predictions mimic what the bases produce at serving time.

followUps.question: The bases are three GBMs with different seeds. Worth stacking?
followUps.html: Rarely. They make highly correlated errors, so there's little to combine; simple averaging captures the small variance reduction. Stacking pays off with genuinely different model families or feature views.

followUps.question: How would you monitor a stacked model in production?
followUps.html: Monitor each base's score distribution and the meta-model's inputs, not just the final output, and periodically re-check the meta-weights on recent data. A shift in one base explains most incidents; you need to see it separately.

followUps.question: Is 0.4 AUC points large?
followUps.html: Depends on the operating point and volume. It could be meaningful at the top of a fraud queue, or it could all come from reordering cases below the threshold that nobody looks at. Measure precision/recall at the actual operating point.

followUps.question: When is stacking clearly worth it?
followUps.html: Competitions and high-stakes, high-volume systems with strong MLOps, where each point of accuracy is worth money and the team can maintain several models. Even then, check that a blend or distillation doesn't get you there cheaper.

dontSay: "Ship it, it's higher." — verify, then price.
"Never use ensembles in production." — sometimes worth it.
"The meta-learner should be a GBM too." — keep it simple.

ml-dl-q44.testing: whether you know what each importance measures and its biases.
ml-dl-q44.trap: picking one as "the truth" without saying what it measures.
ml-dl-q44.spoken:
"I'd trust SHAP more, but first say what each one measures, because they answer different questions.

XGBoost's default importance, gain or split count, measures how much each feature was used during training. It's biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features, which offer more split points; correlated features split the credit unpredictably; and it describes the training set, not generalisation.

Permutation importance shuffles a feature on validation data and measures the drop in performance. That's closer to what the model actually relies on, but correlated features mask each other: shuffle one and its twin covers for it.

SHAP allocates each prediction's difference from the baseline across features, with consistency guarantees from Shapley values, and gives both local and global views. TreeSHAP computes it exactly and fast for trees. It's generally the most trustworthy of the three, though it also spreads credit across correlated features rather than resolving them.

None of them is causal. They all describe the model, not the world, and a leaky feature will top all three charts.

In practice I use SHAP for rankings and explanations, permutation as a cross-check, and treat disagreements as a diagnostic: they usually point to correlated clusters or leakage."

stages.name: What gain importance counts
stages.html:
• Gain: total loss reduction from splits on the feature.
  • Weight / split count: how often the feature is used.
  • Cover: how many samples those splits affected.
  • All measured on training data, inside the fitting process.

stages.name: Its biases
stages.html:
Bias Effect
High cardinality / continuous more candidate splits → inflated importance
Correlated features arbitrary credit split between twins
Training-set based rewards features the model overfit on
Metric choice gain, weight, cover can rank differently from each other

stages.name: Permutation importance
stages.html:
• Shuffle one column in validation data; importance = metric drop.
  • Model-agnostic, generalisation-aware.
  • Weakness: correlated features cover for each other; shuffling creates unrealistic rows.

stages.name: SHAP
stages.html:
• Local: each prediction's deviation from the baseline, split across features, summing exactly.
  • Global: mean |SHAP| per feature; beeswarm shows direction and spread.
  • TreeSHAP: exact and fast for tree ensembles.
  • Still shares credit among correlated features.

stages.name: None is causal
stages.html: Every method explains the model's behaviour. A leaked feature, or a proxy for something else, can top every chart. Importance ≠ cause ≠ acceptable-to-use.

stages.name: Use disagreements as a diagnostic
stages.html:
Pattern Likely reason
High gain, low permutation/SHAP high-cardinality feature used for noisy splits
High SHAP, low permutation correlated twin covers when shuffled
One feature tops all three by far check for leakage

followUps.question: How do you handle correlated features in importance?
followUps.html: Group them: compute permutation or SHAP importance for the group together (shuffle the whole cluster). Or cluster features by correlation and pick representatives. Report group importance instead of pretending to split credit precisely.

followUps.question: Why is a random ID feature sometimes "important"?
followUps.html: High-cardinality features give many split options; trees can use them to memorise training rows, inflating gain. Permutation importance on validation data usually exposes it as near zero. If it stays high, check whether the ID encodes time or leakage.

followUps.question: Which would you show a regulator?
followUps.html: SHAP-based reason codes per decision, with documentation of the method, a stability check across retrains, and review of whether top features are legitimate to use. Never gain importance: it's unstable and not tied to individual decisions.

followUps.question: Is permutation importance on training data useful?
followUps.html: It measures what the model memorised, not what generalises. Always compute it on held-out data to see what the model relies on for new cases.

followUps.question: How do importances help with drift monitoring?
followUps.html: Track mean |SHAP| per feature over time. A sudden change in a feature's contribution flags a data or pipeline change even before labels arrive.

dontSay: "Gain importance shows what matters most." — it shows training usage, with biases.
"SHAP tells us the causes." — it explains the model.
"They disagree, so I'll average them." — investigate the disagreement.

ml-dl-q45.testing: whether you read assumptions off the objective and resist the elbow heuristic.
ml-dl-q45.spoken:
"K-Means minimises the within-cluster sum of squared distances to centroids, and that objective hides its assumptions. It prefers spherical clusters of similar size and similar density, separable by Euclidean distance. Give it a crescent, or one big and one small cluster, and it will carve them wrongly while the loss looks fine. It also always returns exactly K clusters, whether or not structure exists.

Mechanics worth saying: Lloyd's algorithm only reaches a local optimum, so use K-Means++ initialisation and several restarts. Scaling is mandatory, because it's distance-based. And for large data, mini-batch K-Means trades a little quality for a lot of speed.

For choosing K, the elbow method reads a bend off a curve that always decreases, and often there's no clean bend. Silhouette, which compares separation to cohesion per point, is more honest. Stronger still is stability: do the clusters survive resampling and different seeds?

The real validation is external: do the clusters differ on business variables they weren't built from, and do they stay stable over time? A clustering nobody can act on is a scatter plot with extra steps.

If shapes or densities are the problem, I'd switch: Gaussian mixtures for elliptical clusters and soft assignment, HDBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise."

stages.name: The objective
stages.html:
minimise  Σₖ Σ_{x ∈ Cₖ} ‖x − μₖ‖²

Lloyd's algorithm: assign points to the nearest centroid, move centroids to their cluster means, repeat.

stages.name: The assumptions it hides
stages.html:
Assumption When it fails
Spherical clusters elongated or curved shapes
Similar sizes one large and one small group get split or merged
Similar densities sparse clusters absorbed by dense ones
Euclidean geometry categorical or mixed data
K clusters exist returns K groups from structureless data

stages.name: Mechanics that matter
stages.html:
• K-Means++ initialisation, n_init ≥ 10 restarts.
  • Standardise features; consider PCA first in high dimensions.
  • Mini-batch K-Means for millions of rows.

stages.name: Choosing K honestly
stages.html:
Method Honest?
Elbow (inertia vs K) weak: inertia always drops; elbows are often ambiguous
Silhouette better: cohesion vs separation per point
Stability (ARI across seeds/bootstraps) strongest internal evidence
Gap statistic compares to a null reference distribution

stages.name: Validate outside the geometry
stages.html:
• Clusters differ significantly on variables not used to build them (revenue, churn).
  • Stable month over month.
  • Each can be named in one actionable sentence.

stages.name: Alternatives when shapes are wrong
stages.html:
Structure Use
Elliptical, overlapping, soft membership Gaussian Mixture Models
Arbitrary shapes, noise, unknown K DBSCAN / HDBSCAN
Nested groupings, dendrogram hierarchical clustering
Categorical data K-modes / K-prototypes

followUps.question: Why does K-Means need scaling?
followUps.html: It uses Euclidean distance, so a feature in large units dominates the assignment. After scaling, each feature contributes comparably, unless you deliberately weight some.

followUps.question: The silhouette peaks at K = 2 but the business wants 6 segments. Now what?
followUps.html: Tell them the data supports 2 strong groups; 6 would be partly arbitrary. Options: hierarchical sub-segmentation within the 2, or define 6 segments by business rules and use clustering to inform them. Don't present forced clusters as natural.

followUps.question: Can K-Means work on categorical data?
followUps.html: Not directly: means of one-hot vectors aren't meaningful categories and Euclidean distance on them is crude. Use K-modes / K-prototypes, or embed categories first.

followUps.question: How do you check the clusters aren't just noise?
followUps.html: Compare against a null: run the same pipeline on data with features shuffled independently (destroying structure) and see whether your silhouette or stability is clearly better. The gap statistic formalises this.

followUps.question: How do you assign new customers to segments?
followUps.html: Apply the same fitted scaler, then assign to the nearest stored centroid. Monitor the distribution of assignments and distances over time; drift in either means the segmentation needs refitting.

dontSay: "The elbow method gives K." — often ambiguous; use silhouette and stability.
"K-Means finds natural groups." — it always returns K spherical-ish groups.
"No need to scale." — distance-based.

spine: Not a bug: a density verdict
Where DBSCAN still earns its place
ml-dl-q46.testing: whether you understand density-based clustering well enough to read its output as information.
ml-dl-q46.trap: "lower the threshold until noise goes away."
ml-dl-q46.spoken:
"It's not a bug; it's a verdict and a diagnostic.

DBSCAN grows clusters from core points: a point with at least minPts neighbours within radius eps. Points reachable from a core point join its cluster; points reachable from none are labelled noise. So 40% noise means 40% of the data doesn't sit in any region as dense as I specified. Either that's true, the data is sparse and noisy, or my eps is too tight for how the features are scaled.

Eps is the neighbourhood radius, best chosen from the knee of a k-distance plot. MinPts is the density bar, roughly the dimensionality plus a margin. Both are meaningless without scaled features, and eps degrades in high dimensions because distances concentrate.

The structural weakness is one global eps. If clusters have different densities, no single eps is right: the dense cluster merges with neighbours while the sparse one shatters into noise.

That's exactly what HDBSCAN fixes: it builds a density hierarchy and extracts clusters at different densities, with essentially one parameter, the minimum cluster size.

So my steps: check scaling, redo the k-distance plot, and if densities visibly vary, switch to HDBSCAN rather than tuning DBSCAN harder."

stages.name: Not a bug: a density verdict
stages.html:
Point type Rule
Core ≥ minPts points within eps
Border within eps of a core point, not core itself
Noise neither

stages.name: What eps and minPts control
stages.html:
• eps: how far a neighbourhood reaches. Too small → everything is noise; too large → clusters merge.
  • minPts: how many neighbours make a region dense. Rule of thumb ≥ dimensions + 1, often 2× dimensions.

stages.name: Check scaling and eps
stages.html:
Step 1 — Scale features. Unscaled units make eps meaningless in some dimensions.

Step 2 — k-distance plot. Sort each point's distance to its k-th neighbour (k = minPts); choose eps at the knee.

Step 3 — Reduce dimensions. In high dimensions distances concentrate; PCA or UMAP first can help.

stages.name: The one-global-eps weakness
stages.html:
• A single eps can't fit both a tight cluster and a diffuse one.
  • Symptom: tuning eps trades "sparse cluster becomes noise" for "dense clusters merge".

stages.name: Switch to HDBSCAN
stages.html:
• Builds clusters across all densities; keeps the most persistent ones.
  • Main parameter: min_cluster_size; also gives membership probabilities and outlier scores.
  • Usually the better default for exploratory clustering.

stages.name: Where DBSCAN still earns its place
stages.html:
• Arbitrary shapes; no need to choose K.
  • The noise label is useful for anomaly triage.
  • Deterministic for core points; simple to explain.

followUps.question: Could 40% noise be the right answer?
followUps.html: Yes. In fraud logs or sensor data, most points may be isolated and only a few dense patterns exist. If the clusters found are meaningful and stable, a large noise fraction is a finding, not a failure.

followUps.question: How does DBSCAN handle new points?
followUps.html: It has no native predict. You can assign new points to the cluster of the nearest core point within eps, else noise. HDBSCAN offers approximate_predict for this.

followUps.question: Why not just increase eps until noise drops to 5%?
followUps.html: You'd merge distinct clusters and redefine "dense" to fit a target number rather than the data. Noise percentage isn't an objective; cluster quality and stability are.

followUps.question: DBSCAN on 50 million points?
followUps.html: Standard implementations are memory- and time-heavy (neighbourhood queries). Use a spatial index, subsample to find structure then assign the rest, GPU implementations (cuML), or HDBSCAN on a sample with approximate prediction for the remainder.

followUps.question: DBSCAN vs K-Means in one line?
followUps.html: K-Means assumes K spherical clusters and assigns every point; DBSCAN finds arbitrary shapes by density, discovers the number of clusters, and leaves low-density points as noise.

dontSay: "It's a bug; I'll raise eps." — noise is information.
"DBSCAN doesn't need parameter tuning." — eps and minPts are everything.
"It works fine without scaling." — eps depends on units.

ml-dl-q47.testing: whether you can build evidence without labels, in layers a stakeholder trusts.
ml-dl-q47.trap: "the silhouette score is 0.6, so it's good."
ml-dl-q47.spoken:
"I'd build the case in layers, from weakest to strongest evidence.

Internal metrics first: silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz. They measure cohesion against separation, but they share the same geometric prejudices as the algorithms, favouring compact round clusters. So they're consistency checks, not truth.

Stability is stronger evidence. Re-run the clustering under bootstrap resampling, different seeds and small feature perturbations, and measure agreement between runs with something like the adjusted Rand index. Structure that evaporates under resampling was noise wearing a costume.

External validation is what convinces a sceptic: the clusters differ significantly on variables they weren't built from, revenue, churn, support tickets, and they persist over time. That's the difference between 'the algorithm returned groups' and 'these segments exist'.

The final test is actionability. Name each cluster in one sentence a marketer or product manager can act on. If a cluster can't be described, it's a mathematical artifact.

And I'd guard against the meta-risk: try enough algorithms and values of K and you'll find clusters in anything. So I'd fix the pipeline, features, algorithm and selection metric, before looking, rather than p-hacking geometry."

stages.name: Internal metrics: consistency, not truth
stages.html:
Metric Measures Bias
Silhouette per-point cohesion vs nearest other cluster favours convex, well-separated clusters
Davies-Bouldin average similarity of each cluster to its closest same
Calinski-Harabasz between- vs within-cluster dispersion favours spherical, more clusters

stages.name: Stability under resampling
stages.html:
• Bootstrap samples, different seeds, small feature noise.
  • Agreement: adjusted Rand index or Jaccard per cluster between runs.
  • Report per-cluster stability: some clusters may be solid, others not.

stages.name: External validation on unseen variables
stages.html:
• Hold out business variables from the clustering features.
  • Test differences between clusters (ANOVA / Kruskal-Wallis, effect sizes).
  • Check persistence: re-cluster next month; do the segments reappear?

stages.name: Actionability
stages.html:
• "Price-sensitive weekend shoppers who churn after promotions end."
  • If a cluster has no crisp description or distinct action, merge or drop it.

stages.name: Guard against p-hacking geometry
stages.html:
• Decide features, algorithm and selection metric up front.
  • Compare to a null (shuffled features) to show structure beats chance.
  • Report the choices tried, not only the winner.

followUps.question: How do you present this to a sceptical VP?
followUps.html: Lead with the external evidence: segment A has 3× the churn and half the order value of segment B, stable for three months. Then stability, then one slide on method. Business differences persuade; silhouette scores don't.

followUps.question: Silhouette is low but segments differ strongly on revenue. Which wins?
followUps.html: The external evidence, if it's stable. Low silhouette often means clusters touch or aren't spherical, which doesn't make them useless. Report both honestly.

followUps.question: How do you compare two clusterings?
followUps.html: Adjusted Rand index or normalised mutual information between label assignments, plus comparing which one yields stronger external differences and more actionable segments.

followUps.question: Isn't using business variables for validation circular?
followUps.html: Only if they were used as clustering features. Hold them out; then differences on them are independent evidence that the clusters capture real structure.

followUps.question: What if the segments change every month?
followUps.html: Either behaviour is genuinely shifting, or the clustering is unstable. Check stability within a month first; if stable within but not across months, the population is changing and the segmentation needs a refresh cadence and a mapping between old and new segments.

dontSay: "Silhouette 0.6, done." — internal metrics share the algorithm's biases.
"The clusters look clear on the plot." — plots aren't evidence (see Q36).
"I tried 12 algorithms and picked the best-looking." — that's p-hacking.

spine: Two axes: trial cost and important dimensions
ml-dl-q48.testing: whether you choose search strategy by budget structure.
ml-dl-q48.spoken:
"I choose along two axes: how expensive one trial is, and how many hyperparameters actually matter.

Grid search grows exponentially with dimensions and wastes budget on parameters that don't matter. It's defensible for one or two parameters, or when you need an exhaustive, auditable sweep.

Random search beats grid because usually only a few hyperparameters matter. Random sampling covers each important dimension densely instead of repeating the same few values. It's the right default when trials are cheap.

Bayesian optimisation, like Optuna's TPE or a Gaussian-process approach, builds a model of score versus configuration and spends each trial where improvement is likely. It earns its overhead when a single trial is expensive and the budget is tens of trials, not thousands. It's sequential by nature, though batched versions exist.

Hyperband and successive halving attack a different axis: cheap partial evaluations. Start many configurations, kill the losers early at increasing budgets. It wins when learning curves are informative early, epochs or boosting rounds. Combine it with Bayesian sampling, BOHB or Optuna with pruning, and you get both.

Whatever the method: search rates and regularisation on log scales, repeat top configurations across seeds, keep the test set out, and remember tuning gains are usually smaller than one good feature."

stages.name: Two axes: trial cost and important dimensions
stages.html:
Few params matter Many params matter
Cheap trials random search random search, large budget
Expensive trials Bayesian optimisation Bayesian + early stopping (BOHB)
Informative early curves Hyperband / pruning BOHB / Optuna with pruning

stages.name: Grid
stages.html:
• Cost = product of values per parameter.
  • Fine for 1–2 params or a required audit sweep.

stages.name: Random
stages.html:
• With 60 random trials, there's a 95% chance of hitting the top 5% of a single important dimension.
  • Each trial explores new values on every dimension.

stages.name: Bayesian
stages.html:
• Surrogate model (TPE, GP) + acquisition function (expected improvement).
  • Worth the overhead for hour-long trainings with a budget of 20–100 trials.
  • Sequential; parallelism needs batched suggestions.

stages.name: Hyperband
stages.html:
• Successive halving: train many configs briefly, keep the best fraction, give them more budget, repeat.
  • Hyperband runs several halving brackets to hedge against early curves being misleading.
  • Needs a meaningful "partial budget": epochs, rounds, data subset.

stages.name: Discipline for any method
stages.html:
• Log-scale search for learning rate, regularisation.
  • Re-run top configs across seeds; differences within noise are ties.
  • Tune on validation/CV only; test once at the end (nested CV if data is small).
  • Features and data usually beat tuning.

followUps.question: Why does random search beat grid with the same budget?
followUps.html: If only one of three parameters matters, a 5×5×5 grid tests just 5 values of it; 125 random trials test 125 different values. Random search spends budget where it counts.

followUps.question: When is Hyperband misleading?
followUps.html: When early performance doesn't predict final performance: small learning rates that start slowly but win, or strong regularisation that looks bad early. Use a sensible minimum budget and Hyperband's multiple brackets.

followUps.question: How do you tune a model that takes 8 hours to train?
followUps.html: Shrink the problem: tune on a data subset or fewer epochs to narrow ranges, use Bayesian optimisation with pruning, parallelise across GPUs, and transfer settings from similar past models. Confirm the final few configurations at full scale.

followUps.question: Your tuned model beats the baseline by 0.2%. Ship it?
followUps.html: Check it's outside noise (repeat seeds, CI) and not selection bias from many trials. Small tuning gains often vanish on new data; a better feature or more data usually matters more.

followUps.question: Which hyperparameters matter most for gradient boosting?
followUps.html: Learning rate with number of rounds (via early stopping), tree depth or leaves, min child weight / leaf samples, and row/column subsampling. Regularisation terms are secondary.

dontSay: "Grid search to be thorough." — exponential waste.
"Bayesian is always best." — overhead isn't worth it for cheap trials.
"I tuned on the test set." — no.

ml-dl-q49.testing: statistical judgement plus business sense, delivered constructively to a PM.
ml-dl-q49.trap: "B is higher, ship it" or a flat "no".
ml-dl-q49.spoken:
"I'd say: maybe, but first let's check the difference is real and worth something.

First, is 0.004 inside the noise? A single test-set score has sampling variance. I'd bootstrap the test set to get a confidence interval on the difference, or run a paired test on per-example results, like McNemar's for classification, since both models saw the same examples. With typical test sizes, 0.004 is very often a tie.

Second, selection effects. If B was the best of many candidates evaluated on this same test set, part of its edge is the winner's curse.

Third, translate it to the business metric. Does 0.004 change revenue or cost at our operating threshold? Offline differences this small often vanish online.

If it might matter, settle it with an A/B test on the business KPI. If we can't A/B test, the offline gain should clear a practical-significance bar agreed in advance, not just statistical significance.

And I'd weigh what the metric hides: latency, cost, calibration and per-segment performance. B can win on average and lose on the segment that matters most. If B is no worse on those and the gain survives, ship it."

stages.name: Is 0.004 inside the noise?
stages.html:
• Bootstrap the test set 1,000+ times; CI of (B − A).
  • Paired tests: McNemar's on per-example correctness; for AUC, DeLong's test.
  • If the CI includes 0, it's a tie.

stages.name: Selection bias
stages.html:
• Many candidates compared on one test set → the best one's score is inflated.
  • The test set is now partly a validation set; refresh it or hold back a final one.

stages.name: Does it move the business?
stages.html:
• Recompute the business outcome at the actual threshold for both models: approvals, fraud caught, revenue.
  • A metric gain spread below the threshold changes nothing users see.

stages.name: Settle it online
stages.html:
• A/B test on the business KPI with a pre-registered duration and metric.
  • If not possible: require a pre-agreed practical-significance bar offline.

stages.name: Weigh what the metric hides
stages.html:
Dimension Question
Latency / cost is B slower or pricier?
Calibration do B's probabilities still mean what they say?
Segments does B lose on a key segment?
Robustness stable across time slices?

followUps.question: How big should the test set be to detect 0.004?
followUps.html: Depends on the metric's variance and base rate, but often tens or hundreds of thousands of examples for accuracy-scale differences this small. Power-analyse before claiming a difference; with a few thousand examples, 0.004 is almost never detectable.

followUps.question: The PM says "higher is higher, why not?"
followUps.html: Because switching has costs (validation, deployment, monitoring, risk), and if the difference is noise we pay them for nothing, or even ship a slightly worse model. Offer a fast path: a quick paired test today and an A/B test if it's promising.

followUps.question: What if B is statistically better but only by 0.004?
followUps.html: Statistical significance isn't practical significance. With a huge test set, tiny differences become "significant". Ask whether the business impact beats the switching cost.

followUps.question: Is McNemar's test right for AUC?
followUps.html: McNemar's compares paired correct/incorrect predictions at a threshold. For AUC differences use DeLong's test or a paired bootstrap of AUC. Pick the test that matches the metric you're comparing.

followUps.question: How would you avoid this situation next time?
followUps.html: Agree in advance on the decision metric, the minimum meaningful improvement, and the evaluation protocol (repeated CV or fresh holdout, paired test). Then shipping decisions are mechanical instead of negotiated.

dontSay: "B is better, ship it." — no uncertainty estimate.
"The difference is too small, never." — test it; it might be real.
"Statistically significant, so it matters." — practical significance is separate.

spine: It's a theorem, not a bug
Choose the definition that matches the harm
ml-dl-q50.testing: whether you know the impossibility result and treat fairness as a governed trade-off.
ml-dl-q50.trap: "we'll tune the model until all metrics pass," or "we removed the protected attribute."
ml-dl-q50.spoken:
"It's a theorem, not an engineering failure. When base rates differ between groups, demographic parity, which is equal approval rates, equalised odds, which is equal true- and false-positive rates, and predictive parity, which is equal precision or calibration, can't all hold at once, except with a perfect predictor. Any calibrated model with unequal base rates violates the others.

So the job isn't to satisfy every metric. It's to choose the definition that matches the harm in this domain. Equal opportunity among qualified applicants, equal true-positive rates, means something different from equal approval rates, and that choice encodes values and law, not statistics.

That makes it a governance decision. Legal, compliance and product own it, and it's documented, for example in a model card. My role as architect is to give them the quantified trade-off: what each definition costs in the others and in accuracy.

Once chosen, there are technical levers: reweighting data before training, constrained optimisation during training, or group-specific thresholds after training, which is simple and auditable. Removing the protected attribute alone doesn't work, because proxies like postcode carry it back in.

And fairness is monitored per segment in production, not audited once, because drift breaks fairness just like it breaks accuracy."

stages.name: It's a theorem, not a bug
stages.html:
Definition Requires equal across groups
Demographic parity approval rate P(ŷ=1)
Equalised odds TPR and FPR
Equal opportunity TPR only
Predictive parity / calibration precision / P(y=1 | score)

With different base rates P(y=1), calibration and equalised odds can't both hold (Kleinberg et al., Chouldechova), and demographic parity conflicts with both.

stages.name: Choose the definition that matches the harm
stages.html:
• Lending: equal opportunity (qualified applicants approved equally) is common; regulation may prohibit disparate impact.
  • Risk scoring used by humans: calibration within groups often matters most.
  • The choice is ethical and legal first, statistical second.

stages.name: Make it a governance decision
stages.html:
• Present the trade-off curve: accuracy and each fairness metric under different constraints/thresholds.
  • Decision owners: legal, compliance, product, with documentation (model card, decision log).
  • Record who decided, which definition, and why.

stages.name: Apply technical levers
stages.html:
Stage Lever Trade-off
Pre-processing reweighing, resampling simple; indirect control
In-processing constrained optimisation, adversarial debiasing precise; complex
Post-processing group-specific thresholds simple, auditable; may need legal review

Dropping the protected attribute ("fairness through unawareness") fails: proxies (postcode, name, school) reintroduce it, and you lose the ability to measure disparity.

stages.name: Monitor in production
stages.html:
• Track chosen metric per group on live decisions and delayed outcomes.
  • Alert on divergence; include in model reviews and retraining gates.

followUps.question: Isn't using the protected attribute for thresholds illegal?
followUps.html: It depends on jurisdiction and domain; some lending rules restrict using protected attributes in decisions even to correct bias. That's why legal must own the choice. Sometimes the attribute is used only for measurement and for choosing mitigations that don't use it directly.

followUps.question: Why does removing the protected attribute fail?
followUps.html: Other features correlate with it, so the model reconstructs it implicitly. You also lose the ability to measure disparities, making the problem invisible rather than solved.

followUps.question: How much accuracy does fairness cost?
followUps.html: It varies; often less than people fear, sometimes significant. The honest answer is to measure it: plot the frontier of accuracy versus the chosen fairness metric and let decision-makers pick a point.

followUps.question: What goes in the model card?
followUps.html: Intended use, training data description, performance and fairness metrics per group, the chosen fairness definition and rationale, known limitations, and monitoring plan. It makes the decision reviewable and auditable.

followUps.question: Can labels themselves be biased?
followUps.html: Yes: historical approvals or repayment observed only for approved applicants reflect past decisions. Equalising metrics on biased labels can entrench bias. Consider reject inference, outcome definitions, and data audits.

dontSay: "We'll satisfy all fairness metrics." — mathematically impossible with different base rates.
"We removed race, so it's fair." — proxies.
"The data scientists decide the fairness definition." — governance decides.

spine: Honest scheme: walk-forward with a gap
ml-dl-q51.testing: both leaks (folds and features) and a concrete honest scheme.
ml-dl-q51.trap: fixing the split but not the feature engineering.
ml-dl-q51.spoken:
"There are two leaks.

The first is the fold structure. Random K-fold trains on the future to predict the past. With autocorrelation, neighbouring time points are near-duplicates, and they land in different folds, so the score measures interpolation, not forecasting. The inflation can be dramatic.

The second leak hides in the features. Rolling means, lags or normalisation computed over the whole series before splitting carry future information into past rows, even if the split itself is correct.

The honest scheme is walk-forward validation: train on an expanding or rolling window, test on the next block, step forward, and aggregate across several origins. Add a gap, an embargo, between train and test when features look back over a window, so no training row overlaps the test period through its features. Use a rolling window when old regimes actively mislead.

I'd report performance per fold over time rather than pooled: decay across folds tells you how fast things drift and sets the retraining cadence. And I'd always compare against naive baselines, last value and seasonal naive, which forecasting models embarrassingly often fail to beat."

stages.name: Leak 1: the fold structure
stages.html:
Random K-fold:   train ■□■■□■■□■   test □ scattered through time → interpolation
Walk-forward:    train ■■■■■|gap|test ■  → next origin: train ■■■■■■■|gap|test ■

stages.name: Leak 2: the features
stages.html:
• A 30-day rolling mean at day t computed centred, or normalisation using full-series statistics.
  • Fix: compute features using only data ≤ t, inside each fold's training window.
  • Target-derived features (lagged target) need the same care at the fold boundary.

stages.name: Honest scheme: walk-forward with a gap
stages.html:
• Expanding window: more data each step; rolling window: fixed length, forgets old regimes.
  • Gap ≥ forecast horizon and feature lookback.
  • TimeSeriesSplit(gap=…) in sklearn, or a custom backtest loop.

stages.name: Report over time
stages.html:
• Metric per fold, in time order: a downward trend is drift speed.
  • Horizon-specific errors: 1-step vs 7-step ahead.

stages.name: Beat the naive baselines
stages.html:
Baseline Forecast
Naive last observed value
Seasonal naive value one season ago
Moving average mean of recent window

A model that can't beat seasonal naive isn't ready. Use scale-free metrics like MASE to compare.

followUps.question: How big should the gap be?
followUps.html: At least the forecast horizon plus the longest feature lookback, so no training row's features or labels overlap the test period. For a label defined over the next 7 days, the last training row must be 7 days before test starts.

followUps.question: Expanding or rolling window?
followUps.html: Expanding when older data remains relevant and more data helps; rolling when the process changes and old regimes mislead (post-pandemic demand, a pricing change). Compare both in the backtest.

followUps.question: Is K-fold ever OK for time-series models?
followUps.html: For purely autoregressive models on stationary series, some research shows blocked or purged CV can be acceptable. For production forecasting with features, walk-forward is the safe default because it mirrors deployment.

followUps.question: How many origins?
followUps.html: Enough to cover the seasonal patterns and some regime variety, often 5–12. More origins give a better estimate of both average error and its variance.

followUps.question: How do you tune hyperparameters with walk-forward?
followUps.html: Tune on the earlier origins and hold the most recent window(s) for a final untouched evaluation. Otherwise tuning across all folds reuses the latest period for both selection and reporting.

dontSay: "Shuffle and 5-fold." — trains on the future.
"I computed rolling features on the full series first." — feature leak.
"Our MAPE is 8%." (without a naive baseline) — meaningless alone.

spine: Sort by what each is structurally good at
ml-dl-q52.testing: whether you match method to problem shape, not fashion.
ml-dl-q52.spoken:
"I'd sort them by what they're structurally good at.

ARIMA and SARIMA are principled for a single, well-behaved series: explicit autoregressive and moving-average structure on a stationary series, interpretable orders from ACF and PACF, and proper prediction intervals. The cost is per-series care, stationarity work, and weakness with covariates and with many series.

Prophet decomposes trend, seasonality and holidays, is robust to missing data and outliers, and was built for many business series with strong calendar effects, run by analysts who aren't statisticians. The cost is a rigid functional form: it underperforms when dynamics aren't calendar-driven, and it isn't a magic upgrade over naive baselines.

Gradient boosting with engineered features, lags, rolling statistics, calendar, promotions and price, wins when external drivers matter and you have many related series: one global model learns across all of them. The cost is that you own the feature engineering, the temporal validation discipline, and the multi-step strategy, and trees can't extrapolate a trend beyond what they've seen.

So: one well-understood series, ARIMA. Hundreds of calendar-driven series and speed, Prophet or seasonal-naive. Drivers plus cross-series signal, a global GBM, today's industry default.

And everything is judged walk-forward against seasonal-naive."

stages.name: Sort by what each is structurally good at
stages.html:
Problem shape Lean toward
One series, clear structure, need intervals ARIMA / SARIMA / ETS
Many series, strong calendar/holiday effects, little tuning Prophet (or ETS), seasonal-naive
Many related series, exogenous drivers (price, promo, weather) global GBM with lags
Very long histories, complex patterns, lots of series consider deep models (N-BEATS, TFT)

stages.name: ARIMA
stages.claim: explicit structure, one series at a time
stages.html:
• Make stationary (differencing, ADF test), choose p, d, q from ACF/PACF or auto-ARIMA.
  • SARIMA adds seasonal terms; ARIMAX adds regressors (awkwardly).
  • Strengths: interpretable, calibrated intervals. Weakness: scale to thousands of series, non-linear drivers.

stages.name: Prophet
stages.html:
• y = trend + seasonality + holidays + error, fitted as a curve.
  • Handles gaps, outliers, changepoints.
  • Weakness: fixed form; doesn't use autoregressive dynamics well; often matched by simple baselines.

stages.name: Global GBM
stages.html:
• One model across all series: shares patterns, handles cold-start series via similarity.
  • Features: lags, rolling means/std, calendar, holidays, price, promotions, series ID/attributes.
  • Multi-step: recursive (feed predictions back) vs direct (one model per horizon).
  • Weakness: can't extrapolate trends; detrend or add trend features.

stages.name: The decision shape
stages.html: Start with seasonal-naive and ETS as baselines, try a global GBM, and keep whichever wins walk-forward by a meaningful margin on MASE.

stages.name: Always against seasonal-naive
stages.html: Many production forecasts don't beat seasonal-naive. Prove yours does, per series segment, walk-forward.

followUps.question: Why can't GBMs extrapolate trends?
followUps.html: Tree predictions are averages of training targets in leaves, so they can't exceed values seen in training. For a rising series, forecast differences or detrended values, or add a linear trend component.

followUps.question: Recursive or direct multi-step forecasting?
followUps.html: Recursive uses one model and feeds predictions back as lags; errors compound. Direct trains a model per horizon; no compounding but more models. Many teams use direct for short horizons, or a single model with horizon as a feature.

followUps.question: When would you pick deep learning?
followUps.html: Many long, related series with complex patterns and enough data, and a team to maintain it. Otherwise global GBMs and statistical baselines usually match it at far lower cost.

followUps.question: How do you forecast a new product with no history?
followUps.html: Use a global model with product attributes so it borrows from similar products, analogous-product curves, or hierarchical priors. Update quickly as early sales arrive.

followUps.question: How do you get prediction intervals from a GBM?
followUps.html: Train quantile models (e.g. 0.1 and 0.9), use conformal prediction on backtest residuals, or bootstrap residuals. Check coverage in the walk-forward backtest.

dontSay: "Prophet is the best forecasting tool." — often matched by naive baselines.
"ARIMA for our 10,000 SKUs." — per-series care doesn't scale.
"Our model has low error." (no baseline) — beat seasonal-naive first.

ml-dl-q53.testing: mechanism per method and which cold-start case kills each.
ml-dl-q53.trap: treating cold start as one problem.
ml-dl-q53.spoken:
"For each, what does it learn from and which cold start kills it?

Content-based matches item features to a profile built from the user's own history. It doesn't need other users, so it handles new items natively, because they have features. It fails for new users with no history, and it over-specialises, recommending more of the same.

Collaborative filtering, user-based or item-based neighbourhoods, learns only from the interaction matrix. It captures taste patterns content can't, 'people who liked X also liked Y', but it fails for both new users and new items, since neither has interactions, and it struggles with sparsity. Item-based aged better because item similarities are more stable and cacheable.

Matrix factorisation, SVD-style or ALS, decomposes the interaction matrix into latent user and item factors, generalising better from the same sparse data. It was the classic quality winner. ALS fits the implicit-feedback formulation. It has the same cold-start weakness as CF.

So production systems are hybrids. New users get onboarding signals, popularity or context priors, and exploration; new items get content features plus an exposure boost.

And implicit feedback, clicks and views, is confidence, not preference: no click isn't dislike. That changes the loss, how you sample negatives, and how you evaluate."

stages.name: Content-based
stages.html:
• Represent items by features (genre, text embeddings, attributes); build a user profile from items they engaged with.
  • ✅ new items; ❌ new users; ⚠️ filter bubble, limited serendipity.

stages.name: Collaborative filtering
stages.html:
• User-based: similar users' items. Item-based: items similar by co-interaction.
  • ✅ captures taste beyond features; ❌ new users and new items; ⚠️ sparsity, popularity bias.

stages.name: Matrix factorisation
stages.html:
R (users × items) ≈ U · Vᵀ     each user and item gets a k-dim vector
  • SVD / SGD for explicit ratings; ALS with confidence weights for implicit feedback.
  • ✅ best classic quality on sparse data; ❌ same cold start as CF.

stages.name: Cold-start playbook
stages.html:
Case Answer
New user onboarding choices, popularity / trending, context (location, device), bandits for exploration
New item content features / embeddings, exposure boost, similar-item mapping
New platform content-based + popularity until interactions accumulate

Hybrids: feed content features into factorisation (e.g. LightFM) or two-tower models.

stages.name: Implicit feedback is confidence
stages.html:
• Clicks, views, dwell time: positive signal with varying confidence; absence is ambiguous.
  • Loss: weighted (ALS-WR), BPR pairwise ranking, or sampled softmax.
  • Evaluation: ranking metrics (NDCG, recall@k) and online tests.

followUps.question: Why did item-based CF age better than user-based?
followUps.html: Items are fewer and their similarity is more stable than users' tastes, so item-item similarities can be precomputed and cached. User-based neighbours shift quickly as users interact.

followUps.question: What's a two-tower model and why is it common now?
followUps.html: Separate encoders map users (history, features) and items (features, content) into the same embedding space; relevance is the dot product. It handles new items via content features and serves with ANN retrieval over item embeddings, scaling to millions of items.

followUps.question: How do you avoid a filter bubble?
followUps.html: Add diversity and novelty in re-ranking, reserve exploration traffic, include popularity-balanced candidates, and measure coverage and diversity alongside relevance.

followUps.question: Does "no click" mean the user disliked it?
followUps.html: No. They may not have seen it, or seen it and been busy. Treat non-interactions as unknown or weak negatives, and use exposure logs to separate "shown and ignored" from "never shown".

followUps.question: How do you evaluate offline?
followUps.html: Time-based split (train on past interactions, test on future), ranking metrics like recall@k and NDCG, per-segment (new vs heavy users), and remember offline bias from the old policy (see Q16). Confirm with A/B tests.

dontSay: "Matrix factorisation solves cold start." — it doesn't.
"No click means dislike." — implicit feedback is confidence.
"Pick the best algorithm." — production uses hybrids.

ml-dl-q54.testing: whether you anchor a technology decision on economics and operations.
ml-dl-q54.trap: comparing vendor feature lists before knowing the cost of a mistake.
ml-dl-q54.spoken:
"Before comparing vendors, I'd price the two errors. A missed fraud costs the loss amount plus chargeback fees. A false positive costs a blocked good customer, support time and maybe churn. Those two numbers set the operating point, the size of the review queue, and the accuracy bar any option has to clear.

Buy when fraud isn't our differentiator and vendors have network effects we can't replicate, like fraud signals shared across thousands of merchants. I'd evaluate them on our own data with a backtest at our operating point, not their marketing metrics, and price integration and per-transaction fees against our loss rate.

Build when our fraud patterns are proprietary, we have enough labelled data, and at our scale the economics beat vendor pricing. And cost the full lifecycle, the team, serving, monitoring, retraining, compliance, not just the notebook.

In practice the answer is usually a hybrid: the vendor score becomes one feature inside our own model, plus a rules layer for known patterns and instant response. We keep control of the operating point, and the vendor covers our cold start.

Whoever supplies the model, fraud drifts adversarially: fraudsters adapt to what you deploy. So we own monitoring, retraining cadence and the human-review loop, and that ongoing cost usually decides the question."

stages.name: Price the two errors first
stages.html:
Error Cost components
False negative (missed fraud) loss amount, chargeback fees, scheme penalties
False positive (blocked good customer) lost sale, support cost, churn, reputation
  • Combined with review capacity, these set the threshold and the precision/recall needed at it.

stages.name: When to buy
stages.html:
• Consortium data across merchants (device, email, card signals) you can't collect alone.
  • Faster time to value; vendor handles model upkeep.
  • Evaluate: backtest on your labelled history, at your threshold, with cost per decision.
  • Watch: per-transaction fees, latency, data-sharing terms, explainability for disputes.

stages.name: When to build
stages.html:
• Your fraud is specific to your product (promo abuse, account takeover in your app).
  • Enough labels and volume; costs at scale beat vendor pricing.
  • Full lifecycle cost: engineers, feature pipelines, real-time serving, monitoring, model risk, compliance.

stages.name: Hybrid is usual
stages.html:
transaction → rules layer (hard blocks, known patterns)
            → model (own features + vendor score) → threshold → approve / review / decline
            → human review queue → labels back into training
  • "Fine-tune" here usually means adapting a vendor or foundation model to your data where the vendor allows it; check what's actually tunable.

stages.name: Own the ongoing loop
stages.html:
• Fraudsters probe and adapt; performance decays faster than in normal drift.
  • Needed regardless of source: monitoring by segment, delayed-label evaluation, fast retraining, rule updates, feedback from investigators.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate a vendor fairly?
followUps.html: Give them (or score locally) a historical, time-split dataset with known outcomes, compare at your operating point (precision at review capacity, dollar loss caught), include latency and cost per call, and check stability across segments. Their headline AUC on other clients' data doesn't transfer.

followUps.question: Labels arrive after 60 days (chargebacks). How does that affect the choice?
followUps.html: Slow labels make it hard to detect decay and retrain quickly, favouring a partner with faster signals, or building proxy labels (investigator decisions, customer confirmations). Either way, invest in label-free monitoring: score and feature distributions.

followUps.question: Why keep a rules layer if you have a model?
followUps.html: Rules respond in minutes to a new attack while the model needs retraining; they encode hard policy (sanctions, velocity limits); and they're auditable. The model handles the nuanced cases.

followUps.question: What does it cost to build, roughly?
followUps.html: Don't invent numbers; estimate by components for your context: engineers and data scientists, real-time feature infrastructure, serving, monitoring, investigator tooling, compliance reviews, over at least a year. Compare to vendor fees × volume.

followUps.question: How do you handle explainability for declined customers?
followUps.html: Reason codes from your model (SHAP-based) and clear rule descriptions; with a black-box vendor, confirm they provide reasons for disputes and regulatory requests before signing.

dontSay: "We'll build because we have data scientists." — cost the lifecycle.
"Vendor X has 0.98 AUC." — on whose data, at what threshold?
"Once deployed, it'll keep working." — fraud adapts.

ml-dl-q55.testing: numerical stability reasoning and the free fix.
ml-dl-q55.trap: "clip the logits" or "lower the learning rate."
ml-dl-q55.spoken:
"exp of a large logit overflows the float range to infinity, so you get infinity divided by infinity, which is NaN. Very negative logits underflow to zero, and if they all do, the denominator collapses.

The fix is free because softmax is shift-invariant: subtracting the same constant from every logit doesn't change the output. So subtract the maximum logit first. The largest exponent becomes exp of zero, which is one, and nothing overflows.

The same idea in log space is the log-sum-exp trick for log-probabilities. In practice you use the fused log_softmax or cross-entropy functions that take raw logits, instead of composing log of softmax yourself.

And this pressure comes back in attention at long context, with many logits and growing magnitudes, which is why fused attention kernels compute softmax with a running maximum and sum."

stages.name: Overflow and underflow
stages.html:
• float32 exp overflows above ~88.7 (float16 above ~11): exp(1000) = inf → inf/inf = NaN.
  • Very negative logits: exp → 0; if all underflow, 0/0 = NaN; log(0) = −inf in log-softmax.

stages.name: Softmax is shift-invariant
stages.html: softmax(z)ᵢ = e^{zᵢ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ} = e^{zᵢ − c} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ − c}   for any c

stages.name: Subtract the max
stages.html:
z = z - z.max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values
p = z.exp() / z.exp().sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
  • Largest term becomes e⁰ = 1; denominator ≥ 1, never 0.

stages.name: Log-sum-exp and fused losses
stages.html:
log Σ e^{zⱼ} = m + log Σ e^{zⱼ − m},   m = max z
  • F.log_softmax, F.cross_entropy(logits, y), BCEWithLogitsLoss: stable internally.
  • Never torch.log(torch.softmax(z)).

stages.name: Where it reappears
stages.html:
• Attention scores QKᵀ/√d over thousands of keys; FlashAttention-style kernels use an online softmax with running max and sum.
  • Growing logits during training also cause instability (z-loss, QK-norm as mitigations; see Q69).

followUps.question: Why does fp16 hit this sooner?
followUps.html: fp16's max is ~65,504, so exp overflows for inputs above about 11. That's why softmax and reductions are usually computed in fp32 even in mixed-precision training.

followUps.question: Why divide attention scores by √d?
followUps.html: Dot products of d-dimensional vectors grow with d; without scaling, logits get large, softmax saturates toward one-hot, and gradients vanish. Scaling keeps variance roughly constant.

followUps.question: Would clipping logits fix it?
followUps.html: It avoids NaN but changes the output distribution and gradients. Max-subtraction is exact and free, so there's no reason to distort values.

followUps.question: The NaN appears only after thousands of steps. Is it still softmax?
followUps.html: Possibly logits growing over training (weights drifting large), or it's elsewhere: log of zero, division by a zero norm, fp16 gradient overflow. Find the first op that produced inf/NaN with anomaly detection and check logit magnitudes over time.

followUps.question: What does temperature do numerically?
followUps.html: Dividing logits by T < 1 enlarges them (sharper distribution, more overflow risk without max-subtraction); T > 1 flattens. The max-subtraction trick still applies after scaling.

dontSay: "Lower the learning rate." — may delay it, doesn't fix the arithmetic.
"Compute log(softmax(x))." — unstable.
"Clip the logits." — distorts outputs when an exact fix exists.

ml-dl-q56.testing: the collapse argument, plus a practical default.
ml-dl-q56.spoken:
"Without a nonlinearity, any stack of linear layers collapses into a single linear map, because a product of matrices is just another matrix. Depth would buy nothing.

Which one: sigmoid and tanh saturate. Their derivatives go to near zero in the tails, so gradients vanish in deep stacks. I keep sigmoid for gates and output probabilities only.

ReLU is the cheap default: no saturation for positive inputs and sparse activations. Its failure is dead units, stuck at zero with zero gradient after a bad initialisation or learning rate.

GELU and SiLU are the transformer-era defaults: smooth, with a small leak for negative inputs, and empirically better at scale.

So my rule: hidden layers get ReLU-family or GELU; the output layer is dictated by the task and loss: linear for regression, sigmoid for binary or multi-label probabilities, softmax for multiclass. A sigmoid in a deep hidden stack is a vanishing-gradient bug."

stages.name: Linear layers collapse
stages.html:
W₃(W₂(W₁x)) = (W₃W₂W₁)x = W x

Adding a nonlinearity σ between layers breaks the collapse and lets networks approximate non-linear functions.

stages.name: Saturating activations
stages.html:
• σ'(z) ≤ 0.25; tanh' ≤ 1 but → 0 at the tails.
  • Deep stacks multiply these → vanishing gradients (Q18).
  • Still right for gates (LSTM) and output probabilities.

stages.name: ReLU
stages.html:
• max(0, x): derivative 1 for positive inputs.
  • Dead ReLUs: permanently negative pre-activations get no gradient. Mitigations: Leaky ReLU, careful init (He), sane LR.

stages.name: GELU/SiLU
stages.html:
• GELU ≈ x·Φ(x); SiLU/Swish = x·σ(x).
  • Smooth near zero, small negative outputs → fewer dead units, better optimisation at scale.
  • Gated variants (SwiGLU) in modern LLM FFNs (Q64).

stages.name: The picking rule
stages.html:
Layer Choice
Hidden, CNN/MLP ReLU (or Leaky ReLU)
Hidden, transformer GELU / SwiGLU
Output, regression linear (identity)
Output, binary / multi-label sigmoid (+ BCE)
Output, multiclass softmax (+ cross-entropy)

followUps.question: Why not use the same activation for output layers?
followUps.html: The output activation defines what the output means: an unbounded value, a probability, or a distribution over classes. It must match the loss (MSE, BCE, cross-entropy) so the likelihood interpretation and gradients are correct.

followUps.question: How do you detect dead ReLUs?
followUps.html: Track the fraction of units that are zero for all inputs in a batch, per layer. A growing fraction signals dying units; lower the LR, use He init, or switch to Leaky ReLU/GELU.

followUps.question: Is ReLU differentiable at 0?
followUps.html: Not strictly; frameworks define the gradient as 0 (or 1) there. It doesn't matter in practice because exact zeros are rare with real-valued inputs.

followUps.question: Why did transformers move to GELU?
followUps.html: Empirically better results in BERT/GPT-style models; smoothness helps optimisation and the small negative region keeps gradients flowing. Later, gated variants (SwiGLU) improved further per FLOP.

followUps.question: Does the activation affect initialisation?
followUps.html: Yes: He init assumes ReLU zeroes half its inputs; Xavier assumes symmetric activations like tanh. Mismatches change activation variance across depth (Q20).

dontSay: "We add activations to make it non-linear." (without the collapse argument) — circular.
"Sigmoid in hidden layers is fine." — vanishing gradients in depth.
"Softmax for multi-label." — use independent sigmoids.

ml-dl-q57.testing: that you can demystify embeddings and argue against one-hot concretely.
ml-dl-q57.trap: "a vector that captures meaning" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q57.spoken:
"An embedding is a learned dense vector: a row of a matrix selected by a token or item ID, trained by backpropagation like any other weight. It's a lookup table with gradients; nothing mystical.

Its geometry becomes meaningful because training pushes things used in similar contexts toward similar vectors. Similarity in that space means 'useful for the same predictions'.

One-hot vectors can't do that. Every pair is orthogonal and equally far apart, so related words share no statistical strength, and the dimension equals the vocabulary size, which is huge and sparse.

Upstream, tokenisation decides the units. Subword schemes like BPE give a bounded vocabulary with no true out-of-vocabulary words, at the cost of splitting rare words into pieces.

A detail that lands well: in many language models the input embedding matrix and the output projection are weight-tied, sharing parameters.

And the same idea is everywhere beyond text: user and item embeddings in recommenders, categorical embeddings for tabular data, and embedding search for retrieval."

stages.name: A learned lookup table
stages.html:
E ∈ ℝ^{V × d}          V = vocabulary size, d = embedding dim (e.g. 768)
embed(token_id) = E[token_id]     ≡ one_hot(token_id) · E

Gradients update only the rows used in a batch.

stages.name: Why the geometry means something
stages.html:
• Tokens that predict similar next tokens, or appear in similar contexts, get similar gradients → similar vectors.
  • Distance/cosine reflects usefulness for the model's objective, not a dictionary definition.

stages.name: What one-hot can't do
stages.html:
One-hot Embedding
dimension = V (50k+) d (hundreds)
all tokens equidistant related tokens close
no sharing between related tokens statistical strength shared
sparse, memory-heavy input layer dense, efficient

stages.name: Tokenisation decides the units
stages.html:
• Word-level: huge vocab, out-of-vocabulary words.
  • Character-level: tiny vocab, long sequences.
  • Subword (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece): bounded vocab, rare words split into pieces.

stages.name: Where embeddings go next
stages.html:
• Weight tying: output logits = h · Eᵀ, saving parameters.
  • Sentence/document embeddings for retrieval (contrastive training).
  • Categorical embeddings in tabular and recommender models.

followUps.question: How do you choose the embedding dimension?
followUps.html: Trade capacity against memory and overfitting; common heuristics scale with vocabulary size (e.g. roughly the fourth root of cardinality for categorical features), but tune by validation. For LLMs it's tied to the model width.

followUps.question: Is an embedding the same as word2vec?
followUps.html: word2vec is one way to train embeddings (predict context words). In modern models, embeddings are trained end-to-end with the task, and contextual models produce different vectors for the same word in different sentences.

followUps.question: Why can't embeddings from two models be compared directly?
followUps.html: Each model's space has its own arbitrary basis and scale; distances are only meaningful within one space. Mixing them needs alignment or re-embedding everything with one model.

followUps.question: How do embeddings help a tabular model with a 1M-level categorical?
followUps.html: One-hot is infeasible; an embedding table maps each level to a small dense vector learned from the task, letting similar levels share strength. Handle rare and unseen levels with a shared "other" embedding or hashing.

followUps.question: What does weight tying buy?
followUps.html: Fewer parameters (the V×d matrix is used twice) and often better generalisation, because input and output representations of a token are forced to agree.

dontSay: "Embeddings capture the meaning of words." (only) — say how.
"One-hot works fine for big vocabularies." — size and no sharing.
"Embeddings are pre-computed." — usually learned with the task.
