ml-dl-q58.trap: "deeper is more powerful" without saying in what sense.
ml-dl-q58.spoken:
"The universal approximation theorem is an existence result: for any continuous function on a bounded domain, some single hidden layer that's wide enough can approximate it arbitrarily well.

It's silent on three things that matter in practice.

How wide: the required width can grow exponentially with the input dimension. Depth buys compositionality: hierarchical functions, features built on features, can be expressed with exponentially fewer units when stacked.

Whether gradient descent finds it: existence says nothing about training. Deep networks with residuals and normalisation turn out to be trainable in practice.

Whether it generalises: fitting the training data isn't learning the function. Depth is an inductive bias that matches the compositional structure of real data, edges into textures into objects, characters into words into meaning, so deep models learn more from less data.

So the one-liner: approximation isn't optimisation isn't generalisation. The theorem only covers the first."

stages.name: What UAT actually says
stages.html: For continuous f on a compact set and any ε > 0, there exists a one-hidden-layer network with enough units such that |network(x) − f(x)| < ε everywhere.

stages.name: What it doesn't: size
stages.html:
• Some functions need exponentially many units in one layer but polynomially many across several layers (depth-separation results).
  • Composition reuses intermediate features instead of re-deriving them.

stages.name: What it doesn't: findability
stages.html:
• UAT guarantees parameters exist, not that SGD reaches them.
  • Practical trainability comes from residuals, normalisation, good init and optimisers.

stages.name: What it doesn't: generalisation
stages.html:
• A huge shallow net could memorise training data without learning the underlying function.
  • Generalisation depends on inductive bias, data and regularisation.

stages.name: Depth as inductive bias
stages.html:
Domain Hierarchy depth exploits
Vision pixels → edges → textures → parts → objects
Language characters → words → phrases → meaning
Audio samples → phonemes → words

followUps.question: Is deeper always better then?
followUps.html: No. Without residuals and normalisation, very deep plain networks train poorly (vanishing gradients), and past a point returns diminish relative to width, data and compute. Scaling laws treat depth, width and data together.

followUps.question: Does UAT apply to ReLU networks?
followUps.html: Yes; versions exist for ReLU and other non-polynomial activations, and for bounded-width deep networks too. The condition is that the activation isn't a polynomial.

followUps.question: Why do wide shallow networks sometimes do well?
followUps.html: For simple or smooth targets, width suffices, and wide networks are easier to optimise in some regimes (neural tangent kernel). For compositional problems like vision and language, depth wins clearly.

followUps.question: How does this connect to CNNs vs ViTs?
followUps.html: Both illustrate inductive bias: CNNs bake in locality and translation equivariance, which helps with little data; ViTs have weaker priors and need more data but scale further (Q71). UAT says both can represent the function; bias decides which learns it from your data.

followUps.question: What's the one sentence to remember?
followUps.html: "UAT is about representation; depth matters for efficiency, trainability and generalisation, which the theorem doesn't address."

dontSay: "One layer is enough, so depth is just fashion." — ignores size and learnability.
"Deeper networks can represent more functions." — both can represent; efficiency differs.
"UAT guarantees we can train it." — existence ≠ findability.

spine: The cell state is an additive highway
ml-dl-q59.testing: the arithmetic of the cell state, then one job per gate.
ml-dl-q59.trap: listing gates without explaining why the design fixes vanishing gradients.
ml-dl-q59.spoken:
"The core trick is the cell state: an additive highway through time. The new cell state is the old one, scaled by a gate, plus new information. Addition instead of repeated matrix multiplication is what lets gradients survive over long sequences; it's the same insight residual connections use across layers.

Each gate has one job. The forget gate decides what fraction of the old cell state to keep. The input gate decides what new information to write. The output gate decides how much of the cell to expose as the hidden state at this step.

A GRU merges this into two gates, update and reset, with fewer parameters and usually comparable results; it's the pragmatic default if you must use a recurrent model.

The honest limit: gating fixed vanishing gradients, but not the sequential bottleneck. An LSTM still processes one step at a time and can't be parallelised across the sequence, which is why attention won anyway."

stages.name: The cell state is an additive highway
stages.html:
c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ g_t
h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t)

∂c_t/∂c_{t−1} = f_t: when the forget gate is near 1, gradients pass through almost unchanged.

stages.name: Forget gate
stages.html:
• f_t = σ(W_f [h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_f), per dimension in (0, 1).
  • Initialise its bias positive (e.g. 1) so the cell remembers by default early in training.

stages.name: Input gate
stages.html:
• i_t = σ(…) chooses how much of the candidate g_t = tanh(…) enters the cell.
  • Separating "write" from "keep" lets the cell hold values unchanged for many steps.

stages.name: Output gate
stages.html:
• o_t = σ(…) controls what the next layer and next step see as h_t.
  • The cell can store information that isn't shown yet.

stages.name: GRU and the honest limit
stages.html:
LSTM GRU
Gates forget, input, output update, reset
Separate cell state yes no
Parameters more ~25% fewer
Quality similar on most tasks similar

Both still compute step t after t−1: no parallelism over time.

followUps.question: Why does the additive update help gradients?
followUps.html: The gradient path through c is a product of forget-gate values, not of full weight-matrix Jacobians. With f ≈ 1 it stays near 1 over many steps instead of shrinking exponentially (Q23).

followUps.question: Why sigmoid for gates and tanh for candidates?
followUps.html: Gates are soft switches, fractions between 0 and 1 (sigmoid). Candidate values are signed content, centred around 0 (tanh), which keeps the cell state bounded and balanced.

followUps.question: Do LSTMs have infinite memory?
followUps.html: No. Forget gates are rarely exactly 1, so information decays over hundreds of steps. Longer leash than a vanilla RNN, but finite.

followUps.question: Where are LSTMs still used?
followUps.html: Streaming or on-device settings needing constant memory per step (keyword spotting, some time series), and small-data sequence tasks. State-space models (Mamba) now revive recurrent inference with parallel training.

followUps.question: What's peephole LSTM?
followUps.html: A variant where gates also see the cell state directly. It helps precise timing tasks slightly but is rarely used; standard LSTM or GRU are the defaults.

dontSay: "Gates let the LSTM remember everything." — decays, just slower.
"LSTMs solved long sequences, so why transformers?" — the sequential bottleneck remained.
Listing gates without the additive cell update.

spine: The reframe: the retrofit became the model
ml-dl-q60.testing: the origin story with mechanism, and the conceptual leap to transformers.
ml-dl-q60.trap: "attention lets the model focus on important words" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q60.spoken:
"Vanilla sequence-to-sequence models squeezed the whole source sentence into one fixed-size vector, the encoder's final hidden state. That was an information bottleneck: translation quality visibly dropped as sentences got longer.

Bahdanau attention fixed it. At every decoder step, compute a relevance score between the decoder's state and every encoder state, softmax those scores into weights, and feed the weighted sum of encoder states, a context vector, into the decoder. It's content-based addressing over the source, and the alignment between source and target words is learned jointly with translation.

Luong attention simplified the scoring, dot-product or a bilinear form instead of a small MLP, and changed where the context vector enters the decoder. Worth naming to show you know the lineage.

The reframe that matters: attention started as a retrofit to fix an RNN's memory. The transformer's move was to delete the RNN and keep only the retrofit."

stages.name: The fixed-vector bottleneck
stages.claim: one vector for a whole sentence
stages.html:
encoder: x₁ … x_T → h_T  (single vector)  → decoder generates y₁ … y_U

Long sentences lose detail; BLEU dropped with length.

stages.name: Bahdanau: soft lookup per step
stages.html:
score(s_{t−1}, h_i) = vᵀ tanh(W s_{t−1} + U h_i)
α_{t,i} = softmax_i(score)
c_t = Σ_i α_{t,i} h_i        → fed into decoder step t
  • Differentiable, learned alignment; attention maps looked like word alignments.

stages.name: Luong: simpler scoring
stages.html:
Bahdanau Luong
Score small MLP (additive) dot / general (bilinear)
Decoder state used previous step current step
Cost higher cheaper, matmul-friendly

stages.name: The reframe: the retrofit became the model
stages.html:
• Attention gave every output direct access to every input.
  • The transformer removed recurrence: self-attention within encoder and decoder, plus cross-attention between them, all parallel.

followUps.question: What's the difference between attention and self-attention?
followUps.html: In seq2seq attention, decoder states query encoder states (two sequences). In self-attention, a sequence attends to itself: each token's query compares against all tokens' keys in the same sequence. Transformers use both (self-attention and cross-attention).

followUps.question: Are attention weights explanations?
followUps.html: Not reliably. They show where information was pulled from in one layer, but other paths (residuals, other heads) matter, and different weightings can produce the same output. Use them as a hint, not proof.

followUps.question: Why did dot-product scoring win?
followUps.html: It's a matrix multiplication, which GPUs do extremely fast and in parallel. With scaling by √d it trains stably, making it the basis of transformer attention.

followUps.question: Did attention fix the RNN's sequential training?
followUps.html: No. Encoder and decoder were still RNNs, trained step by step. Attention fixed the information bottleneck; the transformer fixed parallelism by removing recurrence (Q61).

followUps.question: What does the context vector represent?
followUps.html: A weighted summary of the source, specific to the current output step: mostly the parts of the input relevant to what the decoder is generating now.

dontSay: "Attention was invented for transformers." — it came from seq2seq RNNs.
"Attention focuses on important words." (alone) — give the scoring and weighted sum.
"Attention made RNNs parallel." — it didn't.

ml-dl-q61.testing: hardware, optimisation and economic reasons, plus the costs.
ml-dl-q61.spoken:
"Three real reasons.

One, parallelism. Training computes every position at once as dense matrix multiplications, exactly what GPUs and TPUs are built for. An RNN's step-by-step chain leaves most of the hardware idle.

Two, path length. Any two tokens are one attention step apart, versus a number of hops proportional to their distance through a recurrent chain. Credit assignment over long ranges stops decaying with distance.

Three, the economics those two unlock. More tokens and more parameters trained per dollar, which let transformers ride scaling laws that recurrent networks couldn't reach in practice.

And the price: attention costs grow quadratically with sequence length, and the architecture has no built-in sense of order, so position has to be injected explicitly with positional encodings. Long-context inference also needs a KV cache that grows with the sequence."

stages.name: Reason 1: parallel training
stages.html:
• Self-attention for all positions = a few large matmuls per layer.
  • RNNs: step t waits for step t−1 → poor GPU utilisation during training.
  • Teacher forcing plus causal masking lets decoder training run in parallel too.

stages.name: Reason 2: constant path length
stages.html:
RNN / LSTM Transformer
Max path between tokens O(n) O(1)
Gradient over long range decays with distance direct
Sequential ops per layer O(n) O(1)

stages.name: Reason 3: scaling economics
stages.html:
• Efficient training at scale → bigger models on more data.
  • Performance improves predictably with compute (scaling laws), which justified the investment.

stages.name: The price paid
stages.html:
Cost Mitigations
O(n²) attention compute/memory FlashAttention, sparse/sliding attention, linear attention
No inherent order positional encodings (sinusoidal, learned, RoPE, ALiBi)
KV cache grows with context at inference GQA/MQA, paged attention, quantised caches
Weak inductive bias needs more data (Q71)

followUps.question: Isn't inference still sequential for transformers?
followUps.html: Generation is token by token, yes, but training and prompt processing are parallel, and the KV cache avoids recomputing past tokens. The training speedup is what drove the scaling advantage.

followUps.question: Why do transformers need positional encodings?
followUps.html: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: shuffle the inputs and the outputs shuffle identically, so without position information the model can't tell word order. Positional encodings inject it.

followUps.question: Are RNNs coming back?
followUps.html: State-space models (Mamba) and linear-attention RNNs offer parallel training with constant-memory recurrent inference, attractive for long contexts. They're competitive in some settings; transformers remain dominant, often hybridised with them.

followUps.question: "Transformers understand context better." Fair?
followUps.html: Too vague. The concrete advantages are direct token-to-token paths and parallel training; better "understanding" is the result of scale that those properties made affordable.

followUps.question: When would an LSTM still be the right choice?
followUps.html: Small data, strict streaming or on-device constraints with constant memory per step, or very long streams where quadratic attention is prohibitive and a small recurrent model is enough.

dontSay: "Attention is all you need." — a slogan, not a reason.
"Transformers are more accurate." — explain why.
Forgetting the costs (quadratic attention, positional encodings).

ml-dl-q62.testing: the mechanism of the coupling, not just "AdamW is better".
ml-dl-q62.trap: "AdamW adds weight decay to Adam." Adam with L2 already had it; the difference is where it's applied.
ml-dl-q62.spoken:
"Adam keeps two moving averages per parameter. The first moment is an average of recent gradients, which is momentum: it steers and smooths the direction. The second moment is an average of squared gradients, which acts as a per-parameter step-size scaler: parameters with large recent gradients take smaller steps. Bias correction fixes both averages being underestimated in the first steps, since they start at zero.

The problem with classic Adam plus L2 regularisation is where the decay goes. Adding λ times the weights to the loss puts the decay term into the gradient, and then it gets divided by the square root of the second moment like everything else. So parameters with a large gradient history get less decay. The regularisation strength becomes tangled with the gradient scale.

AdamW decouples it: weight decay is applied directly to the weights at the update step, outside the adaptive scaling. Decay then means what it says, uniformly. That changed results enough that it's the default for transformer training, hence the new name.

One cost worth naming: those two extra states per parameter mean optimizer memory is about twice the model size in fp32, a big part of the training-memory budget."

stages.name: First moment steers
stages.html:
m_t = β₁ m_{t−1} + (1 − β₁) g_t        β₁ ≈ 0.9

Smooths noisy gradients; direction of travel.

stages.name: Second moment scales
stages.html:
v_t = β₂ v_{t−1} + (1 − β₂) g_t²       β₂ ≈ 0.95–0.999
step ∝ m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)

Large, frequent gradients → smaller effective steps; rare ones → larger.

stages.name: Bias correction
stages.html: m̂ = m / (1 − β₁ᵗ), v̂ = v / (1 − β₂ᵗ); matters most in early steps (and interacts with warmup, Q63).

stages.name: The coupling bug
stages.html:
Adam + L2:  g ← g + λθ ;  θ ← θ − η m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)
            → decay term also divided by √v̂: parameters with big gradients decay less

stages.name: AdamW's fix
stages.html:
AdamW:  θ ← θ − η ( m̂ / (√v̂ + ε) + λθ )
            → uniform shrinkage regardless of gradient history
  • Typical: weight decay ~0.01–0.1, often excluded for biases and norm parameters.

stages.name: The memory cost
stages.html:
• Two fp32 states per parameter: 8 bytes/param.
  • 7B parameters → ~56 GB of optimizer state alone (see Q65); motivates ZeRO sharding and 8-bit optimizers.

followUps.question: Isn't L2 regularisation the same as weight decay?
followUps.html: For plain SGD, yes, they're equivalent up to scaling of λ. For adaptive optimizers they differ, because the adaptive denominator rescales the L2 gradient per parameter. That difference is exactly what AdamW fixes.

followUps.question: Why exclude LayerNorm and bias parameters from weight decay?
followUps.html: They're few, don't cause overfitting in the same way, and shrinking norm gains toward zero can hurt training. Common recipes apply decay only to weight matrices.

followUps.question: Why β₂ = 0.95 in LLM training instead of 0.999?
followUps.html: A shorter memory for the second moment reacts faster to changing gradient scales, improving stability in large-scale training where gradient statistics shift, reducing loss spikes.

followUps.question: How do you reduce Adam's memory?
followUps.html: Shard optimizer state across GPUs (ZeRO stage 1+), use 8-bit optimizer states, or use lower-memory optimizers like Adafactor, which factorises the second moment. Each trades some fidelity or communication for memory.

followUps.question: What does ε do?
followUps.html: Prevents division by zero and caps the step for parameters with tiny v. Too small can cause instability with tiny gradients in low precision; it's occasionally tuned (e.g. 1e-8 vs 1e-6).

dontSay: "AdamW adds weight decay to Adam." — the point is decoupling.
"Both moments are momentum." — the second one scales.
"Adam has no memory overhead." — 2× parameters in fp32.

ml-dl-q63.testing: the mechanism behind a recipe step everyone copies.
ml-dl-q63.spoken:
"Two things are wrong at step ten.

First, Adam's second-moment estimate. It's an average of squared gradients built from only a handful of noisy samples, so the adaptive denominator is unreliable. Some parameters with tiny early estimates get enormous effective steps.

Second, the network itself is raw. Attention distributions and output logits are unformed, gradients are large and badly conditioned. A full-size learning rate at that moment can push weights into divergence or saturation you never recover from. The original post-norm transformers were notoriously dependent on warmup; pre-norm reduced the need but didn't remove it.

Warmup ramps the learning rate from near zero to its peak over the first few hundred or thousand steps, so the optimizer statistics and the network settle before full-size steps land. Then a decay schedule, cosine or linear, takes over: large steps to cover ground, small steps to converge.

And I'd pair it with gradient clipping: warmup prevents the early blow-ups, clipping insures against a rare bad batch later in training."

stages.name: Culprit 1: Adam's noisy second moment
stages.html:
• v̂ estimated from very few gradients early; bias correction fixes its mean but not its noise.
  • Parameters with small early v̂ get step ≈ η·m̂/√v̂ that's far too large.

stages.name: Culprit 2: an unformed network
stages.html:
• Random init: attention nearly uniform, logits poorly scaled, residual stream statistics unsettled.
  • Large early updates can blow up activations, saturate softmax, or create dead units.
  • Post-norm (norm after residual add) amplifies this; pre-norm is more stable.

stages.name: What warmup does
Then decay
stages.html:
• Cosine or linear decay to ~10% of peak (or lower).
  • Alternatives: inverse square root (original transformer), warmup-stable-decay schedules for continued training.

stages.name: Pair it with clipping
stages.html:
• Global-norm clipping (e.g. 1.0) caps any single catastrophic step.
  • Log the pre-clip norm: frequent clipping late in training means the LR is too hot (Q67, Q69).

followUps.question: How long should warmup be?
followUps.html: Commonly a few hundred to a few thousand steps, or ~1–5% of training. Longer for larger learning rates, larger batches and deeper models. Too short risks early instability; too long wastes training at a low LR.

followUps.question: Does warmup matter with SGD?
followUps.html: Less for the second-moment reason, but still useful with large batches and large learning rates (the "linear scaling rule" pairs with warmup), because early gradients are large and the network is fragile.

followUps.question: Why does pre-norm need less warmup?
followUps.html: In pre-norm the residual path is an identity, so gradients flow directly and activations stay bounded early. Post-norm puts normalisation after the residual addition, making early gradients to lower layers larger and less stable.

followUps.question: Can you skip warmup by lowering the peak LR?
followUps.html: You can stay stable, but you give up the benefit of a high LR later, training slower or ending worse. Warmup lets you use a high peak safely.

followUps.question: Your loss explodes at step 300 during warmup. What do you check?
followUps.html: Peak LR too high for this model/batch, too short a warmup, fp16 overflow without proper loss scaling, bad init, or a data problem. Lower the peak, lengthen warmup, check the numerics and the first NaN layer.

dontSay: "Warmup helps the model converge." (only) — give the two mechanisms.
"It's needed because the LR is too high." — the point is safely using a high LR.
"Clipping replaces warmup." — they solve different problems.

ml-dl-q64.testing: what "smooth" and "gated" buy, and honesty about the cost.
ml-dl-q64.trap: "GELU is just better" with no mechanism.
ml-dl-q64.spoken:
"ReLU is cheap and sparse, but it has a hard zero: any unit with negative input gets no gradient at all, so units can die, and the kink makes the loss surface less smooth.

GELU is roughly x times the probability that a standard normal is below x. It gates each input smoothly by its own magnitude, and it lets small negative inputs through with a small gradient, so units don't fully die. Empirically it trains better at transformer scale.

SwiGLU goes further: the feed-forward layer becomes a gated product of two projections, one passed through SiLU and multiplied element-wise by the other. So the gate is learned and input-dependent for every hidden unit. It's consistently better quality per FLOP and standard in Llama-style models, usually with the hidden dimension trimmed to keep the parameter count comparable.

What's worse: slightly more compute, and for gated FFNs an extra projection matrix. That's negligible next to the matmuls, which is why everyone pays it.

One tie-in: activation choice interacts with initialisation assumptions; He initialisation was derived for ReLU."

stages.name: ReLU's hard zero
GELU: smooth gating
stages.html:
• GELU(x) = x · Φ(x); negative inputs produce small negative outputs with non-zero gradient.
  • Smoothness helps optimisation in deep, wide networks.

stages.name: SwiGLU: a learned gate
stages.html:
FFN_ReLU(x)   = W₂ · ReLU(W₁ x)
FFN_SwiGLU(x) = W₂ · ( SiLU(W₁ x) ⊙ (W₃ x) )      three matrices
  • Hidden size often set to ~⅔ of 4d so total parameters match the ReLU FFN.
  • The gate W₃x decides, per input, which hidden features pass.

stages.name: The costs
stages.html:
Cost Size
Extra projection (W₃) offset by smaller hidden dim
Activation compute (erf/sigmoid) tiny vs matmuls
Kernel support universal in modern frameworks

stages.name: The init tie-in
stages.html: He init assumes ReLU's halving of variance; smooth or gated activations change activation statistics slightly, and deep recipes also scale residual projections at init.

followUps.question: Why not Leaky ReLU instead of GELU?
followUps.html: Leaky ReLU fixes dead units but keeps the kink. GELU/SiLU are smooth everywhere, which empirically optimises better in transformers. Gated variants add input-dependent gating Leaky ReLU lacks.

followUps.question: Is the SwiGLU gain large?
followUps.html: Modest but consistent: a better loss at the same compute, reported across several studies. It's adopted because the cost is negligible, not because it's dramatic.

followUps.question: What's SiLU?
followUps.html: SiLU/Swish = x · σ(x): smooth, non-monotonic dip below zero, similar shape to GELU and cheaper to compute exactly.

followUps.question: Why doesn't activation choice matter much for inference latency?
followUps.html: FFN time is dominated by the matrix multiplications (and memory bandwidth); element-wise activations are a small fraction, often fused into the matmul kernel.

followUps.question: Would you switch an existing ReLU model to GELU?
followUps.html: Not by swapping on a trained model: weights were learned for ReLU. For a new training run, yes, as the modern default; validate on your task since gains are empirical.

dontSay: "GELU is better." (no mechanism) — smoothness and non-zero negative gradients.
"SwiGLU is free." — an extra projection; small cost, compensated by hidden size.
"ReLU is obsolete." — still the default in many CNNs.

ml-dl-q65.testing: fluency with memory arithmetic and what it implies for infrastructure.
ml-dl-q65.spoken:
"Before activations, count bytes per parameter.

In mixed-precision AdamW you keep the working weights in bf16, 2 bytes; an fp32 master copy of the weights, 4 bytes; two fp32 Adam moments, 8 bytes; and the gradients, 2 to 4 bytes. That's about 16 bytes per parameter, the standard figure from the ZeRO paper.

Seven billion times 16 bytes is about 112 gigabytes of state, already more than a single 80-gigabyte GPU before a single activation.

Activations come on top and scale with batch size times sequence length times depth times width. They're attacked with activation checkpointing: store only some activations and recompute the rest during the backward pass, trading roughly a third more compute for much less memory.

For contrast, inference needs about 2 bytes per parameter in bf16, less when quantised, plus the KV cache. So training and serving memory are almost an order of magnitude apart.

And this arithmetic is the reason sharded optimizers like ZeRO and FSDP exist: in plain data parallelism most of those 16 bytes are duplicated on every GPU."

stages.name: Count bytes per parameter
Multiply
stages.html:
Item Bytes/param 7B total
bf16 weights 2 14 GB
fp32 master weights 4 28 GB
Adam moments (fp32) 8 56 GB
Gradients (bf16) 2 14 GB
Total state 16 ~112 GB

stages.name: Add activations
stages.html:
• Scale with batch × sequence length × layers × hidden size (attention adds more at long context).
  • Activation checkpointing: recompute in backward; ~⅓ extra compute for large savings.
  • Micro-batching with gradient accumulation keeps activations bounded (Q67).

stages.name: Contrast with inference
stages.html:
• bf16 inference: ~14 GB weights; int8 ~7 GB; int4 ~3.5 GB.
  • Plus KV cache, growing with batch × context length.

stages.name: What the arithmetic justifies
stages.html:
• ZeRO-1/2/3 / FSDP: shard optimizer states, gradients, then parameters across data-parallel GPUs (Q68).
  • 8-bit optimizers, CPU/NVMe offload, LoRA for fine-tuning (only adapter weights get optimizer state).

followUps.question: Why keep fp32 master weights at all?
followUps.html: Updates are tiny relative to weights; in bf16 many would round to zero and be lost. Accumulating updates into fp32 masters preserves them; the bf16 copy is used for compute.

followUps.question: How does LoRA change the budget for fine-tuning?
followUps.html: Base weights are frozen (just 2 bytes/param, or less if quantised as in QLoRA), and only small adapter matrices need gradients and Adam state. A 7B model can then be fine-tuned on a single 24–48 GB GPU.

followUps.question: With ZeRO-3 on 8 GPUs, what's per-GPU state?
followUps.html: Roughly 112 GB / 8 ≈ 14 GB of sharded state per GPU, plus activations and temporary gathered parameters for the layer being computed, plus communication buffers.

followUps.question: What dominates memory at long context?
followUps.html: Activations, especially attention intermediates, which grow with sequence length (quadratically for naive attention). FlashAttention avoids storing the full attention matrix; checkpointing and sequence parallelism help further.

followUps.question: "7B × 2 bytes = 14 GB, so one GPU is fine." Response?
followUps.html: That's inference weights only. Training adds master weights, optimizer state and gradients (16 bytes/param total) plus activations, so about 8× more before activations.

dontSay: "14 GB for a 7B model." (for training) — that's inference weights.
"Activations are negligible." — they often dominate at long context.
"Just use a bigger GPU." — 112 GB of state exceeds any single one today.

ml-dl-q66.testing: number formats and the practical fix, not just "use bf16".
ml-dl-q66.trap: "fp16 is less precise." It's the range, not the precision, that bites.
ml-dl-q66.spoken:
"The two formats spend their 16 bits differently.

fp16 has more mantissa bits, so better precision, but a narrow exponent range. Small gradients underflow to zero, and large intermediate values overflow to infinity, and one infinity cascades into NaNs.

Loss scaling is the fp16 patch. Multiply the loss by a large factor, which scales all gradients up into the representable range, then unscale them before the optimizer step. Dynamic loss scaling lowers the factor automatically when it sees infinities, skipping that step, and slowly raises it again.

bf16 keeps fp32's exponent range with fewer mantissa bits. No underflow drama, no loss scaling needed, it's essentially drop-in, and it's the default on modern accelerators. The lost precision is tolerable because stochastic gradient descent is noise-tolerant anyway.

Both schemes still keep fp32 master weights, and numerically sensitive operations like softmax, normalisation and large reductions typically run in fp32 regardless."

stages.name: Same 16 bits, different split
stages.html:
Format Exponent bits Mantissa bits Max value Smallest normal
fp32 8 23 ~3.4e38 ~1.2e−38
fp16 5 10 ~65,504 ~6.1e−5
bf16 8 7 ~3.4e38 ~1.2e−38

stages.name: fp16's narrow range
stages.html:
• Gradients smaller than ~6e−5 (subnormals down to ~6e−8) become zero: silent loss of learning signal.
  • Activations or logits above 65,504 → inf → NaN downstream.
  • "Mid-training" failures often come from gradually growing activations or logits.

stages.name: Loss scaling
stages.html:
loss_scaled = loss × S            (e.g. S = 2¹⁶)
grads_scaled = ∇ loss_scaled       stays representable
grads = grads_scaled / S           before clipping and the optimizer step
if inf/NaN in grads: skip step, S ← S/2 ;  else occasionally S ← S×2

stages.name: bf16 keeps fp32's range
stages.html:
• Same exponent range as fp32: underflow/overflow behave like fp32.
  • Coarser precision (~3 significant digits) is acceptable for gradients and activations.
  • Supported on A100/H100, TPUs; the default for LLM training.

stages.name: What stays in fp32
stages.html:
• Master weights and optimizer states.
  • Softmax, LayerNorm/RMSNorm statistics, loss computation, large reductions.
  • Autocast handles this per op.

followUps.question: Why unscale before clipping?
followUps.html: Clipping thresholds refer to true gradient norms. Clipping scaled gradients would use a threshold S times too large, effectively disabling clipping. Unscale, then clip, then step (Q67).

followUps.question: If bf16 is so easy, why did anyone use fp16?
followUps.html: Older GPUs (V100 and earlier) had fast fp16 but no bf16 support. fp16's extra precision can also matter for some inference workloads. On current hardware bf16 is the default for training.

followUps.question: Could bf16's lower precision hurt?
followUps.html: Occasionally: accumulating many small values can lose precision, which is why accumulations and master weights stay fp32. For standard training it's a non-issue in practice.

followUps.question: Where does fp8 fit?
followUps.html: Newer GPUs support fp8 formats (E4M3, E5M2) for matmuls with per-tensor scaling factors, giving more throughput. It needs careful scaling recipes and is used for large-scale training and inference with library support (e.g. Transformer Engine).

followUps.question: How do you find which op produced the first inf?
followUps.html: Enable anomaly detection or forward hooks checking for non-finite outputs per module, log max activation values per layer, and replay the failing batch. The first non-finite output localises the problem.

dontSay: "fp16 is less precise, that's why it NaNs." — fp16 is more precise; range is the issue.
"bf16 needs loss scaling too." — it doesn't.
"Mixed precision means everything is 16-bit." — masters and sensitive ops stay fp32.

ml-dl-q67.testing: both knobs and the subtle interaction: when clipping is applied.
ml-dl-q67.spoken:
"Two knobs.

Gradient accumulation fakes the bigger batch: run eight micro-batches, add up their gradients, and take one optimizer step. Mathematically that's the large batch, as long as the loss is averaged correctly over all micro-batches. It's safe in transformers because LayerNorm has no statistics across examples, unlike BatchNorm.

Gradient clipping handles the spikes: compute the global gradient norm, and if it exceeds a threshold, scale the whole gradient down. It caps the size of any single step, turning a catastrophic batch into a survivable one.

The interaction is timing. Clip once, after accumulation is complete, and after unscaling any fp16 loss scale. Clipping each micro-batch clips a different quantity and changes what the large batch means.

And one habit that reads senior: log the gradient norm before clipping. It's the vital sign that shows whether spikes are building, or whether the clip is doing work every step, which usually means the learning rate is too high."

stages.name: Gradient accumulation fakes the batch
stages.html:
opt.zero_grad()
for micro in micro_batches:                 # 8 × 512k tokens
    loss = model(micro).loss / len(micro_batches)
    loss.backward()                          # gradients add up
# one step for the full 4M-token batch
  • Scale the loss (or average) so the accumulated gradient equals the large-batch mean.
  • BatchNorm would see only micro-batch statistics; LayerNorm is per-example, so it's unaffected.

stages.name: Clipping caps the bad step
stages.html:
‖g‖ = sqrt(Σ over all params of ‖gᵢ‖²)
if ‖g‖ > c:  g ← g · c / ‖g‖            (e.g. c = 1.0)
  • Keeps the direction, limits the magnitude.
  • Insurance against rare outlier batches; not a fix for a bad LR.

stages.name: Order of operations
stages.html:
1. Accumulate all micro-batch gradients.
  2. Unscale (if using fp16 loss scaling).
  3. Compute the global norm and clip.
  4. Optimizer step; zero gradients.

stages.name: Log the pre-clip norm
stages.html:
Pre-clip norm pattern Reading
Rare spikes clipping doing its job
Clipped most steps LR too high or instability building
Steady rise before a spike growing logits / numerics (Q69)

followUps.question: Is accumulation exactly equal to a large batch?
followUps.html: For gradient math, yes, with correct averaging. Differences: BatchNorm statistics (per micro-batch), dropout masks (fine), and data ordering effects. Throughput is lower since micro-batches run sequentially.

followUps.question: Why clip by global norm instead of per value?
followUps.html: Per-value clipping changes the gradient direction; global-norm clipping rescales uniformly, keeping direction. It also treats the model as one vector, so one exploding layer triggers the cap.

followUps.question: Should you retune the LR when changing batch size?
followUps.html: If you change the effective batch, yes: larger batches usually tolerate or need larger LR (roughly linear or square-root scaling) with warmup. With accumulation reproducing the recipe's batch, keep the recipe's LR.

followUps.question: What's a sensible clip threshold?
followUps.html: 1.0 is a common default for transformers. Set it from the observed pre-clip norm distribution: high enough that normal steps aren't clipped, low enough to cap outliers.

followUps.question: Clipping each micro-batch "for safety" — harmless?
followUps.html: No. It clips partial gradients whose norms differ from the full batch's, biasing the combined update and making results depend on how the batch was split.

dontSay: "Just use a smaller batch." — changes the recipe's dynamics.
"Clip every micro-batch." — wrong quantity.
"Clipping fixes a too-high learning rate." — it hides it.

ml-dl-q68.testing: whether you pick parallelism by the specific bottleneck and know each cost.
ml-dl-q68.trap: listing the three types without saying when to use each.
ml-dl-q68.spoken:
"I'd organise it by what exactly stopped fitting.

Data parallelism replicates the model on every GPU, splits the batch, and all-reduces gradients. It scales throughput, but every GPU holds the full training state, about 16 bytes per parameter. It dies when the model plus state doesn't fit on one device.

ZeRO or FSDP is still data parallelism, but it shards the redundancy: first the optimizer state, then gradients, then the parameters themselves, gathering each shard only when it's needed. Same maths, far less memory per GPU. It's the first thing I'd reach for.

Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices across GPUs. Activations must be synchronised inside every layer, so it needs NVLink-class bandwidth and stays within a node. Use it when a single layer is too big or too slow.

Pipeline parallelism assigns blocks of consecutive layers to different GPUs and feeds micro-batches through so stages stay busy, but the ramp-up and ramp-down 'bubble' is idle time. It's for spreading depth across nodes.

Frontier training composes all three, so-called 3D parallelism. The design rule is to pick the cheapest parallelism that fixes what specifically doesn't fit."

stages.name: Ask what stopped fitting
stages.html:
What doesn't fit / too slow Reach for
Throughput (model fits) data parallel
Training state (optimizer, grads, params) ZeRO / FSDP
One layer's weights or compute tensor parallel
Total depth across nodes pipeline parallel
Very long sequences sequence / context parallel

stages.name: Data parallel
stages.html:
• All-reduce gradients each step; scales well with good interconnect.
  • Memory per GPU: full model + full optimizer state.

stages.name: ZeRO/FSDP
stages.html:
Stage Sharded Memory per GPU (N GPUs)
ZeRO-1 optimizer state ~ (4 + 12/N) bytes/param
ZeRO-2 + gradients smaller
ZeRO-3 / FSDP + parameters ~16/N bytes/param + working set

Cost: more communication (all-gather params per layer, reduce-scatter grads).

stages.name: Tensor parallel
stages.html:
• Column/row splits of attention and FFN weights (Megatron-style).
  • Communication inside every layer → needs NVLink/NVSwitch; usually ≤ 8 GPUs in a node.

stages.name: Pipeline parallel
stages.html:
• Layers grouped into stages on different GPUs/nodes; activations passed between stages.
  • Micro-batching (GPipe, 1F1B schedules) reduces the bubble; bubble fraction ≈ (stages − 1) / (micro-batches + stages − 1).

stages.name: Compose: 3D
stages.html:
• Tensor parallel within a node, pipeline across nodes, data parallel (often FSDP/ZeRO) across replicas.
  • Plus activation checkpointing and mixed precision throughout.

followUps.question: Why is tensor parallelism kept inside a node?
followUps.html: It communicates activations in every layer, forward and backward. That needs very high bandwidth and low latency, which NVLink within a node provides and cross-node networks usually don't.

followUps.question: You're fine-tuning a 13B model on 8 GPUs in one node. What do you use?
followUps.html: FSDP (or ZeRO-3) with activation checkpointing and bf16, likely enough on its own. If it still doesn't fit, add LoRA or CPU offload before reaching for tensor or pipeline parallelism, which add complexity.

followUps.question: Does ZeRO change the training maths?
followUps.html: No. It's the same data-parallel algorithm; it only changes where state lives and adds communication to gather it. Results match plain data parallelism up to numerical noise.

followUps.question: How do you shrink the pipeline bubble?
followUps.html: More micro-batches per step, interleaved schedules (virtual stages), and balancing stages so each takes similar time.

followUps.question: What's sequence parallelism?
followUps.html: Splitting the sequence dimension across GPUs for operations like LayerNorm and dropout (or for attention itself, as in ring attention), reducing activation memory for very long contexts.

dontSay: "Use data parallel." (for a model that doesn't fit) — it replicates everything.
"Tensor parallel across nodes." — bandwidth-bound.
"Pipeline parallel has no cost." — the bubble.

spine: Look first: grad norms and the first NaN
ml-dl-q69.testing: an ordered incident response for training, not a guess.
ml-dl-q69.trap: "lower the learning rate and keep training."
ml-dl-q69.spoken:
"First I look, before changing anything. The gradient-norm history around the spike: a sudden wall suggests a bad batch, a slow build suggests numerics or logit growth. And which layer produced the first infinity or NaN. That split alone separates a data problem from a numerics problem.

The four usual suspects: a bad data shard, corrupt, duplicated or adversarial, which I confirm by replaying that exact batch; a learning rate too hot for this phase of training, or a schedule bug; fp16 numerics overflowing; and growing logits, attention or output logits drifting upward until softmax breaks, which is what z-loss and QK-normalisation mitigate.

To recover: restore a checkpoint from before the spike, skip or reshuffle the offending data window, and resume with a lower learning rate or tighter clipping. 'Never recovers' usually means the weights are poisoned, so continuing forward throws good compute after bad.

To prevent the next one: checkpoint often enough that losing work is acceptable, keep data ordering deterministic so the bad batch can be bisected, and put pre-clip gradient norms on a dashboard as the early warning."

stages.name: Look first: grad norms and the first NaN
stages.html:
• Grad-norm history: sudden jump vs gradual build.
  • First non-finite tensor: which layer and op.

stages.name: Four usual suspects
stages.html:
Suspect Evidence Confirm
Bad data shard sudden spike at a specific step replay that batch; inspect samples
LR too hot / schedule bug spikes cluster after LR changes check schedule logs
fp16 numerics inf in activations or grads loss-scale history, switch to bf16
Growing logits slow rise in logit magnitudes log max attention/output logits per layer

stages.name: Recover from a checkpoint
stages.html:
Experiment 1

Restore and skip

Reload the last checkpoint before the spike and skip or reshuffle the offending data window.

Why? Weights after the spike are damaged; continuing wastes compute.

Best suited when the spike aligns with a specific batch.

Experiment 2

Restore and cool down

Resume with a lower LR (or longer warmup back to it) and tighter clipping.

Why? Gives the model a stable path through the region that destabilised it.

Best suited when spikes aren't tied to one batch.

Experiment 3

Fix the numerics

Switch to bf16, add z-loss on output logits, add QK-norm.

Why? Removes the mechanism, not just the symptom.

Best suited when logits or activations were growing before the spike.

stages.name: Prevent the next one
stages.html:
• Checkpoint cadence sized to acceptable lost work.
  • Deterministic data order and logged batch indices, so batches can be bisected.
  • Dashboards: pre-clip grad norm, loss-scale, max logits per layer, per-shard loss.
  • Automatic rollback on non-finite loss.

followUps.question: Why not just keep training? Loss sometimes recovers.
followUps.html: Sometimes it does, but "never recovers" means it hasn't. Continuing burns compute on damaged weights; restoring costs only the steps since the last checkpoint.

followUps.question: What's z-loss?
followUps.html: A small penalty on log of the softmax normaliser (log Σ e^z) squared, which discourages output logits from drifting large, improving stability in large-scale training.

followUps.question: How do you find the bad batch?
followUps.html: With deterministic data order you know exactly which samples were in the steps before the spike. Replay those batches on the pre-spike checkpoint and bisect until one reproduces the gradient explosion; then inspect it (corrupted text, extreme lengths, duplicates).

followUps.question: How often should you checkpoint?
followUps.html: Trade storage and write time against lost work: at scale, every few hundred to few thousand steps, with the cadence set by how much GPU-time you're willing to lose and how fast you can write checkpoints (async/sharded saves help).

followUps.question: Spikes keep happening at random points. What's structural?
followUps.html: Likely LR too high for this model/batch, missing stabilisers (pre-norm, QK-norm, z-loss), or β₂ too high for Adam. Lower peak LR, use β₂ ≈ 0.95, add stabilisers, and check data quality filters.

dontSay: "Lower the LR and continue." — the weights are already damaged.
"Probably a random fluctuation." — spikes have causes.
"We don't know which data it saw." — make data order deterministic.

spine: Diff the request path against the eval path
Fix: replay a golden set through production
ml-dl-q70.testing: whether you know the model you evaluated isn't the system you deployed.
ml-dl-q70.spoken:
"I'd walk the production request path and diff it against the evaluation path, because the model you evaluated is rarely exactly the system you deployed.

Suspect number one in the LLM era is tokenisation and formatting: different chat templates, missing special tokens, a different truncation side or padding. The eval harness and the serving stack silently disagree.

Second, numerics. It was trained and evaluated in bf16 but served quantised, int8, int4 or fp8, so offline eval scored a different model than the one in production. Re-run the eval on the deployed artifact.

Third, decoding. Eval used greedy decoding or a fixed seed; production uses temperature and top-p, different maximum lengths and stop conditions. That's a different generation policy.

Fourth, the data and the mode. Real prompts don't look like the benchmark, and custom serving paths can leave dropout or normalisation in training mode.

The fix pattern: a golden set replayed end-to-end through the real production stack as a release gate, plus regular re-evaluation of sampled live traffic."

stages.name: Diff the request path against the eval path
stages.html:
Stage Eval harness Production
Input formatting ? ?
Tokeniser + version ? ?
Precision / quantisation ? ?
Decoding params ? ?
Inputs benchmark real users

Every difference is a suspect.

stages.name: Tokeniser and template
stages.html:
• Chat template mismatch (roles, system prompt, BOS/EOS tokens).
  • Different tokeniser version or normalisation.
  • Truncation from the left vs right; max context differences cutting instructions.

stages.name: Numerics
stages.html:
• Quantisation (int8/int4/fp8) and kernel differences change outputs, sometimes a lot on specific tasks.
  • Evaluate the exact deployed artifact, not the training checkpoint.

stages.name: Decoding settings
stages.html:
• Temperature, top-p/top-k, repetition penalties, max tokens, stop sequences.
  • Batch-dependent effects in some serving engines (padding, speculative decoding settings).

stages.name: Real traffic and mode flags
stages.html:
• Distribution shift: longer, messier, multilingual or adversarial inputs.
  • Mode bugs: dropout active or BatchNorm using batch statistics in a custom path (Q21).
  • Preprocessing differences for images/audio (resizing, normalisation constants).

stages.name: Fix: replay a golden set through production
stages.html:
• Golden set with expected outputs/grades run through the full serving stack before each release.
  • Log production inputs/outputs (with privacy controls); sample and grade regularly.
  • Pin tokeniser, template and decoding config with the model version.

followUps.question: How do you catch a template mismatch quickly?
followUps.html: Log the exact token IDs sent to the model in production for a few requests and compare them with the eval harness's token IDs for the same prompt. Any difference in special tokens or ordering shows immediately.

followUps.question: Quantisation dropped quality on one task only. Why?
followUps.html: Some capabilities (arithmetic, long-context retrieval, rare languages) are more sensitive to precision loss. Evaluate quantised models per task, and consider higher precision or quantisation-aware methods for sensitive layers.

followUps.question: Is it ever the model after all?
followUps.html: Yes, when the benchmark doesn't represent real usage. But rule out pipeline differences first; they're cheaper to fix and more common in the first weeks after launch.

followUps.question: How do you evaluate production quality without labels?
followUps.html: LLM-as-judge with a calibrated rubric on sampled traffic, user feedback signals, task-specific checks (format validity, tool-call success), and periodic human review to keep the judge honest.

followUps.question: Who owns the serving config?
followUps.html: It should be versioned with the model: tokeniser, template, decoding parameters and quantisation recipe in one release artifact, reviewed like code, so eval and prod read the same config.

dontSay: "Retrain the model." (first) — check the pipeline.
"Benchmarks are just different from real life." — find the specific skew.
"We evaluated the checkpoint, so prod is the same." — not after quantisation and templates.

ml-dl-q71.testing: inductive bias as a data-budget trade-off.
ml-dl-q71.spoken:
"Convolution hard-codes two assumptions that happen to be true of images. Locality: nearby pixels relate more than distant ones. And translation equivariance through weight sharing: a cat detector works anywhere in the image. Because those are baked in, a CNN doesn't spend data learning them.

A vision transformer has almost no spatial prior: image patches plus positional encodings, and attention between everything. It has to learn locality from data. With enough data that flexibility wins, and it can learn things convolution can't express. With little data, it loses to the CNN's head start.

That's the general law: a stronger inductive bias gives better sample efficiency but a lower ceiling; a weaker bias is data-hungry but has a higher ceiling. Match the prior to your data budget.

In practice, with a small dataset, I'd fine-tune a pretrained model, CNN or ViT, rather than train from scratch, because pretraining supplies the missing data. And hybrid designs like ConvNeXt or convolutional stems for ViTs borrow the CNN's bias where it helps."

stages.name: Convolution's two built-in assumptions
stages.html:
Assumption Mechanism
Locality small kernels see neighbourhoods; receptive field grows with depth
Translation equivariance the same kernel weights slide over every position
(Plus) hierarchy pooling and stacking build parts into objects

stages.name: What a ViT must learn
stages.html:
• Image → 16×16 patches → linear embeddings + positions → transformer.
  • Every patch can attend to every other from layer 1; locality isn't given.
  • With little data it overfits or learns poor spatial structure.

stages.name: The general law
stages.html:
Strong bias (CNN) Weak bias (ViT)
Small data ✅ better ❌ worse
Huge data good ✅ often better, higher ceiling
Long-range relations limited by receptive field native

stages.name: What to do in practice
stages.html:
• Small dataset: fine-tune a pretrained backbone; data augmentation; freeze early layers.
  • ViT from scratch on small data: use strong augmentation/distillation (DeiT) or hybrid stems.
  • Latency-sensitive edge deployment: efficient CNNs often still win.

followUps.question: Is translation equivariance the same as invariance?
followUps.html: No. Equivariance: shift the input, the feature map shifts correspondingly. Invariance: the output doesn't change. Convolutions are equivariant; pooling and global aggregation add approximate invariance for classification.

followUps.question: With a pretrained ViT, does the small-data problem go away?
followUps.html: Largely, for fine-tuning: the pretraining already taught spatial structure. Pretrained ViTs often fine-tune very well on small datasets. The CNN advantage is mostly for training from scratch.

followUps.question: Why not always use the higher-ceiling model?
followUps.html: The ceiling only matters if you have the data and compute to reach it. Below that, the stronger prior gives better results for your actual budget.

followUps.question: Where else does this bias-vs-data law show up?
followUps.html: Everywhere: GBMs vs deep nets on tabular data, graph networks vs generic transformers on graphs, physics-informed models vs pure data-driven ones. Pick the prior that's true of your data when data is scarce.

followUps.question: Name the generative lineage in one breath.
followUps.html: Autoencoder (no sampling) → VAE (blurry samples) → GAN (sharp but unstable, mode collapse) → diffusion (stable, high quality, slower sampling), each fixing the previous one's failure.

dontSay: "CNNs are just better for images." — only with limited data.
"ViTs don't work on small data." — pretrained ones do.
"More flexibility is always better." — only with enough data.

spine: The working picture: MLPs store, attention moves
ml-dl-q72.testing: mechanistic interpretability tools, and judgement about using them in production.
ml-dl-q72.trap: presenting model editing as a routine fix.
ml-dl-q72.spoken:
"I'd localise it in two steps.

First, the logit lens: project the residual stream at each layer onto the vocabulary and watch where in depth the wrong answer starts to dominate. Fact recall tends to emerge in a band of layers, not everywhere.

Second, causal localisation with activation patching, also called causal tracing. Run a clean prompt and a corrupted one, swap activations component by component, and see which swap restores or flips the answer. That tells you which layers, heads and MLPs are causally responsible, not just correlated.

The working picture from this research: mid-layer MLPs behave like key-value memories that store associations, and attention heads move information between token positions. Factual recall lives disproportionately in those MLPs.

Model editing methods like ROME rewrite the located MLP weights directly. They work impressively on the target fact but are brittle: side effects on related facts and paraphrases. So I'd verify with a neighbourhood evaluation, not a single prompt.

Two caveats: attention maps aren't explanations, and superposition, features sharing neurons, is why current work uses sparse autoencoders to find interpretable features.

Would I ship an edit for one fact? No. I'd fix it with data, retrieval or the system prompt first; editing is a research tool until side-effect evaluation matures."

stages.name: Localise in depth: logit lens
stages.html:
• At each layer, apply the final unembedding (after norm) to the residual stream.
  • Track the probability of the false token vs the true one by layer.
  • A sharp rise over a few layers suggests where the association is retrieved.

stages.name: Localise causally: activation patching
stages.html:
1. Clean prompt ("The Eiffel Tower is in") → model's answer.
  2. Corrupted prompt (subject noised) → answer lost.
  3. Restore one component's clean activation at a time (layer × position × MLP/attention).
  4. Components whose restoration recovers the answer are causally involved.

stages.name: The working picture: MLPs store, attention moves
stages.html:
Component Role in factual recall
Early/mid MLPs at the subject token retrieve attributes (key → value)
Attention heads move retrieved attributes to the final position
Late layers shape the output token

stages.name: Editing as surgery
stages.html:
• Treat an MLP layer as a linear associative memory; compute a rank-one update mapping the subject key to a new value.
  • Evaluate: efficacy (target fact), generalisation (paraphrases), specificity (unrelated facts unchanged), fluency.

stages.name: Caveats
stages.html:
• Attention weights ≠ causal importance.
  • Superposition: many features share neurons; sparse autoencoders (SAEs) extract more interpretable features.
  • Localisation can be distributed; one fact may involve several layers.
  • Edits can ripple to related entities or break consistency.

stages.name: What you'd actually ship
stages.html:
• Short term: system prompt correction or retrieval (RAG) with an authoritative source.
  • Medium term: fix training/fine-tuning data; add the fact to evaluation suites.
  • Editing: research and diagnosis tool; if ever used, only with a large neighbourhood and regression eval.

followUps.question: Why not just fine-tune on the correct fact?
followUps.html: You can, but a small fine-tune on one fact can overfit, cause forgetting, or fail to generalise to paraphrases. It needs mixed data and regression evaluation. Retrieval is often simpler and more reliable for factual accuracy.

followUps.question: What's the difference between logit lens and patching?
followUps.html: Logit lens is observational: it shows what the representation encodes at each layer. Patching is interventional: it tests which components cause the output. Use the lens to form hypotheses, patching to confirm them.

followUps.question: Would you ship a ROME edit to fix a customer complaint?
followUps.html: No. The side effects aren't well characterised, it doesn't survive retraining, and a system-prompt or retrieval fix is faster and auditable. Editing is for understanding, and maybe targeted fixes with extensive evaluation.

followUps.question: What are sparse autoencoders for?
followUps.html: They learn an overcomplete, sparse dictionary of features from model activations, so each feature is more interpretable than individual neurons (which mix many concepts due to superposition). They let you find and steer specific features.

followUps.question: How do you know the false fact isn't from training data?
followUps.html: Search the training corpus (or a proxy) for the claim; if it's common, the model learned it faithfully and the fix is data or retrieval. Localisation tells you where it's stored, not why it's there.

dontSay: "Look at the attention maps to see where the fact is." — not causal.
"Just edit the weights with ROME." — side effects.
"Fine-tune on one example." — overfits, may not generalise.
